full_judgment:
Gobinda Chandra Tagore J : On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order dated 21-3-2012 passed by the learned Judge, Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka in Artha Rin Suit No. 115 of 2010, now pending in the Court of Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka, rejecting an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 for rejection of the plaint should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or why such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper, should not be passed.

2. Pending hearing of the Rule, all further proceedings of Artha Rin Suit No. 115 of 2010 was stayed for a period of 6 (six) months. Subsequently, the order of stay was extended from time to time and lastly, by the order dated 7-12-2015 the same was extended for a period of 4 (four) months. Accordingly, the order of stay is still in force.

3. Shortly stated the relevant facts necessary for disposal of the Rule are as follows:

The petitioner is one of the Sponsor Directors of Al-Arafah Islami Bank Ltd. The respondent No. 2. Al-Arafah Islami Bank Ltd. VIP Road Branch, Shantinagar, Dhaka as the plaintiff filed Artha Rin Suit No.115 of 2010 before the Artha Rin Adalat on 25-7-2010 against the petitioner and one Md Abdul Quayum Khandaker stating, inter alia, that the defendant No.1, a Sponsor Director of the bank (now his position of Directorship is under suspension) is also the Managing Director of Kazi Air International (Pvt.) Ltd. and defendant No.2 is the relative of the defendant No.1 and also an ex-officer of the said company and later on worked for some time in the bank. The defendant No.1, while transacting travelling agency business opened 08 Mudaraba Term Deposit Receipt (MTDR) Accounts, in particular, MTDR A/C Nos.004391/1905 for Taka-7,35,000, 007618/2176 for Taka 25,00,000, 007709/309 for Taka 10,00,000, 007710/310 for Taka 10,00,000, 007711/311 for Taka 10,00,000, 007712/312 for Taka 10,00,000, 003377/774 for Taka 10,00,000 and 007783/383 for Taka 25,00,000 amounting in total Taka-1,07,35,000 in his personal name. By exercising his influence as a Director of the bank, he in collusion with the defendant No.2 while, working in the bank used to withdraw profits accrued on those accounts in excess from time to time. The defendant No.1 also used to avail/enjoy Quard facility in his name against the security of the said MTDRs and at times even in excess of the prescribed ratio, within a period from 1998 to 2002. Thus, the defendant No.1 took away fraudulently a total sum of Taka 5,05,702 against his 6 MTDRs, which after deduction of less profit of Taka-71,314 taken against 2 (two) other MTDR accounts in his name, became Taka 4,34,388 as on 22-3-2002. The cause of action for filing the suit arose on 16-4-2002, when taking of excess profit by the defendant No.1-petitioner in collusion with the defendant No.2 and in collaboration of his wife, father and son was detected and 'later on, on 9-2-2002', when the plaintiff wrote letters followed by reminders at different dates. Thereafter, on 25-7-2010, the plaintiff-respondent filed the instant suit in the Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka. The plaint of the suit has been annexed to the Writ Petition as Annexure-A. After receiving the summons, the petitioner appeared in the suit on 11-8-2010. Thereafter, the petitioner, on 31-10-2010, filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, Annexure-C, for rejection of the plaint. After hearing the application, the Artha Rin Adalat by the impugned order dated 21-3-2012 as contained in Annexure-B, rejected the application. There were MTDRs in the personal names of the Managing Director of the petitioner's company, his wife, father and children for an amount of Taka 2,70,35,000 with the Al-Arafah Islami Bank Ltd., VIP Road Branch, Dhaka, respondent No.2. The Managing Director of the petitioner's company has the Current Account (CD), Short Notice Deposit Account (SND) in his name and Mudaraba Saving Deposit Account (MSD) in the personal name of the petitioner. In course of banking transaction, an amount of Taka 1,66,32,548 was misappropriated by the officers of the bank. The petitioner filed Money Suit No.45 of 2006 for recovery of the said misappropriated money in the Court of Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka against the respondent No. 2 and others as defendants and the suit is pending. The petitioner also filed five criminal cases against the officers of the respondent No. 2. The criminal cases are also pending in the Court of learned Sessions Judge and the Court of Divisional Special Judge, Dhaka. The respondent No.2 informed the petitioner by their letters dated 8-10-2006 and 29-1-2007 that the Money Suit would be settled through arbitration as per the decision of the Board of Directors and accordingly, the arbitrators were appointed by both the parties through their respective letters dated 8-6-2007 and 27-8-2007. The respondent No.2 suddenly informed the petitioner by its memo dated 23-10-2007 that it had been decided at the meeting of the Board of Directors of Al-Arafah Islami Bank Ltd. held on 20-10-2007 that the earlier decision to settle the matter involved in Money Suit No.45 of 2006 through arbitration was cancelled and that an excess amount of profit to the tune of Taka 26,32,515 given to the petitioner against the MTDRs would be recovered and by a subsequent letter dated 17-9-2008, the respondent No.2 asked the petitioner to repay the excess profit within 15 days. The petitioner replied to the said letter by his letter dated 29-9-2008 denying the so called excess profit and describing the entire story of misappropriation of money by the officers of the bank, the Money Suit and the Criminal Cases and also requested the respondent No. 2 to refund the money amounting to Taka 1,66,32,548 to the petitioner, which was misappropriated by the officers of the respondent No.2. Earlier, the petitioner also filed Writ Petition Nos.6395 of 2009 and 8470 of 2009 challenging the enlistment of the name of the petitioner in the list of Credit Information Bureau (CIB) of Bangladesh Bank treating the petitioner as defaulter and after hearing the above mentioned Writ Petition, Rules were made absolute by the judgment and order dated 22-8-2010, Annexure-D passed by this Court with an observation that, "since no such judicial pronouncement is there, it is our reckoning that the idea of forced loan, leading to 'Demand Loan' was erroneous". The respondent No.2 has filed the Artha Rin Suit No.115 of 2010 on 25-7-2010 with a mala fide intention against the petitioner and another defendant for realisation of dues with up to date profit, which was detected on 9-2-2002 and, as such, the order of rejection of the application filed under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. Having no other equally efficacious remedy, the petitioner has filed the instant Writ Petition and obtained the Rule and the order of stay.

4. The respondent No.2 contested the Rule by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition thereto contending, inter alia, that the petitioner has not come with clean hands and he is not entitled to any relief and the Writ Petition involves disputed question of facts, which are required to be proved by adducing oral and documentary evidence and accordingly, the same cannot be adjudicated upon summarily under the writ jurisdiction. None has misappropriated any money from the petitioner; rather, the petitioner in connivance with others received the money of the bank illegally; instead of paying back the money, he filed various criminal cases against the employees of the bank with a mala fide intention to evade the payment. Due to non-co-operation of the petitioner in resolving the matter out of Court, the Board of Directors of the bank was forced to abandon the idea of amicable settlement and demanded the money. Although at the Board meeting the petitioner agreed to pay the entire money he received from the bank illegally, subsequently, he refused to settle the same; rather, he made frivolous claims against the bank. Whether the money received by the petitioner can be converted to forced loan or demand loan can be addressed to in a judicial pronouncement in accordance with the provision of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and the BRPD Circulars issued from time to time by Bangladesh Bank as decided by a Division Bench of this Court in Writ Petition No.6395 of 2009. The petitioner did not violate any the provision of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Moreover, the delay is not a bar in filing any suit under the special law, such as, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and, as such, the question of filing an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground of delay is misconceived. However, the defect in filing the suit under section 18(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain may be cured by way of amendment of the plaint at any stage of the trail. Similarly, misjoinder of a party can never be a ground for rejecting a suit under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

5. During the hearing, the petitioner filed a Supplementary Affidavit annexing thereto the judgment and order passed by a Division Bench in Writ Petition No.4243 of 2004 and the judgment and order passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1835 of 2008 by the Appellate Division. The Leave Petition arose out of the said Writ Petition No.4243 of 2004. Upon filing those judgments, it was stated that the principle laid down therein is fully applicable and relevant to the facts and circumstances of the instant Writ Petition.

6. Having placed the Writ Petition, Mr AKM Bodruddoza along with Mr Md Zakir Hossain, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that it ex facie appears from the plaint that the cause of action of the suit arose on 16-4-2002, but the suit was filed on 25-7-2010 i.e. after more than 8 years from the date on which the cause of action of the suit arose and, as such, the suit is barred by section 46(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and accordingly, the Artha Rin Adalat ought to have rejected the plaint under section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 read with Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but the Artha Rin Adalat rejected the application by the impugned order and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

7. The learned Advocate further submits that as per the statements made in the plaint, the petitioner did not receive any loan from the bank which is regulated in accordance with the Islamic Shariah inasmuch as the bank did not invest nor did grant any financial favour or facilities to the petitioner and, as such, the alleged demand made by the bank in the plaint does not come within the ambit of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 as well as under the jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat and, as such, the suit being barred under section 5 and section 46 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, the Artha Rin Adalat ought to have allowed the application for rejection of the plaint and therefore, the impugned order is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

8. Having referred to an unreported judgment passed in Writ Petition No.4243 of 2004 which gave rise to the judgment passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1835 of 2008 by the Appellate Division submits that any Artha Rin Suit in its given facts and circumstances may be barred by limitation and the present suit being filed after more than 8 years from the date on which, as per the plaintiff's claim, the cause of action arose, the present suit is also barred by limitation, specially under section 46 of the Ain, but the Artha Rin Adalat having passed the impugned order rejecting the application for rejection of the plaint on the ground of limitation acted contrary to the expressed provision of law and hence, the impugned order is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

9. On the contrary, Mr M Moksadul Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No.2 submits that the question of limitation is a mixed question of law and facts and the same cannot be decided without taking evidence both oral and documentary at the time of trial and, as such, the learned Artha Rin Adalat rightly rejected the application for rejection of the plaint on the ground of limitation and therefore, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

10. The learned Advocate having referred to the decision passed in the case of Shahabuddin Khan (Md) vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, reported in 14 BLC 111 and the case of Shitalakhaya Ice and Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. vs Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka, reported in 64 DLR 487 submits that the provisions under section 46 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 are directory and thus, delay is not a bar to filing any suit under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, which is a special law and, as such, the Artha Rin Adalat rightly and justly rejected the application for rejection of the plaint and therefore, there being no legal infirmity in the impugned order, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

11. The learned Advocate further submits that the cause of action for filing the suit arose on 16-4-2002, when taking of the excess profit by the petitioner was detected and 'later on, on 9-2-2002' when the plaintiff wrote letters followed by reminders on different dates and on several dates, when the excess profit was taken and lastly on 7-6-2010, when the plaintiff issued a legal notice demanding the payment of the outstanding dues and thus, the cause of action is still continuing and, as such, the suit being filed within time, the Artha Rin Adalat justly rejected the application for rejection of the plaint on the ground of limitation and hence, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

12. The learned Advocate lastly submits that on making the demand by issuing the legal notice for the payment of the money illegally taken away by the petitioner the money became converted to a forced loan and the same is payable on demand and since, the bank made the demand by the legal notice dated 7-6-2010 and filed the suit on 25-7-2010, the suit was filed very much within the time and accordingly, the Artha Rin Adalat having passed the impugned order did not commit even any error of law and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

13. We have perused the Writ Petition and the Affidavit-in-Opposition thereto along with the documents annexed thereto, and heard the learned Advocates from both the sides.

14. The petitioner is a sponsor Director of Al-Arafah Islami Bank Ltd. Now his Directorship is under suspension. He is also the Managing Director of Kazi Air International (Pvt.) Ltd. While, the petitioner, as per the plaintiff's case, was doing his travel agency business opened 08 MTDR accounts, in particular, MTDR account Nos.004391/1905 for Taka 7,35,000, 007618/ 2176 for Taka 25,00,000, 007709/309 for Taka 10,00,000, 007710/310 for Taka 10,00,000, 007711/311 for Taka 10,00,000, 007712/312 for Taka 10,00,000, 003377/774 for Taka 10,00,000 and 007783/383 for Taka 25,00,000 amounting in total Taka 1,07,35,000 in his personal name. By exercising influence as a Director of the bank, he in collusion with defendant No.2, who was a junior officer of the bank received excess profit against the said 8 MTDRs. The bank instituted Artha Rin Suit No.115 of 2010 for realisation of the said excess profits, which stood at Taka 60,88,120 including the interest thereon as on 30-4-2010. As per the plaintiff's case, the petitioner took away the excess amount in collusion with the defendant No.2 during the period from 1998 to 2002. The cause of action of the suit first arose on 16-4-2002, when taking of the excess profit by the petitioner in collusion with defendant No.2 was detected and 'later on, on 9-2-2002', when the plaintiff wrote letters followed by reminders on different dates and on several dates, when excess profits were taken and lastly on 7-6-2010, when the plaintiff served a legal notice on the petitioner demanding repayment of the outstanding dues and then the plaintiff instituted the suit on 25-7-2010. The defendant No.1-petitioner on 31-10-2010, filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 for rejection of the plaint. The Artha Rin Adalat No.4, Dhaka by the impugned order dated 21-3-2012 rejected the application on the findings that the defendant did not file the written statement in the suit, but the claim made in the application cannot be proved without evidence and the same is not consistent with the provision of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure nor were there any ingredients of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code in the application and the question of limitation cannot be decided at this stage.

15. The petitioner's case centred round the point as to whether the Artha Rin Suit was filed within time as stipulated in section 46 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and whether the suit is barred by limitation.

16. With regard to the arising out of the cause of action of the suit, the plaintiff made a specific statement in paragraph No.12 of the plaint. For the convenience of discussion paragraph No.12 of the plaint is quoted below:

"12. That the cause of action for suit first arose on 16-4-2002 when taking of excess profit by defendant No.1 in collusion with defendant No. 2 and in collaboration of the wife, father and the son of the defendant No.1 was detected and later on, on 9-2-2002 when plaintiff wrote letters followed by reminders at different dates and on several dates when excess profit was taken and lastly on 7-6-2010 when plaintiff issued legal notice demanding payment of the outstanding dues of the Bank and the same is continuing till full adjustment of the dues of the Bank, within jurisdiction of this court."

17. Therefore, it appears from the plaint that the facts about allegedly taking away the excess profit was detected on 16-4-2002 and before that on 9-2-2002 the plaintiff wrote letters followed by reminders on different dates and on several dates when the excess profit was allegedly taken. Be that as it may, the plaintiff on 7-6-2010 issued a legal notice demanding payment of the outstanding dues. Therefore, the legal notice was issued after about long 8 years and 2 months from the date of detection of the allegedly taken away of excess profit, i.e. 16-4-2002 and the suit was filed on 25-7-2010 i.e. after 8 years 3 months and 9 days. It does not appear from the plaint that the petitioner upon receiving the legal notice in writing or otherwise conceded or admitted or denied the demand made in the legal notice and, as such, by issuing the legal notice on 7-6-2010 the plaintiff cannot legally fill up the long gap of 8 years and 2 months. Thus, it is apparent on the face of the plaint that the suit has been filed after 8 years, 3 months and 9 days from the date of detection of the allegedly taking away of the excess profit. Accordingly, it is not required to decide by taking evidence that the suit was filed after more than 8 years and 3 months.

18. In this regard the bank in its Affidavit-in-Opposition asserted that, "delay is not a bar in filing any suit under the special law such as Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003". In support of this assertion the learned Advocate for respondent No.2-bank also relied upon two decisions of this Court made in the cases of (1) Md Shahabuddin Khan vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, reported in 28 BLD 294 = 14 BLC 111 and (2) Shitalakhaya Ice & Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. vs. Artha Rin Adala No.1, Dhaka, reported in 64 DLR 487. In the case of Shahabuddin Khan vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, reported in 28 BLD 294 = 14 BLC 111, the facts that the outstanding amount had been overdue was detected on 17-9-2003 and the Artha Rin Suit was filed on 9-6-2005, but the Court found that the provision of section 46 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 being directory in nature, the suit was not barred by limitation. Accordingly, in that case the order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, rejecting an application for rejection of the plaint on the ground of limitation was upheld. Similarly, in the case of Shitalakhaya Ice & Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. vs Artha Rin Adala No.1, Dhaka, reported in 64 DLR 487, the cause of action of the suit arose on 30-8-2001 and respondent No.1 therein filed the Artha Rin Suit on 1-12-2008 i.e. after about 7 years. But, another Division Bench of this Court found therein that the provision of section 46 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 being directory, the suit was not barred by limitation.

19. From the above decisions made by two different Benches of this Court, it appears that the provisions of section 46 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 are directory and for that matter any Artha Rin Suit may be filed after 7 years or at any time whenever the concerned bank or financial institution feels the necessity for filing of such a suit.

20. On the contrary, in this regard the petitioner annexed the judgment passed in Writ Petition No.4243 of 2004 by a Division Bench of this Court wherein, it was found that the suit was barred by limitation as the cause of action therein arose on 28-4-1991 and the suit was filed on 29-2-2004. The petitioner also annexed the judgment passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1835 of 2008, which arose out of the judgment passed in Writ Petition No.4243 of 2004. By the judgment, the Appellate Division affirmed the judgment of the High Court Division and rejected the Leave Petition on the following observation:

"The High Court Division observed that in this case it is rather admitted fact that the Artha Rin Suit in question was filed beyond the statutory period of limitation. So, the learned Judge of the Artha Rin Adalat evidently, has committed error and illegality in rejecting the petitioner's application under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint on the ground of limitation.

In view of the above, we find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed."

21. Therefore, from the above decision of both the Divisions of this Court, it appears that a Artha Rin Suit may be barred by limitation in the given facts and circumstances of the suit. The judgment passed on this point by the Appellate Division is binding upon this Court.

22. Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, except sections 46 and 47 thereof, came into force with effect from 1-5-2003, while, sub-section (6) of section 46 declares that the provision of section 46 will be applicable after one year from the date of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain came into force, but any financial institution could give effect to this section before the provision of section 46 came into force. Section 46 provides for special provisions and limitations of time for filing any suit under the Ain, which is apparent on its heading. Section 46 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 runs as follows:

“৪৬। মামলা দায়ের সম্পর্কিত বিশেষ বিধান ও সময়মীমা।–(১) The Limitation Act, 1908 (Act No. IX of 1908) এ ভিন্নতর বিধান যাহাই থাকুক না কেন, আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান সম্পাদিত চুক্তি বা চুক্তির শর্ত অনুযায়ী ঋণ গ্রহীতার নিকট হইতে ঋণ পরিশোধ সূচি (Repayment schedule) অনুাযায়ী ঋণ পরিশোধ শুরু হইবার পরবর্তী-

(ক) প্রথম এক বৎসরে প্রাপ্য অর্থের অন্যূন ১০%, অথবা

(খ) প্রথম দুই বৎসরে প্রাপ্য অর্থের অন্যূন ১৫%, অথবা

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, এই ধারার বিধান কার্যকর হইবার পূর্বেও কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান এই ধারার বিধানকে কার্যকর করিতে পারিবে ।”

23. Section 46(1)(Ka) contemplates that notwithstanding anything contained in the Limitation Act, 1908, subject to the provision of section 46(2), if at least 10% of the outstanding loan is not realised within the 1st one year from the commencement of the repayment schedule, a financial institution shall have to file a suit within the next one year; similarly, section 46(1)(Kha) mandates that if during the first 2 years at least 15% of the outstanding loan is not realised, the financial institution shall file the suit within the next one year; and section 46(1)(Ga) also mandates that if during the first 3 years at least 25% of the outstanding loan is not realised, the financial institution shall file the suit within the next one year.

24. Section 46(2) stipulates that if the loan is rescheduled within the period of limitation prescribed in section 46(1) the provisions of section 46(1) shall, subject to necessary changes accordingly, be applicable mutatis mutandis.

25. Section 46(3) ordains that if as per the repayment schedule mentioned in section 46(1) the accumulated period for repayment of the loan is less than 3 years and the loan amount realised during that accumulated period is less than 20%, the financial institution, subject to the provisions of section 46(4), shall file the suit within the next one year.

26. Section 46(4) stipulates that if the loan is rescheduled within the period of limitation prescribed in section 46(3), the provisions of section 46(3) shall, subject to necessary changes accordingly, be applicable mutatis mutandis.

27. Section 46(5) provides that if any suit is filed after the prescribed period of limitation precribed in sections 46(1), 46(2), 46(3) or section 46(4) as the case may be, the Court shall immediately inform the matter in writing to the Chief Executive Officer of the concerned financial institution; and if the suit was not filed within the period of limitation due to the negligence of any officer, the competent authority having taken disciplinary action against the concerned officer shall inform the Government and the Court about the same within 90 days from the date of being informed under this sub-section.

28. In the present case, no repayment schedule was fixed either mutually or by unilaterally. From the plaint it appears that the bank did not sanction any loan in favour of the petitioner, rather it has been stated therein that the petitioner took away the excess profits against his 8 MTDRs accounts by using his influence in collusion with the defendant No.2, who was a junior officer of the bank. Therefore, at best, as per the claim of the bank, the money allegedly taken away by the petitioner in excess of his profits was repayable on demand and, as such, the amount was repayable from 16-4-2002, the date of detection of the allegedly taking away of the money by the petitioner. It appears from the plaint that the petitioner did not pay any single farthing before or after 16-4- 2002. Therefore, the bank ought to have filed the suit within 15-4-2004 as per the provision of section 46(1)(Ka). But the provisions of section 46 came into effect on 1-5-2004 and, as such, the suit was to be filed within the next one year from 1-5-2004 i.e. within 30-4-2005. Since the petitioner did not repay any amount after 16-4-2002, the clauses (Kha) and (Ga) of sections 46(1) or 46(2), 46(3) or section 46(4) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 are not applicable to the case in hand.

29. From the plain reading of the provision of section 46(1)(Ka), it appears that as no money was realised within the first one year from 16-4- 2002, the plaintiff ought to have filed its suit within the next one year from 1-5-2004 on which the provisions of section 46 came into effect. But it is the submission of respondent No.1 that the provision of section 46(1)(Ka) is directory and not mandatory. Accordingly, whenever the suit was filed after the cause of action had arisen the same was not barred by limitation.

30. It has already been found that the present suit has been instituted after more than 8 years and 3 months from the date of arising out of the cause of action. As per the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondent No.2, even the bank could have filed the suit later on. But the Latin maxims goes as to read, "Currit tempus contra desides et sui juris contemplores"-Time runs against the slothful and those who slight their own rights. This is in keeping with the other Latin maxims read 'Vigilantibus, non dormientibus jura subvenient'-Laws come to the assistance of the vigilant, not of the sleepy and "Vigilantibus, non dormientibus, aquitas subvenit"- Equity assists those who are vigilant and not those who are sleeping. Accordingly, a statute has to be interpreted in accordance with the maxim that the laws serve the persons, who are vigilant and not those who sleep upon their rights. In this regard the case of Grice vs Dudley Corporation, (1957) 2 All ER 673 may be relied on.

31. TM Cooley in his book 'A TREATISE ON THE CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITATIONS', first Indian reprints of the first edition, at page-365 observed on the limitation of time in filing any suit or litigation as follows:

"A limitation law fixes upon a reasonable time within which a party is allowed to bring suit to recover his rights, and, if he fails to do so, establishes a legal presumption against him that he has no rights in the premises. It is a statute of repose. Every government is bound in good faith to furnish its citizens all needful legal remedies; but it is not bound to keep its courts open indefinitely for one who neglects or refuses to apply for redress until it may fairly be presumed that the means by which the other party might disprove the claim are lost in the lapse of time."

32. It is a settled principle of law that no limitation in filing any suit or litigation should be imposed suddenly. The concerned party should be given ample opportunity to take recourse to the law of limitation and therefore, the law of limitation should come into force after a good while the substantive law came into force. In this regard, TM Cooley again observed in his book at page- 366 as under:

"All statutes of limitation, also, must proceed on the idea that the party has had opportunity to try his right in the courts. A statute which should bar the existing right of claimants without affording this opportunity, after the time when the statute should take effect, would not be a statute of limitations, but an unlawful attempt to extinguish rights, whatever it might purport to be by its terms. It is essential that they allow a reasonable time after they are passed for the commencement of suits upon existing causes of action; though what shall be considered a reasonable time must be determined by the legislature, into the wisdom of whose decision in establishing a legal bar it does not pertain to the jurisdiction of the courts to inquire."

33. It has already been found that the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, except its section 46 and 47, came into effect with effect from 1-5-2003 and section 46 came into effect after one year from the other provision of the Ain had come into force i.e. the provision of section 46 came into effect on and from 1-5-2004. Therefore, the observation made by TM Cooley has been reflected in enacting the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. The time schedule for filing any suit as has been set out in section 46 of the Ain is a provision of limitation.

34. Chief Justice Murshed in his judgment passed in the case of Debendra Chandra Dev Nath vs Bharat Chandra Singha, reported in 19 DLR 514 set out the policy of limitation in respect of any stature of law wherein it was observed:

"I think this would be asking for too much by way of concession and I am saying so because of a consciousness and awareness of the very nature and purpose of the law of limitation which is undoubtedly designed to set litigations and disputes at rest. The law of limitations, as I read it, and, as it has been held by consistent legal decisions, is a law which is designed to impose a quietus on legal dissensions and conflicts. It requires that persons must come to Court and take recourse to legal remedies with due diligence. Legal yardsticks have, therefore, been formulated, specifying the time, which is allowable for taking recourse to legal reliefs. Therefore, the main purpose of the Limitation Act is to guillotine cases which seek reliefs at a point of time which is beyond the period specified thereunder. The same principle is applied to all other kinds of provisions with regard to limitation in various different statutes."

35. It has already been found that as per the submission made on behalf of respondent No.1 that any suit under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain may be filed at any time from the date of arising out of the cause of action and that there is no limitation for filing the suit under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. It is a universal truth that a man is mortal, but disputes or controversies between or among men cannot be immortal. In this regard John Voet, a Dutch jurist said, "Controversies are restricted to a fixed period of time, lest they should become immortal while men are mortal". As such any dispute or controversy should be ended within a reasonable time for the sake of establishing and living in a peaceful society; that is why it is a settled principle of law that the law of limitation is a law of repose, peace and harmonies. Therefore, there should be an ending time of litigation. On the principle as has been discussed above, no law, specially dealing with civil rights can be presumed without the thought of limitation for seeking relief thereunder. Even though there is no limitation under the writ jurisdiction, the petitioner must have to come before the Court with his application within a reasonable time and without any laches and thus, even under the writ jurisdiction the law of limitation is impliedly applicable. There is no limitation in filing any criminal cases as because, offence never abates. Even, then the inordinate delay in filing any First Information Report or any Petition of Complaint creates reasonable doubt over the case of the prosecution or the complainant. Thus, the concept of limitation is based on consideration of public policy and expediency. The Latin maxim 'Interest republicae ut sit finis litium' postulates that the interests of the State require that a ceiling period should be put to terminate all litigations. Therefore, it is not conceivable that there can be any law, specially dealing with the civil lights, without any provision of limitation of time.

36. Now, it has been argued on behalf of the respondent bank that the provisions of section 46 of the Ain are directory and not mandatory. Such interpretation is contrary to the observations made above. Moreover, from the language of the contingency conditions attached to all three circumstances under section 46(1), which has been used in the same term, " ....পরিমাণ অর্থ আদায় না হইলে, উপ-ধারা(২) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, উহার পরবর্তী এক বৎসরের মধ্যে মামলা দায়ের করিবে।" it appears that the institution of a suit under the Artha Rin Ain is subject to the condition of non-payment or non-realisation of the stipulated amount of loan within the time prescribed under section 46(1). Section 46(3) also contemplates similar condition if the accumulated period under section 46(1) for the realisation of loan is less than 3 years. Therefore, the provisions of section 46(1) or those of section 46(3) with regard to the filing of a suit are clothed in a positive command following a negative condition. If the negative condition exists, the positive command is to be obeyed. Thus, the negative condition and the positive command are strong indication of the intent of the Legislature to make the provision mandatory.

37. With regard to the effect of employment or failure to employ negative words, which have imported that the act should be done in a particular manner or time, and not otherwise, TM Cooley said in his book at page-74 as under:

"There are cases where, whether a statute was to be regarded as merely directory or not, was made to depend upon the employment or failure to employ negative words which imported that the act should be done in a particular manner or time, and not otherwise. The use of such words is often very conclusive on an intent to impose a limitation; but their absence is by no means equally conclusive that the statute was not destined to be mandatory."

38. The Supreme Court in the judgment and order passed on 28-10-1970 in the case of Atta Muhammad Qureshi vs The Settlement Commissioner, Lahore Division, Lahore and 2 others, reported in 1971 PLD (SC) 61 decided the question as to when an enactment is to be considered as absolute and when as merely directory as follows:

"It is not possible to lay down a general rule of universal application in this behalf, but the one which is suggested by the reported authorities in this connection is the affirmative or negative character of the language in which the provision is couched. If it is negative, that is to say, if the statute enacts that certain action shall be taken in a certain manner and in no other manner, it has been held that the requirements are absolute and that neglet to attend them will invalidate the whole procedure. If, on the other hand, the language is affirmative, it may be considered as a directory provision."

39. In the said case reported in 1971 PLD (SC) 61 the Supreme Court further held—

"One other principle which has been enunciated in this behalf is that as a general rule, statutes, which enable persons to take legal proceedings under certain specified circumstances, demand that those circumstances must be accurately obeyed, notwithstanding the fact that the provisions thereof are expressed in merely affirmative language."

40. It is another settled principle of law that where the expression 'shall' or 'must' is used, it prima facie indicates the mandatory nature of the provision. In this regard, the case of Mozibur Rahman Moznu vs Abdul Halim, 53 DLR (AD) 93 may be relied on. Their Lordships held therein as follows:

"The word 'shall' in the sub-rule, as it appears to me, has made obligatory counting of votes by the Presiding Officer after the scrutiny of the ballot papers in the ballot box or boxes."

41. Therefore, apart from the principle that if the failure to comply with a legal provision is visited with any consequence, the provision is generally treated as mandatory, there are other principles under which a provision of any statute may be considered as mandatory or absolute.

42. In fact, in order to determine whether a provision is mandatory or directory it is required to look into the real intention of the Legislature upon considering the whole scope of the statute. In this regard, in the case of Liverpool Borrough Bank vs Turner, (1848) 13 QB 30 Lord Campbell observed as follows:

"No universal rule can be laid down as to whether a mandatory enactment shall be construed directory only or obligatory with implied nullification for disobedience. Is the duty of the Courts of justice to try to get at the real intention of the Legislature by carefully attending to the whole scope of the statute to be construed."

43. Having cited the above decision in the case of Howard vs Bollingdon, (1877) 2 PD 203, Lord Penzance held as follows:

"I believe as far as any rule is concerned, you cannot safely go further than that. In each case you must look to the subject-matter, consider the importance of the provision and the relation of that provision to the general object to be secured by the Act and upon review of the case in that aspect, decide whether an enactment is, what is called, imperative or only obligatory."

44. It appears from the preamble of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 that the intention of the Legislator in enacting the law is to further amend and consolidate the existing law in order to realise the loan disbursed by the financial institutions. The preamble of the Ain reads as follows:

“আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক ঋণ আদায়ের জন্য প্রচলিত আইনের অধিকতর সংশোধন ও সংহতকরণকল্পে প্রণীত আইন।

যেহেতু আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত ঋণ আদায়ের জন্য প্রচলিত আইনের অধিকতর সংশোধন ও সংহতকরণ প্রয়োজনীয়;

সেহেতু এতদদ্বারা নিম্নরুপ আইন করা হইলঃ-

45. It appears from the text of the Ain that under the Ain the loan may be realised in two ways firstly by selling the properties placed as the securities against the loan under section 12 and or then by filing a suit in the Artha Rin Adalat established under section 4 if the sale proceeds of the securities does not entirely satisfy the loan amount or there is no security at all. However, a suit may be disposed of amicably by way of mediation. Therefore, if the loan is not realised otherwise there cannot be legally any other option but to file a suit within the prescribed time; otherwise, the entire purpose and intention of the law shall be frustrated.

46. The Legislature has made the provisions of section 46(1) applicable subject to the provisions of section 46(2). From a joint reading of sections 46(1) and 46(2) it appears that the filing of a suit under section 46(1) is subject to the rescheduling of the loan under section 46(2) within the prescribed period of limitation i.e. if the loan is rescheduled, no suit can be filed within the prescribed period. In the other words, if the loan is not rescheduled, the suit must have to be filed within the period prescribed in section 46(1) and not after that period. Similarly, the provisions of section 46(3) being subject to the provisions of section 46(4), if the loan is not rescheduled, the suit must be filed within the period prescribed in section 46(3).

47. Since the filing of any suit under the Ain depends on the circumstances as to non-realisation of the stipulated amount of loan and non-rescheduling of the loan within the prescribed period, if the circumstances exist the concerned financial institution is legally bound to file the suit within the prescribed period in accurately obeying the circumstances, which contemplates implied nullification for disobedience thereto.

48. It has also been argued on behalf of the respondent bank that the consequence of the failure to file a suit within the prescribed period has been provided by section 46(5) such as to taking disciplinary action against the concerned officer of the financial institution and not that the plaint is to be rejected. But if the filing of the suit within the prescribed period is not mandatory and for that matter the suit being filed out of time is not affected at all, it will be practically unnecessary, futile and unreasonable to take any disciplinary action against the concerned officer of the financial institution. In that case, virtually there will be no limitation of time in filing any suit under the Ain. Consequently, the other provisions of section 46 will be of no use and shall be rendered unnecessary and redundant. It has already been observed that no law, particularly dealing with the civil rights can be conceived without the provisions of limitation. But the reasonable Legislature cannot enact such an unreasonable legislation having no rational nexus between its provisions and the objective intended to be achieved, while, like other legislations, the Ain also enjoys the presumption of constitutional validity. Therefore, the provision of section 46 (5) does not diminish the force of the other provisions of section 46 of the Ain. Accordingly, the filing of the suit within the period of limitation prescribed under sections 46(1) or section 46(3), as the case may be, is mandatory, which also contemplates implied nullification for disobeying the same provisions.

49. Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1908 provides that if any special law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule to the Act, the provision of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule. The said section 29(2) reads as follows:

"29. Savings—(1)...................

(2) Where any special law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule, the provision of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special law—

(a) the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special law; and

(b) the remaining provisions of this Act shall not apply."

50. Section 3 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 declares that the provisions of this Ain shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force (আপাততঃ বলবৎ অন্য কোন আইনে ভিন্নতর যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, এই আইনের বিধানাবলীই কার্যকর হইবে।) Section 46(1) and section 46(3) of the Ain also prescribe for any suit periods of limitation different from the periods prescribed therefor by the first schedule to the Limitation Act. Section 46(1) by its non-obstante clause 'The Limitation Act, 1908 (Act No. IX of 1908) এ ভিন্নতর বিধান যাহাই থাকুক না কেন has made applicable the periods of limitation prescribed therein and non-applicable the periods prescribed in the Limitation Act. Therefore, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is a special law as contemplated under section 29(2) of the Limitation Act. Now the question arises whether section 29(2) of the Limitation Act is applicable to any suit under the Ain and because of that section 3 of the same Act is also applicable to such suit.

51. The Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. XVIII of 1985) is a special law. Section 3 of the Ordinance also provides exactly a similar overriding clause like section 3 of the Ain (The provisions of this Ordinance shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force). The Ordinance also prescribes different periods of limitation for different purposes, which are different from the periods prescribed in the Limitation Act. In the case of Jamila Khatun vs Rustom Ali, 48 DLR (AD) 110 filed under the Ordinance the Appellate Division held in this regard as follows:

"But in respect of "suits" section 3 of the Limitation Act will apply or section 29(2) of the said Act will apply, if the suit is filed under a special or local law, unless the Limitation Act has been expressly excluded from the purview of such suits. Section 3 of the Ordinance of 1985 only means that if there are provisions in the Ordinance which are different from or are in conflict with the provisions of any other law, then the provisions of the said Ordinance will prevail over the provisions of other laws. If, for example, any special period of limitation is prescribed in the Ordinance of 1985 then that will govern the field, and not the Limitation Act, 1908. Section 3 does not debar the application of Limitation Act to suits filed under the Ordinance of 1985, as contended by Mrs. Bhuiyan."

52. Then, the Appellate Division also held therein—

"Under sub-section (6) of section 9 a defendant may apply to the Court for setting aside a decree passed ex-parte against him within 30 days of the passing of the decree and sub-section (7) of section 9 provides that the provisions of section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 shall apply to an application under sub-section (6). These provisions clearly indicate that the Ordinance of 1985 is a special law. Under section 29(2) of the Limitation Act section 3 thereof shall apply and sections 4, 9 to 18 and 22 are applicable unless excluded and other sections are not applicable unless included."

53. Thus, as per the law enunciated by the Appellate Division, despite the overriding clause of Section 3 of the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 the provisions of section 29(2) or those of section 3 of the Limitation Act are applicable to the suits filed under the said Ordinance.

54. Like the overriding clause of section 3 of the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 the overriding clause of section 3 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 also means that if there are provisions in the Ain which are different from or are in conflict with the provisions of any other law, then the provisions of the said Ain will prevail over the provisions of other laws. By virtue of the non-obstante clause of section 46(1) of the Ain 'The Limitation Act, 1908 (Act No. IX of 1908) এ ভিন্নতর বিধান যাহাই থাকুক না কেন only the periods of limitation prescribed therein shall prevail over the periods of limitation prescribed in the Limitation Act and thereby the application of section 29(2) or section 3 of the Limitation Act to the suits under the Ain has not been debarred.

55. Therefore, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 being a special law the provisions of section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1908 and by virtue thereof, the provisions of section 3 of the same Act are applicable to the suits under the said Ain of 2003.

56. Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908 provides that subject to the provisions contained in sections 4 to 25 (inclusive), every suit instituted, appeal preferred, and application made, after the period of limitation prescribed therefor by the first schedule shall be dismissed, although limitation has not been set up as a defence. Accordingly, by virtue of section 29(2) section 3 of the Limitation Act being applicable to the suits under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, there is a rigorous consequence of the failure to institute a suit after the period of limitation prescribed therefor by the said Ain i.e. the suit shall be dismissed.

57. Therefore, the provisions of section 46(1) and those of section 46(3) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 read with the provisions of sections 29(2) and 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908 are mandatory.

58. We have also found in the unreported decision of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1835 of 2008 that there is limitation in filing an Artha Rin Suit.

59. We have meticulously gone through the judgments passed in the cases of (1) Md Shahabuddin Khan vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, reported in 28 BLD 294 = 14 BLC 111 and (2) Shitalakhaya Ice & Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. vs Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka, reported in 64 DLR 48. It appears that while their Lordships came to the respective decision, their attention was not drawn to the following statutory provisions and precedents—

(1) The precedents on the legal and social significance and importance of the law of limitation referred to above, particularly the case of Debendra Chandra Dev Nath vs Bharat Chandra Singha, 19 DLR 514;

(2) The precedents on the point whether any provision is mandatory, particularly, the case of Atta Muhammad Qureshi vs The Settlement Commissioner, Lahore Division, Lahore and 2 others, reported in 1971 PLD (SC) 61 (the judgment was passed on 28-10-1970); and case of Mozibur Rahman Moznu vs Abdul Halim, 53 DLR (AD) 93.

(3) The statutory contingency provisions of the clause of section 46(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 “....পরিমাণ অর্থ আদায় না হইলে, উপ-ধারা (২) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, উহার পরবর্তী এক বৎসরের মধ্যে মামলা দায়ের করিবে।”, which contemplates a positive command following a negative condition;

(4) The statutory contingency provisions of the clause of section 46(3) of the Ain “.....উক্ত নির্ধারিত সাকুল্য মেয়াদের মধ্যে আদায়ের পরিমাণ ২০% অপেক্ষা কম হেইলে, আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান উপ-ধারা (৪) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, উহার পরবর্তী ১ (এক) বৎসরের মধ্যে মামলা দায়ের করিবে।” which also contemplates a positive command following a negative condition;

(5) The statutory provisions of section 46(1) read with the provisions of section 46(2) and the provisions of  section 46(3) read with the provisions of section 46(4) of the Ain;

(6) The statutory provisions of sections 46(1) and 46(3) of the Ain read with the provisions of sections 29 (2) and 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908;

(7) The precedent on the application of section 3 read section 29(2) of the Limitation Act to any suit under a special law Jamila Khatun vs Rustom Ali, 48 DLR (AD) 110; and

(8) The decision of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1835 of 2008 on the question of limitation of time in filing suits under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain.

<u>60. But each of the decisions of the Court is not binding precedent if it is given per incuriam, i.e. without the Court's attention having been drawn to the relevant statutes or some authority, which is binding upon the Court concerned. The literal meaning of 'per incuriarn' is through inadvertence or through want of care. As per the Black's Law Dictionary 'per incuriam' means a judicial decision wrongly decided, usually, because the judge or judges were ill-informed about the applicable law. In the case of Most. Sufia Khatoon vs Mrs. Mahabuba Rahman, 30 BLD (AD) 41 = 62 DLR (AD) 266 it has been observed that it is a settled principle that a judgment 'per incuriam' or a judgment sub silentio does not constitute a precedent. As per the principle laid down by the Appellate Division in the case of the Public Service Commission vs Mohammad Sohel Rana, 8 ADC 332 = 17 BLC (AFD) 187, one Bench of the High Court Division need not follow the judgment passed per incuriam by another Bench. Their Lordships held therein as follows:</u>

<u>"In the High Court Division Rules as quoted above, we find that a Division Bench should ordinarily respect the opinion of another Division Bench; one Bench of the High Court Division has no jurisdiction to sit over the judgment or the decision of another Division Bench. If it differs, it should refer the question to another larger Bench or a Full Bench. However, if a decision is given per incuriam, it need not be followed."</u>

61. The said two judgments reported in 28 BLD 294 and 64 DLR 48 being passed without the Court's attention having been drawn to the relevant statutory provisions and the precedents as stated above, are the judgments per incuriam. Accordingly, we need not follow the same.

<u>62. In such view of the matter, since not even a single farthing of the alleged loan money was ever realised nor was it rescheduled, the respondent bank was to file its suit within one year from the date of coming into force of the provision of section 46 of the Ain i.e. within 30-4-2005. But the suit was filed on 25-7-2010 and, as such, the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation and as per the provisions of section 46(1)(Ka) of the Ain read with the provisions of sections 29(2) and 3 of the Limitation Act is also liable to be dismissed.</u>

63. Another question has been raised in the Writ Petition as to whether the excess of profit allegedly withdrawn fraudulently against MTDR accounts by the petitioner in collusion with the defendant No.2, a junior officer of the Bank can be treated as loan and realised through the Court under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

64. The suit has been filed for realisation of the excess profit fraudulently withdrawn by the petitioner in collusion with the defendant No. 2, a junior officer of the bank against his MTDR accounts along with profit/compensation thereon. Therefore, admittedly, the petitioner did not receive any loan from the bank, which is regulated in accordance with the Islamic Shariah inasmuch as the bank did not invest nor did grant any financial favour or facilities to the petitioner; rather the petitioner invested certain amounts of money through the said Mudaraba Term Deposit Receipt (MTDR) accounts maintained with the bank for profit. "Loan"(Ee) has been defined in section 2(Ga) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 as follows:

“২। (গ) ঋণ অর্থ_

(১) অগ্রিম ধার, নগদ ঋণ, ওবার ভ্রাফট, ব্যাংকিং ক্রেডিট, বাট্টাকৃত বা ক্রয়কৃত বিল, ইসলামী শরীয়া মোতাবেক পরিচালিত আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক বিনিয়োগকৃত অর্থ বা অন্য যে কোন আর্থিক আনুকূল্য বা সুযোগ-সুবিধা-, যে নামেই অভিহিত হউক না কেন;

(২) গ্যারান্টি ইনডেমনিটি, ঋণপত্র বা অন্য কোন আর্থিক বন্দোবস্ত যাহা কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান ঋণ গ্রহীতার পক্ষে প্রদান বা জারী করে বা দায় হিসাবে গ্রহণ করে;

(৩) কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক উহার কোন কর্মকর্তা বা কর্মচারীকে প্রদত্ত কোন ঋণ; এবং

(8) পূর্ববর্তী ক্রমিক এ উল্লিখিত ঋণ (৩) হইতে (১), বা, ক্ষেত্রমত, ইসলামী শরীয়া অনুযায়ী পরিচালিত আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক বিনিয়োগকৃত অর্থ এর উপর বৈধভাবে আরোপিত সুদ, দণ্ড সুদ বা মুনাফা বা ভাড়া;”

65. Since the bank did not invest nor did grant any financial favour or facilities to the petitioner, the excess profit allegedly withdrawn by the petitioner from his MTDR accounts does not attract the clause ‘ইসলামী শরীয় মোতাবেক পরিচালিত আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক বিনিয়োগকৃত অর্থ বা অন্য যে কোন আর্থিক আনুকূল্য বা সুযোগ-সুবিধা-, যে নামেই অভিহিত হউক না কেন’ of section 2(Ga)(1) or the clause ‘ইসলামী শরীয়া অনুযায়ী পরিচালিত আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক বিনিয়োগকৃত অর্থ এর উপর বৈধভাবে আরোপিত সুদ, দণ্ড সুদ বা মুনাফা বা ভাড়’ of section 2(Ga)(4) of the Ain. Neither the remaining parts of sections 2(Ga)(1) and 2(Ga)(4) nor sections 2(Ga) (2) and 2(Ga)(3) of the Ain relate to the transaction under the MTDR scheme. Accordingly, there was no transaction of loan between the respondent bank and petitioner.

66. It is the contention of the respondent bank that on making demand for payment by issuing a legal notice the excess profit fraudulently withdrawn by the petitioner in collusion with the defendant No.2, a junior officer of the bank was turned to a forced loan or demand loan. In clause 1 of the BRPD Circular No.5 dated 5-6-2006 issued by the Banking Regulation and Policy Department, Bangladesh Bank all loans and advances have been grouped into 4 (four) categories for the purpose of classification, namely (a) Continuous Loan, (b) Demand Loan, (c) Fixed Term Loan and (d) Short-term Agricultural and Micro Credit. In clause 1(b) Demand Loan has been defined as follows:

"1. (b) Demand Loan: The loans that become repayable on demand by the bank will be treated as Demand Loans. If any contingent or any liabilities are turned to forced loans (i.e. without any prior approval as regular loan) those too will be treated as Demand Loans. Such as: Forced LIM, PAD, FBP, and IBP etc."

<u>67. The definition of Demand Loan contemplates that firstly, it must be one kind of loan (lot) as defined in section 2(GA) of the Ain and then it is repayable on demand. The term 'contingent' or the term 'any other liabilities' as appears in the said definition are derived from or incurred on the transaction of loan in any form, such as 'advance', 'debt', 'cash loan', 'over draft' etc. Moreover, any other sorts of loan not covered by the definition of loan (11/5) under section 2(Ga) of the Ain cannot be realised under the Ain. Nevertheless, it has already been found that there was no transaction of loan between the respondent bank and petitioner. Accordingly, the suit is beyond the jurisdiction of the Court established under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.</u>

<u>68. The provisions of section 18(1) of the Ain contemplate that any amount of money misappropriated by any officer or employee of the bank cannot be treated as a loan and realised through the Court under the Ain. Section 18(1) of the Ain runs as follows:</u>

<u>“১৮। মামলা দায়ের ও শুনানী সম্পর্কিত বিশেষ বিধান ॥</u>

<u>(১) কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের কোন কর্মকর্তা বা কর্মচারী কর্তৃক আত্মসাৎকৃত কোন অর্থ ঋণ গণ্যে এই আইনের অধীন আদালতের মাধ্যমে আদায়যোগ্য হইবে না।”</u>

69. It is the averments of the plaintiff-respondent bank that the defendant-petitioner has fraudulently withdrawn the excess profit against his MTDR accounts in collusion with the defendant No.2, a junior officer of the bank, which contemplates that the petitioner has misappropriated the excess profit in collusion with an officer of the bank. This contemplation also gets support from the submission made by the respondent bank in its affidavit-in-opposition "the defect in filing the suit under section 18(1) of the Artho Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 can easily be cured by filing an amendment application at any stage of the trial." Therefore, the amount of money misappropriated or fraudulently withdrawn by the petitioner in collusion with an officer of the bank cannot be realised upon treating the same as loan through the Court under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Accordingly, the Court established under the Ain has no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the suit.

70. In view of the discussions made above, the suit being hopelessly barred by limitation and beyond the jurisdiction of the Court established under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, we find merit in the Rule.

71. Hence, the Rule is made absolute.

72. Accordingly, the application dated 31-10-2010 filed under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 57 of the Artha Rin Adalat AM, 2003 in Artha Rin Suit No.115 of 2010, now pending in the Artha Rin Adalat No.4, Dhaka, stands allowed, the plaint of the suit stands rejected and the suit stands dismissed.

However, there would be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued, at the instance of purchaser-petitioner calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-8 to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and order dated 21-11-2010 passed by Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet, Miscellaneous Appeal No. 72 of 2009 allowed the appeal setting aside the Judgment and order dated 27-5-2009 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Sylhet, in Miscellaneous (Pre-emption) Case No. 16 of 2002 should not be set aside.

2. Short facts, necessary for disposal of the Rule, is that, the predecessors of opposite party Nos. 1-8 filed Miscellaneous Pre-emption Case No. 16 of 2002 under section 96 of the SA & T Act against the purchaser petitioner alleging, inter-alia, that Ataur Rahman, their predecessor (father of only petitioner witness Abdul Hashim), purchased the 30 decimals of land by kabala deed dated 21-5-1975. Then he sold 11¼ decimals of land to Kala Mia opposite party No. 2 (vendor) by kabala deed dated 20-4-1998. There was oral condition with kala Mia that if Kala Mia sell this land at any time then he would inform their predecessor Ataur Rahman or his heirs. But Ataur Rahman was not informed at the time of the impugned sale to the petitioner Kamaruddin. There was breach of condition of the impugned sale by kabala deed dated 25-8-1999. The pre-emptor Ataur Rahman came to know about the sale on 30-8-1999. Hence the pre-emptor filed the Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case 16 of 2002 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Sylhet.

3. The pre-emptee-purchaser, Kamaruddin contested the case and filed written objection contending that the petitioner knew about the impugned sale to this opposite party, there was no necessity of any notice, moreover petitioner has no necessity for the disputed land of the impugned sale and there had been no disadvantage of the petitioner in possessing the remaining land of the plot during 15 months. There was no condition in the sale by the petitioner to the vendor of the opposite party for return of the land, it is a lie that there was oral agreement as such, the application for pre-emption is liable to be dismissed.

4. The pre-emptor examined 1 witness as OPW, to prove the case in the court Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Sylhet but the pre-emptee-purchaser examined none.

5. The Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Sylhet after hearing on consideration of the evidence on record, rejected the Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 2002 on 27-5-2009. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the Judgment and order dated 27-5-2009 passed Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Sylhet, in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 2002, the pre-emptor preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 72 of 2009 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet which was heard by Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet, who after hearing allowed the Miscellaneous Appeal setting aside the Judgment and order dated 27-5-2009 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Sylhet, in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 2002.

6. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the Judgment and order dated 21-11-2010 passed by Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 72 of 2009, the pre-emptee-purchaser filed this Revisional application before this court and obtained Rule and stay operation of the impugned Judgment and order dated 21-11-2010 passed by Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 72 of 2009.

7. Mr Chowdhury Murshed Kamal Tipu, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the pre-emptee-purchaser, submits that the Trial Court after hearing on consideration of the evidence on record rightly rejected the pre-emption Miscellaneous case. He further submits that the lower appellate court after hearing without consideration of the evidence on record wrongly allowed the Miscellaneous appeal setting aside the Judgment and order passed by the Trial Court. He further submits that the lower appellate court committed error of law in holding that trial Court redundantly and illegally considered the point of necessity of the petitioner according to former law though the instant pre-emption case was filed in 2002 before the amendment of Section 96 of SAT Act in 2006 wherein the former law is applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case and the impugned judgment having occasioned failure of justice is liable to be set aside. He further submits that the petitioner of pre-emption case failed to make out any case of pre-emption adducing corroborative evidence of necessity moreover, apparently pre-emptor failed to make out any case of conditional sale and the appellate court on misconception of the law of pre-emption illegally allowed the pre-emption Miscellaneous case occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that the pre-emptor earlier sold 30 decimals of land to Kala Miah by kabala deed dated 21-5-1975, there-after Kala Miah sold 11¼ decimals to opposite party No. 2 (vendor) by kabala deed dated 20-4-1998. He further submits that pre-emptor already mutated his name in SA Khatian No. 561 (Ext.-1) in deed No. 853 dated 25-9-2002. He further submits that the Trial Court after hearing on consideration of the evidence on record rightly held that:—

“শর্ত দিয়ে কোন সম্পত্তি হস্তান্তর করলে হস্তান্তর বৈধ হয় ও শর্তটি অবৈধ হয়। ছায়েল দাবী করে নালিশী ভূমি ছাড়া ছায়েলের ভূমি ভোগ ব্যবহারে অসুবিধা সৃষ্টি হবে। কিন্তু বাস্তবে দেখা যায় নালিশী ভূমি ছাড়াও ছায়েল তার নিজের জমিতে ভোগ দখলে আছে। নালিশী ভূমি ছায়েলের প্রয়োজন তা নথি দৃষ্টে সাক্ষ্য দ্বারা প্রমাণিত হয় নাই।”

8. He further submits that during pendency of the pre-emption Miscellaneous Case pre-epmptor mutated his name with separate khatian and the pre-emptor was not tenant in the khatian No. 561 as such, the pre-emptor lost his entitle to pre-emption of the case land. In support of his arguments, he cited a decision, in the case of Sushi! Kumar Ghosh vs Md Nurul Hawlader, reported in 14 BLT (AD) 69. Accordingly, he submits that the Rule issued earlier may be absolute for ends of justice.

9. Mr M Azami along with Mr MA Halim Chowdhury, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the pre-emptor opposite parties, submit that the Trial Court without considering the evidences on record wrongly rejected the pre-emption Miscellaneous Case. They further submit that the lower appellate court after hearing on consideration of the evidences on record rightly allowed the Pre-emption Miscellaneous Appeal setting-aside the Judgment and order passed by the trial court. They further submit that the predecessor of the opposite party No. 1 Ataur Rahman purchased 30 decimals of land vide deed No. 19179 dated 21-5-1975 and became co-sharer of the holding by purchase and due to his urgent necessity of money on 20-4-1998 he transferred 11.25 decimals of land to Kala Miah opposite party No. 2 with a oral condition that if Kala Miah wish to sale this land at any time he would sale to his vendor Ataur Rahman of his successor. But without considering the oral condition Kala Miah transferred his portion of land to Kamar Uddin vide deed No. 11058 dated 25-8-1999 as such the impugned transferred accrued pre-emption right of the pre-emptor as a co-sharer of the case holding. They further submit that admittedly the petitioner is stranger in the suit land and prior of purchase of the suit land, the purchaser -pre-emptor did not serve any notice to the co-sharer of the holding and failed to comply the mandatory provision of section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or prior to purchase the petitioner did not in any way notify the co-sharers of the holding about the purchase and by concealing the entire fact of the transfer. They further submit that right of pre-emption is a statutory right of a co-sharer, if a portion or share of a holding is sold to a person who is not a co-sharer tenant of the holding have every right to apply before the court for the said portion of share. They further submit that the pre-emptor sold 11.25 decimals of land to Kala Miah and the co-sharer ship of pre-emptor is in existence as because rest 18.75 decimals of land of disputed holding is under his ownership. They further submit that as per section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the right of pre-emption by a co-sharer of holding accrues against each transfer made by co-sharer to the stranger it such transfer has not fallen under the provision of Section 96(10) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 or any other law. In support of their arguments they cited a decision, in the case of Md Atiqur Rahman Chowdhury, vs M/s Marshu Ltd, reported in 3 ALR (AD) 58. Accordingly, they submit that the present Rule may discharged for ends of justice.

10. Heard the learned Advocate of both sides, perused the Revisional application, judgment and order passed by both the Courts below and other necessary papers/documents are available in record. It appears from the record that the pre-emptor earlier sold 11¼ decimals to opposite party No. 2 by kabala deed dated 20-4-1998, after 15 months Kala Miah sold the rest to one Kamar Uddin on 25-8-1999, it also appears that pre-emptor already mutated his name by separate khatian No. 853 as such the pre-emptor is not a tenant with the khatian No. 561.

11. It also appears that the Trial Court after hearing on consideration of the evidences on record rightly rejected the pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 2002 and held that:—

“শর্ত দিয়ে কোন সম্পত্তি হস্তান্তর করলে হস্তান্তর বৈধ হয় ও শর্তটি অবৈধ হয়। ছায়েল দাবী করে নালিশী ভূমি ছাড়া ছায়েলের ভূমি ভোগ ব্যবহারে অসুবিধা সৃষ্টি হবে। কিন্তু বাস্তবে দেখা যায় নালিশী ভূমি ছাড়াও ছায়েল তার নিজের জমিতে ভোগ দখলে আছে। নালিশী ভূমি ছায়েলের প্রয়োজন তা নথি দৃষ্টে সাক্ষ্য দ্বারা প্রমাণিত হয় নাই।”

<u>12. It also appears that the pre-emptor willfully sold the 11.25 decimals of land in favour of the Kala Miah and after 15 months sold the case land in favour of the preemptee purchaser, the pre-emptor already mutated his name by separate khatian and after mutation he has no right to preempt the case land by filing pre-emption case.</u>

13. It may be mentioned here, our Apex court held that in the case of Sushi! Kumar Ghosh vs Md Nurul Hawlader, reported in 14 BLT (AD) 69, wherein it has been held that:—

"it is not enough that the pre-emptor must have subsisting interest at the time of filing of the pre-emption cases but the pre-emptor also must have interest at the time when the final order pre-emption case is passed. The High Court Division further held that the appellate was wrong in allowing the pre-emption in favour of the added pre-emptor on the ground that there were not co-sharers when the pre-emption cases were filed rather they are subsequent transferees from pre-emptor No. 1 during pendency of the pre-emption cases and, as such, the appellate court had committed gross illegality in allowing pre-emption in favour of the added pre-emptor."

14. It may be mentioned here, in the case of Azadur Rahman @ Azakkor Rahman vs Abdul Musabbir, reported in I LNJ 219 = 17 BLC 472, wherein it has been held that:

State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (XXXVIII of 1951)

Section- 96

"The petitioner's right of pre-emption accrues when the first transferred was effected, pre-emption against subsequent transfer suffers from legal infirmity."

15. It may be mentioned here that the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor opposite parties cited a decision, I have scrutinized the same which is different subject, as such, pre-emptors will not get any benefit by the decision as mentioned above.

16. Considering the above facts and circumstances of the case. I hold and find that the pre-emptor opposite parties failed to prove their case by satisfactory oral and documentary evidences. The preemptor earlier sold 30 decimals of land to Kala Miah by Kabala deed dated 21-5-1975 thereafter Kala Miah sold 11¼ decimals of land to opposite party No. 2 by Kabala deed dated 204-1998. The preemptor did not file any Pre-emption Case against the first sale. The preemptor filed pre-emption case against subsequent sale. Right of Pre-emption accrues when the first transfer was affected, pre-emption against subsequent transfer suffers from legai infirmity.

17. In the result, the Rule issued earlier is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned Judgment and order dated 21-11-2010 passed by Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet, Miscellaneous Appeal No. 72 of 2009 is hereby set-aside, the Judgment and order dated 27-5-2009 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Sadar, Sylhet, in Miscellaneous (Pre-emption ) Case No. 16 of 2002 is hereby affirmed and rejected the Miscellaneous (Pre-emption ) Case No. 16 of 2002.

Send down the LC records along with a copy of this Judgment to the courts concerned at once for information and necessary steps.

End.
