full_judgment:
This rule has been issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 30-7-2017 passed by learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Moulvibazar in Miscellaneous Appeal No.10 of 2009 allowing the application under order 6 Rule 17 read with sections 107 and 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the application of pre-emption of pre-emption case No.23 of 2003 by decreasing the area of the schedule land from 0.23 acres to 0.1150 acres of Khatian No.284 should not be set aside.

2. Opposite party No.1 as pre-emptor filed miscellaneous case No.23 of 2003 before the Assistant Judge, Komolgonj, Moulvibazar claiming the case land as co-sharer by way of pre-emption. The area of land sought to be pre-empted was 23 decimal as mentioned in the disputed sale deed.

3. The pre-emptee opposite party Nos.1-7 contested the case by filing written objection denying the claim of the pre-emptor.

4. During trial, pre-emptor examined 1 witness and pre-emptee examined 2 witnesses in support of their respective claims. After hearing the trial Court dismissed the case by judgment and order dated 10-5-2009 against which the pre-emptor preferred Miscellaneous appeal No.10 of 2009 before the District Judge, Moulvibazar and subsequently the said appeal was transferred to the Court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Moulvibazar.

5. During pendency of the appeal the preemptor-opposite party filed an application under Order VI, rule 17 read with section 107 and 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 30-7-2013 for amendment of pre-emption application contending that as he is co-sharer in the case jote and possessing 8 annas shares i.e. 0.1150 acres, his pre-emption application should be proceeded for remaining 0.1150 acres of land. After hearing the appellate Court allowed the application for amendment which has been impugned here.

6. Mr Choudhury Murshed Kamal Tipu, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that in the impugned deed of sale an area of 23 decimal of land has been transferred for which the pre-emptor filed the case and after hearing the same has been dismissed. In the appellate stage the pre-emptor sought to amend pre-emption application inserting an area of 0.1150 acres which amounts to part pre-emption which cannot be allowed as per law. In support of his contention he referred the case of Haji Tajamal Ali being dead his heirs Kamarunnessa vs Abdus Sattar, 34 DLR (AD) 217. He next submits that the impugned order is a non speaking order and the appellate Court passed the order without assigning any reason and, as such, the impugned order is not sustainable.

7. Conversely Mr M Khaled Ahmed learned advocate appearing for the opposite party-pre-emptor submits that plaint or application as the case may be can be amended at any stage of the proceeding, even at the appellate stage and the appellate Court committed no error in allowing application for amendment of pre-emption petition. In support of his contention he referred the case of Daguram Mandal vs Omela Shundari Bewa 12 DLR 626, Doon Valley Rice Limited vs MV Yue Yang, 48 DLR 531, Rafiqul Islam vs Principal Secretary, President's Secretariat, 49 DLR 476, Jahangir Nagar University Co-operative Housing Society vs Md Mujibar Rahman, 10 BLD 419 = 43 DLR 282, Abdul Motaleb vs Md Ershad Ali, 18 BLD AD 121 = 4 BLC (AD) 150. Radha Krishna Jogani (Agarwalla) vs Dwarka Das Agarawalla 36 DLR AD 253.

8. Having gone through the application for amendment of pre-emption petition and other materials it appears that the pre-emptor as co-sharer filed the pre-emption case regarding a deed of sale by which an area of 23 decimal land has been transferred in the holding. Both the parties led evidence in support of their respective claims and the trial Court after hearing dismissed the case. The pre-emptor adduced evidence in the trial Court claiming entire case land and the trial Court after hearing dismissed his case. At the appellate stage he intends to amend pre-emption petition claiming 0.1150 acres of land on the ground that he is the owner and possessor in the remaining 0.1150 acres of land and, as such, no claim of the pre-emption is required to be laid by him. So it is to be ascertained after proposed amendment whether his claim comes within the perview of partial pre-emption. It is settled proposition of law that partial pre-emption cannot be allowed. In 34 DLR (AD) 217 this proposition has been clearly spelt out by our appellate division in the following manner:

"Pre-emption was disallowed in that case on reversal of the High Court Division's decision as the pre-emptor was not found to have owned any land contiguous to the land transferred. Rule of bar of partial pre-emption was discussed in both the cases referred to above and it was held that this rule is applicable to a case where pre-emption is soughs by a co-sharer tenant who is required to pre-empt the entire land transferred, but is not applicable in a case where a contiguous land holder seeks pre-emption and contiguity being the only basis for his claim. He may pre-empt only that part of the land transferred to which his land is contiguous unless the land transferred is a compact block of area."

<u>9. Since the pre-emptor is claiming the land as co-sharer by inheritance he is obligated to initiate and continue pre-emption proceeding regarding the land transferred by deed of sale. The pre-emptor filed the application for entire quantum of land as transferred by the impugned deed of sale but at the appellate stage he sought to amend his pre-emption application which cannot be allowed. Aforequoted salutary principle has been affirmed by many other decisions of our apex Court and, as such, the appellate Court committed serious error in allowing the application for amendment which cannot be sustained.</u>

<u>10. The principle cited by the learned advocate for the opposite party reported in 49 DLR 477 is to the effect that if a fictitious portion of land is included in a deed of sale, that portion need not be pre-empted, which is not applicable in the instant case. Only exception is that if the pre-emptor is co-sharer in one holding out of many holdings in the transfer deed, then he can seek pre-emption regarding the holding where he is co-sharer which will not be termed as partial pre-emption. In the case of Karimunnesa Begum Chowdhury vs Niranjan Chowdury, 43 DLR (AD) 108 such view has been propounded. The pre-emptor stated that he is owner of half of the land having transferred by impugned sale deed and he need not file pre-emption for that portion but in all fairness his plea is not acceptable because he did not file any suit challenging the purported transfer of his portion of land. So the amendment is not to be allowed for proper adjudication of disputes.</u>

11. Other decisions as referred by the learned advocate for the opposite party is regarding the principle for amendment of plaint wherein the proposition laid down that amendment application can be allowed at any stage of the proceeding, even at the appellate stage. The principal enunciated in those decisions are time honored and there is no disputes regarding the ratios laid down in those decisions. The moot question is whether amendment application can be allowed claiming part pre-emption and given the facts and circumstances of the case, the appellate Court erroneously allowed the application which caused failure of justice.

12. In the above context the rule bears merit and accordingly the rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. 13. The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby re-called and vacated.

Send a copy of the order to the concern Court.

End.

full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: As similar questions of laws and facts are involved in Writ Petition Nos. 9316 of 2007, 9319 of 2007, 9321 of 2007, 9318 of 2007 and 8540 of 2007, they have been heard together and are disposed of by this consolidated judgment. 2. In Writ Petition No. 9316 of 2007, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the sanction given by the respondent No. 2 purportedly under Rule 19(ঞ) (5) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 vide Memo No. গোঃ/২০০৭-১৮৭ dated 16-4-2007 (reproduced in paragraph 8 of the Writ Petition) for proceeding with Debidwar Police Station Case No. 17 dated 21-2-2007 corresponding to GR Case No. 32 of 2007 filed under sections 385/386 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with Rule 14 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, now pending before the Divisional Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong, being hit by section 3(3)(ka) of the Emergency Power Ordinance, 2007 read with Rule 14 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 and violative of Articles 35 and 93(1) of the Constitution, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. In Writ Petition No. 9319 of 2007, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the sanction given by the respondent No. 2 purportedly under Rule 19(43) (5) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 vide Memo No. গোঃ/২০০৭-১৮৮ dated 16-4-2007 (reproduced in paragraph 8 of the Writ Petition) for proceeding with Debidwar Police Station Case No. 19 dated 25-2-2007 corresponding to GR Case No. 34 of 2007 filed under sections 385/386/506 of the Penal Code, 1860 read with Rule 14 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, now pending before the Divisional Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong as Druto Bichar Tribunal Case No. 27 of 2007, being hit by section 3(3)(ka) of the Emergency Power Ordinance, 2007 as well as Rule 14 of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 and violative of Articles 35 and 93(1) of the Constitution, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

4. In Writ Petition No. 9321 of 2007, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the sanction granted by the respondent No. 2 purportedly under Rule 19(ঞ) (1) and 19(ঞ) (5) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 vide Memo No. গোঃ/২০০৭-১৯০ dated 16-4-2007 (as quoted in paragraph 8 of the Writ Petition) for proceeding with Debidwar Police Station Case No. 6 dated 12-3-2007 corresponding to GR Case No. 43 of 2007 under sections 147/341/342/385/323/379/167/34 of the Penal Code, 1860 treating the case as of public importance under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, now pending before the Divisional Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong, being hit by section 3(3)(ka) of the Emergency Power Ordinance, 2007 and Articles 35 and 93(1) of the Constitution, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

5. In Writ Petition No. 9318 of 2007, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the sanction given by the respondent No. 2 vide Memo No. গোঃ/২০০৭-১৮৯ dated 16-4-2007 (as quoted in paragraph 5 of the Writ Petition) for proceeding with Debidwar Police Station Case No. 20 dated 25-2-2007 corresponding to GR Case No. 35 of 2007 filed as per sections 385/406 of the Penal Code, 1860 under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007, treating the case as of public importance, now pending before the Divisional Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong, being hit by section 3(3)(ka) of the Emergency Power Ordinance, 2007 as well as Articles 35(1) and 93(1) of the Constitution, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

6. In Writ Petition No. 8540 of 2007, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the sanction given by the respondent No. 2 purportedly under Rule 19(ঞ) (1) and (ঞ) (5) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 vide Memo No. cctts/k009- dated 16-4-2007 (Annexure-A. to the Writ Petition) for application of the aforesaid Rules of 2007 to Debidwar Police Station Case No. 7 dated 4-3-2007 corresponding to GR Case No. 44 of 2007 filed under sections 385/386 of the Penal Code, 1860, now pending before the Divisional Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong and re-numbered as Druto Bichar Tribunal Case No. 26 of 2007, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

7. Facts giving rise to the issuance of the Rules Nisi may, briefly, be stated as follows:

The petitioner in all the Writ Petitions is a former Member of Parliament from Comilla-4 constituency (Debidwar, Comilla) and a very popular leader in his constituency. He is also an Electrical Engineer who obtained M.Sc. Degree in Electrical Engineering from the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET), Dhaka. He is a prominent business magnate of the country too. However, the informants of the criminal cases as referred to in the Rule-issuing orders initiated the cases against the petitioner for commission of offences punishable under sections 385/386 and some other sections of the Penal Code, 1860. The investigating agencies duly investigated the cases and submitted charge-sheets therein. In view of consideration of public importance, the offences allegedly committed by the petitioner were brought within the purview of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 and accordingly sanctions were accorded by the appropriate authority for proceeding with the cases under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007. As the petitioner was charge-sheeted in all the cases, the Court of 1st instance sent up the same to the Divisional Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong for trial. At that stage, the petitioner invoked the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the Rules Nisi.

8. At the outset, Mr Ajmalul Hossain, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner in all the Writ Petitions, submits that as the facts and circumstances of the cases in question are exceptional, the petitioner, instead of availing himself of any other alternative remedy provided in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, has resorted to Article 102 of the Constitution for proper and effectual remedies and, as such, the Writ Petitions are before this Court for adjudication in accordance with law.

9. Mr Ajmalul Hossain further submits that the Writ Petitions are maintainable, though there is an alternative remedy under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure; but this alternative remedy will not stand in the way of the petitioner in invoking the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division when any question of law and an interpretation of any statute are involved.

10. Mr Ajmalul Hossain also submits that the presence of an alternative remedy does not debar the High Court Division from exercising its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution when the facts and circumstances of a particular case are such that the accused had no reasonable opportunity to avail himself of the statutory remedy provided under the relevant statute.

11. Mr Ajmalul Hossain next submits that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court Division is empowered to quash the proceedings of the cases pending in the Druto Bichar Tribunal below under Article 102 of the Constitution.

12. In support of the above submissions, Mr Ajmalul Hossain adverts to the decisions in the cases of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs lqbal Hasan Mahmood alias lqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku, 60 DLR (AD) 147; Nesar Ahmed also known as Babul vs Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali, 49 DLR (AD) 111; MA Hai, Md Wazed Ali Miah and Md Moslem vs Trading Corporation of Bangladesh, 40 DLR (AD) 206; Chairman, Anti-Corruption Commission vs Enayetur Rahman, 64 DLR (AD) 14 and State of Haryana vs Ch. Bhajan Lal, AIR 1992 SC 604.

13. Per contra, Mr Md Motaher Hossain (Sazu), learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1 in all the Writ Petitions, submits that in view of the 'ratio' enunciated in the case of Chairman, Anti-Corruption Commission vs Enayetur Rahman, 64 DLR (AD) 14, the Writ Petitions are not maintainable inasmuch as no vires of the relevant law has been challenged therein and in this perspective, the petitioner cannot cross the threshold and that being so, the Rules are liable to be discharged as being not maintainable.

14. Mr Md Motaher Hossain (Sazu) also submits that if the petitioner has any genuine grievance with regard to initiation of the cases against him, he can definitely invoke the remedies provided by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 and by this time, it has become a settled proposition of law that the proceedings of a criminal case cannot be quashed under the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division by giving a damn to the provisions of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

15. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, learned Advocate for the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), on our request, has assisted us by referring to the decision in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Sheikh Hasina reported in 60 DLR (AD) 90 and submits that all the contentions that have been raised by Mr Ajmalul Hossain in the present Writ Petitions have already been answered by the Appellate Division in that decision [60 DLR (AD) 90) and in such a situation, the Writ Petitions are misconceived and the petitioner must go through the process of trial before the Divisional Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong.

16. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan further submits that as the Rules Nisi are incompetent, they are liable to be discharged; but at the same time, he asserts that if there is any genuine grievance on the part of the petitioner in connection with any of the cases, he may definitely avail himself of any relief provided for within the four corners of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

17. We have heard the submissions of the learned Advocate Mr Ajmalul Hossain and the counter-submissions of the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr Md Motaher Hossain (Sazu) and the learned Advocate for the Anti-Corruption Commission Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan and perused all the Writ Petitions and relevant Annexures annexed thereto.

18. The Emergency Power Ordinance, 2007 provides for the power of bringing any offence committed before or after the Ordinance as triable under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007. It is true that Rules 3 to 8 of the Emergency Power Rules have created certain offences and provide for their punishment and mode of trial and therefore, offences so created are prospective. So those offences mentioned in the aforementioned Rules of 2007 cannot be punished if committed prior to 12th January, 2007. But that does not mean that the offences mentioned in Rules 14 and 15 providing for trial of offences under various laws are prospective. This is because Rules 14 and 15 have simply brought those offences within the mischief of the Emergency Power Rules of 2007 only for the purpose of trial and the offences mentioned therein were offences since the promulgation of the respective laws. In the instant cases, we find that the offences punishable under sections 385 or 386 or 506 or other relevant sections are as old as the Penal Code itself which came into force in 1860.

19. Article 35(1) of our Constitution is as follows:

"35. (1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than, or different from, that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence."

20. This Article 35(1) of our Constitution is exactly Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India and Article 6 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1956.

21. In the decision in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Sheikh Hasina reported in 60 DLR (AD) 90, it was held in paragraph 56:

"56. But our Article 35(1) is materially different from that of Article 1 section 9 Clause 3 of the US Constitution and it must be interpreted according to its term. What is prohibited under Article 35(1) is only conviction or sentence under an ex post facto law and not trial thereof and a trial under a procedure different from what obtained at the time of commission of the offence or trial by a Court different from that which had competence at the time cannot ipso facto be held to be unconstitutional. A person accused of the commission of an offence has no fundamental right to a trial by a particular Court or by a particular procedure except in so far as any Constitutional objection by way of discrimination or violation of any other fundamental right may be involved. In other words, the prohibition under this clause does not extend to procedural laws and a procedural law would not contravene Article 35(1) merely because retrospective effect is given to it."

22. Similar view was taken in the case of GP Nayyar vs State (Delhi Administration) reported in AIR 1979 SC 602. In that case, the Supreme Court of India articulated itself in the following manner:

"Article 20(1) deals with ex post facto laws, though that expression has not been used in the Article. Usually, a law prescribes a rule of conduct by which persons ought to be governed in respect of their civil rights. Certain penalties are also imposed under the criminal law for breach of any law. Though a sovereign Legislature has power to legislate retrospectively, creation of an offence for an act which at the time of its commission was not an offence or imposition of a penalty greater than that which was under the law provided violates Article 20(1). In the well-known case of Phillips vs Eyre (1870) 6 QBD 1 at pages 23 and 25 and also in the American case of Calder vs Bull (1780 to 1806) 3 Dall 386; 1 Led 648 at page 649, the principle underlying the provision has been fully discussed. All that Article 20(1) prohibits is ex post facto laws and is designed to prevent a person from being punished for an act or omission which was considered innocent when done. It only prohibits the conviction of a person or his being subjected to a penalty under ex post facto laws."

23. In the case of Mohammad Alam vs State reported in 19 DLR (SC) 242, the Pakistan Supreme Court held as follows:

"No accused person has any vested right in procedure which is regulated by the law in force at the time of the trial. It is obvious that at the time of the commission of the offence, the relevant law is to apply to its trial. Obviously, the trial would take place according to the procedure prevalent at the time the case is brought before a Court or a Tribunal."

24. It was further held in that case:

"With regard to the procedural laws, the general principle is that alterations in procedure are retrospective unless there be some good reason against such a view."

25. In that case, the earlier case of the State vs Maulvi Muhammad Jamil reported in PLD 1965 (SC) 681 was considered and it was observed:

"The principle was affirmed in the above decision that when the law is altered during the pendency of an action, the rights of the parties are to be decided according to the law as it existed when the action was begun, unless the new statute shows a clear intention to vary such rights. Where the Legislature has made its intention clear that the amending Act should have retrospective operation, there is no doubt that it must be so construed, even though the consequences may entail hardship to a party. But even without express words to that effect, retrospective effect may be given to an amending law, if the new law manifests such a necessary intendment. With regard to the procedural laws, the general principle is that alterations in procedure are retrospective unless there be some good reason against such a view. If a statute deals merely with the procedure in an action, and does not affect the rights of the parties, it will be held to apply prima facie to all actions pending as well as future.  It is only if it be more than a mere matter of procedure, that is, if it touches a right in existence at the passing of the new Act, that the aggrieved party would be entitled to succeed in giving a successful challenge to the retrospective effect of the new Act. For this proposition, reliance was placed in that case on Maxwell on Interpretation of Statutes, 1962 Edition, pages 212, 216 and 217, Crawford on Statutory Construction, 1940 Edition, pages 568 and 648, Halsbury's Laws of England, Vol. 36, Third Edition, pages 423 and 426, Craies on Statute Law, Fifth Edition, pages 370 and 371 and Corpus Juris, Vol. 59, page 1174. The formulation of the principles in such cases fairly sums up the legal position as envisaged by the decisions cited by both parties before us."

26. In the case of Abdul Wadud vs State reported in 48 DLR (AD) 6, it was held that if a statute deals merely with the procedure in an action, and does not affect the rights of the parties, it will be held to apply prima facie to all actions pending as well as future. But the principle is that procedural laws are always retrospective unless a different intention is manifestly expressed in the statute itself.

27. From the above deliberations, we have no hesitation in holding that a procedural law is always retrospective unless a different intention is expressly made in the statute itself and no one has a right, far less a fundamental right, to trial by any particular Court or a particular procedure.

28. In the decision reported in 60 DLR (AD) 90, it was held in paragraphs 66, 67 and 68:

"66. Neither the EP Ordinance nor the EPR has made sections 385/109 an offence. It was an offence since the enactment of the Penal Code in 1860 and this offence is not a creation of the EPR. What the EPR 14 has done is that it has brought the said offence within the mischief of Rule 14 for the purpose of trial by the Court set up under the EPR. Therefore, it cannot be said that the EPR has made it punishable in 2007; but it was not at all an offence before 2007 or 2000 or 2001 when the offence was allegedly committed. This was an offence under sections 385/109 and it has only been made triable under the EPR. Therefore, by no stretch of imagination, there has been any violation of the rules Against ex post facto law as provided for by Article 35(1) of the Constitution.

67. In such view of the matter, the finding of the High Court Division that any case arising out of an offence committed prior to 11-1-2007 cannot be tried under the Emergency Power Rules is of no substance and is based on a misconception of Article 35(1) of the Constitution and the concept of prohibition against ex post facto law.

68. Sub-section 3(4s) of section 3 of the EPO simply provides that provisions may be made by promulgating rules under section 3 for expeditious and effective enquiry, investigation, trial and appeal of any offence or any other matter relating thereto during the continuance of the proclamation of emergency. The expression "কার্যকরতাকালে" in 3(34s) relates to the framing of rules for the enquiry, investigation, trial, appeal etc. and does not relate to the time of the offence. It does not mean that the offences to be tried under the rules framed under section 3(5) are to be offences committed during the subsistence of the emergency."

<u>29. Reverting to the cases in hand, sections 385 or 386 or 506 and other relevant sections of the Penal Code are not creations of the Emergency Power Ordinance or the Emergency Power Rules of 2007. Those have been brought under Rule 14 only for the purpose of trial and therefore the question of violation of Article 35(1) or, for that matter, any of the provisions of any international instrument on human rights does not arise at all.</u>

30. In the decision reported in 60 DLR (AD) 90, the Appellate Division spelt out in paragraph 103:

"103. It has been argued that Rule 19(a) (1) and (2) is bad because there is no guideline in giving sanction. The reference to public importance is enough guideline given by the law-makers and therefore, the High Court Division was wrong in declaring Annexure-'C' as without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and in quashing Gulshan Police Station Case No. 34(6) of 2007 dated 13-6-2007 under the Emergency Power Rules, 2007..."

<u>31. Keeping the above view of the Appellate Division at the back of our mind, we find that there in nothing wrong in according the sanctions in exercise of the power given under Rule 19(0) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007. Sometimes, the status of the accused is considered in criminal proceedings. In the case of PD Patel vs Emperor reported in 11TR (1933) Page 363, the status of Patel was considered and only because he was a Barrister, his sentence was enhanced. Besides, in the case SA Maquith Chowdhury vs State reported in 11 DLR (SC) 105, the Pakistan Supreme Court did not reduce the sentence only because the accused was an Advocate.</u>

<u>32. In view of what have been stated above, it is ex facie clear that no illegality was committed by bringing the Penal Code within Rule 14 and according the impugned sanctions under Rule 19(ঞ) of the Emergency Power Rules, 2007.</u>

<u>33. It does not stand to reason and logic as to why Mr Ajmalul Hossain has found fault with Article 93(1) of the Constitution. This Article 93(1) relates to the ordinance-making power of the President when Parliament stands dissolved or is not in session. The Emergency Power Ordinance, 2007 was promulgated by virtue of Article 93(1) of the Constitution and the Emergency Power Rules, 2007 were framed pursuant to section 3 of the Emergency Power Ordinance of 2007. So the invocation of Article 93(1) of the Constitution appears to be an exercise in futility.</u>

34. In the decision in the case of Chairman, Anti-Corruption Commission vs Enayetur Rahman, 64 DLR (AD) 14, the Appellate Division spelt out in paragraph 7:

"7. This Court on repeated occasions argued that Article 102(2) of the Constitution is not meant to circumvent the statutory procedures. The High Court Division will not allow a litigant to invoke the extra-ordinary jurisdiction to be converted into Courts of appeal or revision. It is only where statutory remedies are entirely ill-suited to meet the demands of extra-ordinary situations, that is to say, where vires of a statute is in question or where the determination is mala fide or where any action is taken by the executives in contravention of the principles of natural justice or where the fundamental right of a citizen has been affected by an act or where the statute is intro vires, but the action taken is without jurisdiction and the vindication of public justice requires that recourse may be had to Article 102(2) of the Constitution."

35. The facts leading to the issuance to the Rules Nisi, according to us, do not attract any of the extra-ordinary situations that have been specified in the above-mentioned paragraph 7 of the decision reported in 64 DLR (AD) 14.

36. In the decision in the case of Anti-Corruption Commission vs Mehedi Hasan reported in 67 DLR (AD) 137, it was held in paragraph 27:

"27. As regards Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 652 of 2013 arising out of Writ Petition No. 7242 of 2008, we are of the view that there is no scope for quashing a criminal proceeding under the writ jurisdiction unless the vires of the law involved is challenged. Having gone through the Rule-issuing order, we find that the vires of the law involved in the present case has not been challenged. Therefore, there is no scope for aggrandizement of jurisdiction of the High Court Division in quashing a criminal proceeding. Consequently, the High Court Division was not justified in quashing 15 criminal cases (Special Case Nos. 12-26 of 2007) in exercise of its power under Article 102 of the Constitution."

<u>37. As far as we know, the decision reported in 67 DLR (AD) 137 is the latest decision of the Appellate Division on this issue. So the law declared by the Appellate Division in that decision is binding upon the High Court Division in view of the mandate of Article 111 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>38. Furthermore, in the decision in the case of Golam Nabi vs Anti-Corruption Commission reported in 65 DLR 181, it has been unmistakably held that the decision reported in 64 DLR (AD) 14 has ousted the jurisdiction of the writ Court to quash the proceedings of a criminal case unless the 'vires' of any law is found to have been challenged.</u>

39. Coming back to the instant cases, indisputably the petitioner has not challenged the vires of the law involved therein. Given this scenario, it is crystal clear that the petitioner could have sought necessary remedies against the proceedings of the cases pending against him which are available in the relevant statute, that is to say, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

40. The decisions adverted to by Mr Ajmalul Hossain in the cases of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Iqbal Hasn Mahmood alias Iqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku, 60 DLR (AD) 147; Nesar Ahmed also known as Babul vs Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali, 49 DLR (AD) 111; MA Hai, Md Wazed Ali Miah and Md Moslem vs Trading Corporation of Bangladesh, 40 DLR (AD) 206 and State of Haryana vs Ch. Bhajan Lal, AIR 1992 (SC) 604 do not seem to be applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present cases in view of the discussions made hereinabove. So those decisions are of no avail to Mr Ajmalul Hossain.

<u>41. Although Mr Ajmalul Hossain has relied upon the decision in the case of Chairman, Anti-Corruption Commission vs Enayetur Rahman, 64 DLR (AD) 14, yet we find that that decision has supported the contention raised on behalf of the respondent No. 1. The 'ratio' of that decision decisively applies to the present Writ Petitions. Against this backdrop, the reference to the decision reported in 64 DLR (AD) 14 by Mr Ajmalul Hossain, as we see it, does not help him in any way.</u>

42. From the foregoing discussions and regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the cases, we are led to hold that the Rules Nisi have no legs to stand upon. As such the Rules are liable to be discharged. Accordingly, the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

43. The Divisional Druto Bichar Tribunal, Chittagong is, however, directed to proceed with the trial of the cases in accordance with law.

Communicate a copy of this judgment to the Tribunal below at once for information and necessary action.

End.

full_judgment:
Mamnoon Rahman J : All these Rules were heard together and disposed of by a single judgment as they do involve similar questions of fact as well as of law.

2. In Writ Petition No.5198 of 2003-the petitioner, Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha (RAJUK), has challenged the impugned gazette notification dated 2-8-2001 as evident in Annexure-B to the Writ Petition. In Writ Petition No. 11817 of 2006, 11818 of 2006, 11819 of 2006 and 3466 of 2007 the respective petitioners have challenged the gazette notification bearing memo No. Bhu: Ma:/Sha-10/Mu:tha: Dhaka-11/92-3691, dated 13-10-99 (Annexure-D) as published in Bangladesh gazette on 11-11-1999.

3. The short facts leading to the issuance of these Rules are as follows:

(a) In Writ Petition No.5198 of 2003, the property in question was acquired vide LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64 as per the provisions of section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953. The Government vide the impugned gazette notification withdraw 14-68 acres of land from acquisition exercising the power conferred under section 8(b) of the Emergency Acquisition of Property Act 1948. The case of the petitioner is that the authority cannot publish such gazette notification exercising the power conferred under section 8(b) of the Act of 1948 as the same was already repealed with effect from 13-3-1982 and being aggrieved moved this Writ Petitions and obtained the present rule.

(b) In Writ Petition No. 11817 of 2006, 11818 of 2006, 11819 of 2006 and 3466 of 2007 the respective petitioners on an advertisement made by RAJUK applied for allotment of plots. On the basis of their applications the RAJUK issued formal allotment letters in their favour. Pursuant to the allotment letters the respective petitioners paid in full the royalty/premium to the lessor namely RAJUK and after satisfaction the lessor namely RAJUK executed registered lease deeds for 99 years of the respective plots as mentioned in these Writ Petition with the petitioner and also handed over formal possession thereon. The further case of the petitioners is that they have constructed house as per approved plan and enjoying the possession thereon. All on a sudden, some people entered into the premises and claimed ownership of the said plots by virtue of sale deeds obtained from the original owners from whom the aforesaid land was acquired by the lessor as per Town Improvement Act of 1953 (hereinafter referred as Act of 1953). On query the petitioners came to know that the Ministry of Land issued a gazette notification which is impugned in all these Writ Petitioners wherein the Ministry of Land released certain portion of land from acquisition exercising the Power conferred under section 8(b) of the Act of 1948.

4. In Writ Petition No.5198 of 2001; though notices were served in accordance with law, the same was not contested by any respondents in any manner. In Writ Petition No.3466 of 2007 the respondent No.8 (RAJUK) contested the Rule by filing affidavits-in-opposition whereas respondent Nos. 7 (one Mst. Sufia Khatun) contested in Writ Petition Nos. 11817 of 2006, 11818 of 2006 and 11819 of 2006 respectively by filing affidavits-in-opposition as well as respondent No.8 (RAJUK) entered appearance by filing power. The cases of the respondent No.7 in the aforesaid three Writ Petitions are that the contentions raised by the petitioners are misconceived one and the same has been denied by the respondents. The respondent No.7 purchased the land from the persons whose predecessor in interest was the original landlord and admittedly the land was acquired in LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64 but the requiring authority decided to de-requisition certain portion of land which attracts the purchased land of the respondent No.7. In one occasion the authorities refused to release the land to one Mr Khademul Islam Chowdhury who being aggrieved preferred Writ Petition No.835 of 1977 before this Court wherein the High Court Division after hearing the parties made the Rule absolute. On review the High Court Division maintained the earlier order and the appeal by RAJUK to the Appellate Division was summary rejected. The further case of the respondent No.7 is that by virtue of the decision of the Apex Court, the Ministry of Land issued a memo dated 8-2-1999 canceling the entire proceeding of LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64 and by virtue of that letter the Ministry of Land issued the impugned gazelle notification and, as such, the same cannot be interfered with by this Court in a proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution. The further case of the respondent No.7 is that the Writ Petition No.11817 of 2006 is not maintainable as the said application has been preferred by a Constituted Attorney.

5. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing along with Mr Shah Khashruzzaman the learned advocate in Writ Petition No. 5198 of 2003 on behalf of the petitioner submits that the impugned notification issued by the Ministry of Land is without any legal authority or in accordance with law. He submits that the Act of 1953 being an independent special and complete law is fully authorised to deal with any land in any manner and as per the said law RAJUK being the ultimate authority to deal with the land acquired or in requisition under the said law in and manner. The Act of 1953 being an independent, special and separate Law, section 8(b) of the Act of 1948 which is a separate law has no manner of application and in such circumstances, the impugned notification issued by the Ministry of Land pursuant to Act of 1948 is a misconceived one and thus the same is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

6. In Writ Petition Nos. 11817 to 11819 of 2006 and 3466 of 2007 Mr Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners adopted the submission made by the Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Senior counsel appearing in Writ Petitioner No. 5198 of 2003. In addition to the said submission he further submits that the property was acquired under the Act of 1953 which is a separate law, thus the Act of 1948 has no manner of application in the case of any Acquisition and Requisition made under the Act of 1953. He submits that section 8(b) o f the Act of 1948 only empowers the government to withdraw from Acquisition of any land which has been acquired as per section 5 of the Act of 1948 and also before payment of any compensation. He submits that from the plain reading sections 79, 101 and other provisions of the Act of 1953, it is found that any other law including the Act of 1948 has no manner of application in the case of requisition and acquisition of any land by the then DIT at present RAJUK under the Act of 1953. By referring the entire Act of 1953 as well as the subsequent amendments as made up to date he submits that there are different modes for requisition and acquisition of the property by RAJUK as well as disposal of the same. So the Act of 1948 which is completely a separate law cannot be applicable in any case of acquisition or requisition under the Act of 1953 in any manner. He also referred subsection 3 of section 93A of 1953 and submits that immediately after requisition the property shall vest with the RAJUK. Lastly, he submits that the judgment of the High Court Division, upon which, the respondent No.7 relied is a judgment per in curium. In support of his contention he referred to the following reported cases: Managing Director, Rupali Bank vs Tafazal Hossain, 44 DLR (AD) 260, Sadeque Uddin Ahmed vs Jabed Ali, 3 MLR (AD) 91, Jamir Ali vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, 52 DLR 125, Jamir Ali vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, 52 DLR (AD) 176, Abdul Hoque vs Government, 9 MLR (AD) 151 = 9 BLC (AD) 56, Sadeque Uddin Ahmed, vs RAJUK, 46 DLR 205 and Al-liaj Abul Basher vs Bangladesh, 50 DLR (AD) 11.

7. Mr AQM Shafiullah, the learned Advocate along with Mr Abdun Nur appearing on behalf of the.RAJUK in their respective cases supported the contentions of the petitioners. By placing affidavit-in-opposition they supported the case of the petitioner in Writ Petition No.11817-11819 of 2006 and 3466 of 2007. Mr Shafiullah submits that without hearing the requiring body there is no scope to deal with any acquisitioned or requisitioned land by any other authority and in the instant case it appears that though RAJUK is the requiring body but Ministry of Land has released the land without notifying or hearing the RAJUK in any manner. In support of his contention he referred by the case reported in Bangladesh vs M/s Commercial Trust of Bangladesh, 14 BLD (AD) 72 = 46 DLR (AD) 89. He also submits that after acquisition and after payment of compensation the same reaches the finality of a process and after finality there is no scope to release, any land remains vacant or unutilized and such un utilization does not create any right in favour of any person to get back his/her land by way of right. In this respect he referred the case reported in Al-haj Abul Bather vs Bangladesh, 50 DLR (AD) 11.

8. Mr Md Rezaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 7 submits that the Ministry of Land issued the impugned memo and notification in accordance with law and, as such, the same cannot be interfered by this Court. He submits that the Government namely the Ministry concerned enjoys ample authority to release any land either under requisition or acquisition and, as such, the respondent-Government committed no illegality in issuing the impugned memo as well as notifications. He further submits the High Court Division in writ petition No. 835 of 1977 has rightly set aside the entire LA case in question resulting the issuance of the impugned memo and notifications which requires no interference by this Court.

9. Perused the Writ Petitions, affidavits-in-opposition, provisions of law, decisions as referred to and heard the learned Advocates for the contesting parties. On perusal of the same it appears that a common question of law has been raised in all these Writ Petitions. It appears from the record that the then DIT at present RAJUK acquired certain portion of land for the development of Dhaka city and for the implementation of residential scheme in the area specified in the Town Improvement Act of 1953. The said process was initiated and completed as per the provisions laid down in the said Act of 1953. It appears that after completion of acquisition and payment of compensation, the requiring body decided to release some land which appears to be in communication stage in between the authorities. As per the papers submitted by the respondent No. 7, it appears that there are certain conditions stipulated at that time before releasing such properties and as the owners refuse to accept the conditions the authorities cancelled the proposal for release and challenging the same Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 was filed and the Rule was made absolute and on the basis of the said judgment the impugned memo and notifications were made.

10. The pertinent question are raised in these Writ Petitioners is whether a property acquired under a law can be released on the basis of another legislation.

11. Town Improvement Act, 1953 (EB Act XIII of 1953) is enacted in the year 1953 with a special object which runs as follows:

"An Act to provide for the development, improvement and expansion of the Capital of the Republic and Narayanganj and Tongi Municipalities and certain areas in their vicinity and the constitution of a Kartipakkha therefore."

12. In the said Act, section 93A has been inserted by East Pakistan Ordinance No.49 of 1953 and the same was amended from time to time. Section 93A of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 runs as follows:

93A. Requisition of property for any scheme—(1) When any immovable property is required by the Board for carrying out any of the purposes of this Act, the Government may direct the Deputy Commissioner to requisition such property for the Board by an order in writing:

Provided that no property used by the public for the purpose of religious worship shall be requisitioned.

(2) Service of order or requisition—When any order of requisition has been made under previous subsection, it shall be served on the owner of the property personally by delivering or tendering it to him or where the owner with some adult male member of the family of such owner, or if no such adult member can be found, the notice may be served by affixing a copy to some conspicuous part of the premises in which he is known to have last resided or carried on business, or personally worked for gain, and also by affixing such copy to some conspicuous part of the requisitioned property.

(3) Possession of requisitioned property—When the order of the requisition has been served under sub-section (2) in respect of a property, the Deputy Commissioner shall take and deliver possession of the property within 2 weeks to the Board, and the Board may use or deal with the property as may appear to it to be expedient.

(4) Acquisition of requisitioned property—

(a) the Government may, if it thinks fit, acquire any requisitioned property for the Board, and shall if it proposes to so acquire a requisitioned property, direct the Deputy Commissioner to cause a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property proposed to be acquired sating that the property is proposed to be acquired for the Board.

(b) Such notice shall state particulars of the property to be acquired and shall require all persons interested in the property to appear personally or by agent before the Deputy Commissioner at a time and place therein mentioned (such time not being earlier than 15 days after the date of publication of the notice) and to state the nature of the respective interest in the property, the objections (if any) to the acquisition of the property and particulars of their claims, the compensation for their respective interest.

(c) Notice shall also be served to the above effect on the owner of such property and on all such persons known or believed to be interested therein or to be entitled to act for persons so interested as reside or have agents authorised to receive on their behalf within the revenue district in which the property is situated.

(d) In case any person so interested resides elsewhere and has no such agent, the notice shall be sent to him by a registered post in a letter addressed to him at his last known residence, address or place of business.

(e) Every person required to make or deliver a statement under sub-section (2), (3) and (4) shall be deemed to be legally bound to do so within the meaning of sections 175 and 276 of the Penal Code.

(f) The Deputy Commissioner shall after hearing all objections and after making such further enquiry, if any, as he thinks necessary, submit the case for the decision of the Government together with a record of the proceedings held by him and report containing his recommendations on the objections.

(g) The Government after considering the report made under clause (f) shall make a decision about the acquisition of the requisitioned property and such decision of the Government shall be final.

(h) The Government shall then publish in the Official Gazette a notice to the effect that the Government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property for the Board. On and from the beginning of the day on which the notice is so published, the requisitioned property shall vest absolutely in the Board free from all encumbrances and the period of such requisition of such properly shall end.

(i) For the purpose of enquiries in connection with the acquisition of a requisitioned property for the Board the Deputy Commissioner or an officer authorized by him shall have the power to summon and enforce the attendance of witnesses including the parties interested or any of them and to compel the production of documents by the same, and (so far as may be) in the same manner as is provided in the case of a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure.

(5) Whenever any immovable property is requisitioned or is required under the foregoing provisions, compensation shall be paid and the amount of compensation shall be determined in the manner, and in accordance with the principles, hereinafter set out, i.e., to say.

(a) Where the amount of compensation can be fixed by agreement, it shall be paid in accordance with such agreement.

(b) (i) Where no such agreement can be reached, the Deputy Commissioner shall assess a compensation for the immovable property having regard to the provisions of sections 23, 24 and 24 24A, as modified by section 81 of this Act, and sub-section (2) of section 35 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, so far as the same can be made applicable, and he shall give immediate notice of the assessment to the person or persons interested:

Provided that in determining such market-value the Court shall take into account the average value of the properties of the similar description and with similar advantage in the vicinity during the twenty-four months preceding the date of service of the notice under clause (a) of subsection (4) of this section:

Provided further that in assessing compensation for the requisition of any immovable property to which the provision of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 or any other law for the time being in force, for the control of house rent, apply, the Deputy Commissioner shall have regard to those provisions, so that the compensation awarded may not exceed the amount of rent allowable in respect of such property under those pro visions;

(ii) Any person interested who has not accepted assessment, may by written application move the Tribunal to determine the matter;

(iii) The application shall state the grounds on which objection to assessment is taken:

Provided that, every such application shall be made within weeks of the service of the notice by the Deputy Commissioner under clause (b) or within 3 months from the date or the order of assessment, whichever period shall later expire.

(c) At the commencement of the proceedings before the Tribunal, the Board and the persons to be compensated shall state what in their respective opinion is a fair amount for compensation.

(6) When any property is requisitioned or acquired under this section, the provisions of sections 88 and 91 shall not apply.

(7) The Government may, by order in the Official Gazette, direct that any power conferred or any duty imposed on it by this section shall, in such circumstances and under such condition, if any, as may be specified in the direction, be exercised or discharged by such officer as may be specified."

13. Also ii appears that by the Town Improvement (Amendment) Act, 1987 (Act of 29 of 1987) section 79 has been inserted wherein it has been provided as follows:

"79(1) The Kartipakkha may for carrying out the purpose Of this Act, acquire, by purchase, lease, exchange or otherwise, any land or interest in land and dispose of by sale lease, exchange or otherwise, such land or any interest in such land.

(2) The acquisition of any land or interest in land for the Karitipakkha this sections, or for any scheme under this Act, shall be deemed to be an acquisition for a public purpose within the meaning Of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (II of 1982), and the provisions of the said Ordinance shall apply to all such proceedings."

14. Also it appears that by the said Act a special provisions has been introduced which runs as follows:

(ক)-----------

(খ)-----------

(গ)-----------

(ঘ)-----------

(ঙ)এইরুপ প্রবর্তনের অব্যবহিত পূর্বে উক্ত Act এর অধীনে নিষ্পন্নাধীন যে কোন হুকুম দখল এবং অধিগ্রহণের কার্যধারা এইরুপে অব্যহত থাকিবে যেন এই আইন প্রণীত হয় নাই এবং উহা তদাধীনে নিষ্পন্ন হইবেঃ

(চ)-----------

15. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions of law, it appears that the Town Improvement Act, 1953 being a special law enacted for a very special and specific purpose and which is also a complete, law to deal with any land in any manner which included acquisition as well as disposal of the same and as per the said law the then DIT at 'present RAJUK is the ultimate authority in such cases.

16. Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 is the law incorporated in the year 1948 which is an ordinary legislation for the purpose of requisition of the property in connection with the administration and development of the new province, East Bengal and as per section 1(4) of the said Act, the said law namely Act of 1948 shall remain in force for a period of 34 years. As per the said provision of law the Act has been repealed on 16-8-1982 i.e. on the expiry of 34 years. Section 5 of the said law deals with the manner of acquisition of property whereas section 8 as well as 8B of the said Act deals with withdrawal from acquisition and requisition of the property. Section 8B of the said Act deals with the provision relating to withdrawal from acquisition which runs as follows:

8B. Withdrawal from Acquisition—When owner of any property which has been acquired under section 5 is willing to receive back the property, the Government may, at any time before the payment of compensation withdraw from the acquisition of any such property by notification published in the Official Gazette, and on such withdrawal, the property shall be restored to the possession of the owner, and with effect from the date of such restoration, the property shall vest back in the owner with the rights which he had before such property was acquired."

<u>17. So it appears that the Act of 1948 is a separate legislation providing for the provisions for acquisition and requisition under the said law as well as the provisions of release of the same from acquisition or requisition. From the four corners of the said law namely Act of 1948 we do not find any provisions that the said law is applicable to any other law for the purpose of either acquisition and/or release of the same in any manner. In the case of Abdul Huq vs Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary Ministry of Land, reported in 9 MLR (AD) 151 = 9 BLC (AD) 56, Their Lordships deals with the provisions of release of land acquired under the Town Improvement Act, 1953. Their Lordships observed as follows:</u>

<u>"Section 93A(4)(h) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 provides as under:</u>

<u>"(h) The Government shall then publish in the Official Gazette a notice to the effect that the Government has decided to acquire the requisition property for the Board. On and from the beginning of the day on which the notice is so published, the requisitioned property shall vest absolutely in the Board free from all encumbrances and the period of such requisition of such property shall end."</u>

<u>In that view of the matter there is absolutely no scope for any release of the requisitioned property by the Government. Even assuming that there may be some decision of the Board but that was hot acted upon in accordance with law so as to release the property in favour of the original owners thereof."</u>

18. Their Lordships further observed;

"There is no provision in law for release of the property as has been claimed by the petitioners as the land has been admittedly requisitioned with a view to acquire the same for greater Dhaka Development Project by the RAJUK under specified scheme. "

19. In the case of Sadeque Uddin Ahmed vs Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakkha (RAJUK), reported in 3 MLR (AD) 91 wherein their Lordships held that the Act of 1953 is a special law and unlike the Act of 1948 it does not contain any express provision for release of land under requisition. But section 41 to 45 of the said Act provides certain steps to be followed by the RAJUK if it desires to dispose of any property. Deciding the aforesaid case their Lordships held:

"The Act was enacted in 1953 with the avowed purpose of inter alia framing and executing improvement scheme for development of greater Dhaka City. Like the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 section 93A of the Act also provides for requisition but unlike the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 the Act does not contain any express provision for release of land from requisition. Under section 41 of the Act the Board may pass a resolution to the effect that any use of land should be discontinued and upon passing of such a resolution it shall form part of the particulars of the scheme under section 45(1)(c) of the Act, but section 45 of the Act is applicable to an improvement scheme of any area within the municipality (which is now Corporation), whereas Annexure- X(2) of the Supplementary Affidavit-in-opposition or respondent No. 1 shows that the present scheme when it was made had fallen outside the municipal area and therefore the various resolutions taken by the Board of Trustees of the former DIT reducing from time to time the quantum of land to be acquired have neither attained any statutory force nor been implemented by refund of the compensation money.

Although section 51A(4) of the Act requires respondent No. 1 to execute an approved development scheme "Forthwith ", no consequence is provided for in the Act itself if respondent No. 1 cannot, for any reason, comply with the said mandate. In a developing country, various factors such as paucity of fund, unstable political conditions, change of Government and a host of other considerations are to be taken into account not only in interpreting the word forthwith but also in assessing the legal consequence of a failure to comply with it."

20. In the foregoing paragraphs we have already found that the Act of 1953 being special law cannot be interfered by any authority taking shelter of any other legislation. In the case of Managing Director, Rupali Bank Limited vs Tafazal Hossain, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260 their Lordships observed that if any legal remedy is a available under both general law and special law, the remedy prescribed by the special law must be sought in exclusion of the one available under the general law.

21. It appears that after the natural death of Act of 1948 on 16-8-1982 the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 came into force and in the said law certain provisions have been inserted which specifically attracts the Town Improvement Act of 1953. But it appears from section 47 of the said Ordinance that if any proceeding initiated before the enactment of the said Ordinance it shall not affect any provision of this law and those proceeding shall be governed as if the instant Ordinance has not been amended. In the case of Jamir Ali (Md) vs Secretary, Ministry of Land, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 176 their Lordships held:

"Claim for release of unutilized acquired land is not a vested right and nor failure of the requiring body to utilize the land acquired within 3 years from the date of acquisition in view of the decision of the Government for acquisition of land as contemplated under section 12 is not applicable to the facts of the instant cases which were started long before the Ordinance came into force in view of the provision of amended section 79 of the 1953 Act as not retrospectively can be read into section 12 of the 1982 Ordinance."

22. The High Court Division also, while passing the judgment in the same case, held that in spite of repeal of section 93A and 93B of the Act 1953 the pending acquisition of the disputed land shall be continued under the aforesaid provisions as if those provisions have not been repealed and the provisions of section 12 or other provisions of Acquisition and Requisition of Immoveable Property Ordinance, 1982 shall not be applicable to the acquisition proceedings started under section 93 A of the Act of 1953. It appears in the cases in hand that certain communications were stated regarding release of certain land in question. From the Writ Petitions as well as from the affidavits-in-opposition it appears that the requiring authorities issued certain letters to the Deputy Commissioner for taking certain steps and also the Deputy Commissioner intimating the requiring body about the course of action but such type of communication cannot be used or create any legal right in favour of any person to get back any land under acquisition. This view is taken by their Lordships in the Appellate Division in a case reported in Al-Haj Abul Basher vs Bangladesh, 50 DLR (AD) 11. It further appears that in the instant case the impugned notifications were issued by the Ministry of Land exercising the power conferred under section 8(b) of the Act of 1948 long after the natural death of the said Act. It also appears that before issuing such notification, no intimation of the impugned action has been made to the RAJUK who is the requiring body which is a sine-qua-non3 for issuing such notification for taking such step. This view is also supported by a decision reported in Bangladesh vs M/s Commercial Trust of Bangladesh, 14 BLD (AD) 72 = 46 DLR (AD) 89.

<u>23. Section 8(b) of the Act of 1948 has been examined by our Apex Court in several occasions and their Lordships while examining the same consistently held that once compensation has been paid, it reaches it finality and, as such, there is no question of release of any land from acquisition. The decision reported in Md Matiur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 15 BLD 331 = 46 DLR 638 also supports this contention. In a case reported in Rangamati Food Products Ltd. vs Commissioner of Customs, 10 BLC 525 the High Court Division held that a decision of this Court is not binding if it is judgment per in curium. In the instant case the respondent No.7 resorted to the decision passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.835 of 1977. We have carefully" examined the entire judgment passed by their Lordships but it appears that at the time of hearing, no law either the Act of 1953 or Act of 1948 so far as it relates to acquisition and requisition has been referred therein in any manner. In the said judgment their Lordships only set aside the decision of a Joint Secretary of a Ministry so far as it relates to an observation that the RAJUK, the then DIT, may start a fresh process of acquisition. From the plain reading to the aforesaid judgment we do not find any single word to the effect that the High Court Division has cancelled the entire LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64.</u>

24. It appears from the impugned gazette notification that a letter of 1999 has been referred though the said latter was not annexed by the petitioner to the writ petition. But the respondents have annexed such letter in their affidavits-in-opposition as evident in Annexure-D which runs as follows:

গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার

ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয়

শাখা-১০।

স্বারক নং ভূঃমঃ/পাঃ১০/হঃদঃ/ঢাকা ১১/৯২৫৪

তারিখ ৮-২-১৯৯৯ খ্রিঃ

২৬-১০-১৪০৫ বাং

বিষয়ঃ ১০/৬৩ ও ৬৪ এল, এ, কেসের কার্যক্রম প্রত্যাহার প্রসংগে।

উপযুক্ত বিষয়ে মহামান্য সুপ্রীম কোর্টের হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে দায়েরকৃত রীট মামলা নং ৮৩৫/৭৭ এর রায়ের প্রেক্ষিতে ১০/৬৩ ও ৬৪ এল, এ, কেস বাতিল বলিয়া পরিগণিত হওয়ায় সরকার ১০/৬৩ ও ৬৪ নং এল, এ, কেসের সকল কার্যক্রম পূর্ব বাংলা (জরুরী) সম্পত্তি হুকুম দখল আইন, ১৯৪৮ এর ৮(বি) ধারা মোতাবেক প্রত্যাহার করার সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহণ করিয়াছে। জেলা প্রশাসক ঢাকাকে এই ব্যাপারে আইন অনুযায়ী পরবর্তী প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করার জন্য নির্দেশক্রমে অনুরোধ করা হইল।

(মোঃ নুর উদ্দিন আহম্মেদ)

(সিনিয়র সহকারী সচিব)

25. It appears that by referring to the judgment passed by the High Court Division-in Writ Petition No.835 of 1977 the Senior Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Land-intimated the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, that the High Court Division has cancelled the entire proceeding of LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64 and in such view of the matter, the Government decided to release the land in question exercising the power conferred under section 8B of the Act of 1948. It appears that the letter was issued in the year of 1999 though the Act of 1948 lost its force on 16-8-1982. Furthermore, in the judgment passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.835 of 1977 the High Court Division neither adjudicated the legality and property of the said LA Case in question in any manner nor has passed any order canceling the proceeding of the L.A. Case No.10 of 1963-64.

26. As we have pointed earlier in the instant case that the land in question was requisitioned by an authority under section special law namely the Act of 1953, so any land required or acquired under the said Act cannot be released by exercising power conferred in any other law including the Act of 1948 which is an ordinary legislation.

27. From the plain reading of the letter as referred above it appears that the interpretation given by the said Ministry is totally incorrect and misconceived one which causes misinterpretation of law and also creates serious anomalies in the process of law as well as initiation of series of litigations. From the plain reading of the Act of 1948 and the decisions as referred to it has been clearly held that the Act of 1948 has not manner of application in a proceeding under the Town Improvement Act of 1953 and the authority namely RAJUK is to dispose of any land as per the provision laid down in the said Act; and not the Ministry of Land.

28. From the Judgment of the High Court Division as well as the provisions of law it appears that the Ministry of Land is not the authority either in law or by the judgment passed by the High Court Division to issue such letter. It appears that the letter issued pursuant to the judgment is a misinterpreted one and based upon misconception of law. Taking any step by misinterpretation of the judgment of this Court, which is the integral part of the Constitution, tantamount to a serious disobedience to this Court and ultimately to the Constitution and creates serious bottleneck in the property adjudication of the administration of justice. Especially when such interpretation is coming from a respectable officer like Senior Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Land which is the highest executive Office relating to land of the Country. It appears that in numerous decisions Their Lordships of our Apex Court time and again reminded that after finality there is no scope to release any land from acquisition especially after payment of compensation but it appears in the instant proceeding that time and again by violating the direction made by their Lordships in numerous decisions the Government functionaries are issuing different letters and notifications violating the settled principle of law which seriously affected the administrative function as well as violating the process of law and also violating the provisions of law concerned.

29. In the instant case it appears that though there is a procedure of release under the Act of 1953, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 7 failed to show us any document so far as it relates to the final decision to de-requisition for the land in question by the authority concerned and it appears that such communication started in the years 1960 and notifications was issued in the year of 1990 to 2001 to long after 30 years. In the instant case the Act of 1948 has no manner of application in any manner in a case of Acquisition and requisition by the Town Improvement Act of 1953 but it appears that long after 30 years the impugned notifications were made by a different authority referring the Act of 1948. Under such circumstances we are of the view that the Ministry of hand should not be allowed further to issue such misconceived and arbitrary notifications which causes serious problems in the day to day affairs of land management.

30. Considering the facts and circumstances, the provision of law and the decisions as refereed to, we are of the view that the impugned memo and the notifications passed by the Ministry of Land are illegal, malafide and made without lawful authority. All the impugned notifications are hereby set aside and declared to be illegal and are also declared to have been taken without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

31. Thus the Rules issued in Writ Petition Nos. 5198 of 2003,11817,11818,11819 all of 2006 and 3466 of 2007 are made absolute without any order as to cost.

32. Let a copy of the Judgment be forwarded to the Secretary, Ministry of Land, Government of Bangladesh, Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh, Chairman, RAJUK as well as to the Officer the Chief Advisor of the Caretaker Government for information and taking necessary steps in this regard.

End.

lawyer:
AFM Mezbah Uddin Senior Advocate with Oziullah and Kamal Hossain, Advocates ------ For the Petitioners. 
Nurul Amin Senior Advocate with Md Ramzan Ali Sikder Advocate --------- For the Opposite-Party Nos. 1-2.
parties:
Md. Nurul Islam and others ---------- Petitioners
VS
Md. Abul Kashem and others ------- Respondent-Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
On an application under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, this Rule was issued at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 6-5-2018 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 170 of 2017 disallowing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 19-9-2017 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 11 of 2017 should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 11 of 2017 against the petitioners as defendant for a decree of permanent injunction restraining the defendants from obstructing the plaintiff from using the pathway measuring 53'.6" fit x 12'.6" running from east to west, stating that the property originally belonged to one Sheikh Anwar Ali who purchased the same from one Sri Showmendra Mohan by sale deed No. 1209 dated 13-2-1952. The said Sheikh Anwar Ali died leaving his wife Jebunnesa Begum and son Sheikh Golam Rahman. The said Golam Rahman and Jebunnesa by 4 (four) separate sale deeds dated 28-6-1974 transferred the property measuring 0750 sataks to the plaintiffs and 0750 sataks to defendant Nos. 1 and 2. In the deeds of the defendants there has been a covenant that the plaintiffs shall have right of pathway over the north side of the property transferred to the defendants measuring 53'6" x 8' ft and the said property is not transferable by the defendants to anybody.

3. Accordingly, the plaintiffs have been enjoying the said road as mentioned in the sale deeds of both the parties. Subsequently, by two separate deeds dated 24-1-1987 both plaintiffs and defendants again purchased 0.0055 sataks of land each from Golam Rahman and her mother. The plaintiffs claimed that the property purchased by the defendants on 24-1-1987 measuring 0.0055 sataks is situated north side of the existing road and it was purchased for the purpose of widening the existing road. But the defendants in violation of the terms as contained in their sale deeds dated 28-6-1974 most illegally entered into an agreement with the developer, defendant No. 5 Ambit Builders Ltd. for construction of a multistoried building for the entire property purchased by them including the land on which the pathway is existing and the developer after entering into the agreement for development of the property obtained sanction and approval of the building plan from RAJUK showing the entire land measuring 0.804 sataks without excluding the land of the pathway. After obtaining sanction from RAJUK the developer defendant No. 5 started construction of the building encroaching the existing road and obstructing the plaintiffs from using the said road specifically prescribed for them.

4. The plaintiffs raised objection and requested the defendants not to encroach the road and obstruct smooth enjoyment of the road in question but they did not pay any heed to their requests. Consequently, the plaintiffs filed the instant suit for a decree of permanent injunction against the defendants not to obstruct or create any hindrance or disturbances in smooth enjoyment of the road in question. In the suit the plaintiffs filed an application under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure ("CPC") praying for temporary injunction against the defendants. The trial court issued notice to show cause to the defendants who appeared in suit and filed written objection. The trial court though heard the application for injunction but disposed of the same by a short order directing both the parties to the suit to maintain status quo in respect of the suit pathway.

5. The defendants being aggrieved filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 170 of 2017 wherein they filed an application for stay operation of the order passed by the trial court. The lower appellate court stayed the order of status quo passed by the trial court. Against the said order the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 112 of 2018 before this Court and prayed for stay. This Court issued Rule and stayed operation of the order passed by the lower appellate court. Against the said order the defendants moved before the Appellate Division. Appellate Division kept the appeal stand over for one week and directed the appellant petitioners to get the matter heard before the High Court Division. During pendency of the civil revision, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the lower appellate court and disallowed the appeal maintaining order of status quo passed by the trial court by the impugned judgment and order.

6. At this juncture the defendant appellant petitioners moved this Court by filing this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule and order of stay.

7. The plaintiff opposite parties entered into appearance and contested the Rule by filing counter affidavit contending, inter alia, that since 1974 the plaintiffs uninterruptedly without any disturbance from any quarter using and enjoying the suit pathway measuring 53'.6" x 8' ft. Thereafter, for widening the said pathway the defendants by a deed dated 24-1-1987 again purchased 0.0055 sataks of land from original owners which is situated just north side of the existing pathway measuring 53'6" x 4'6" ft. The plaintiffs in addition to the existing 8' ft road along with subseqiuently purchased 4½' ft land measuring 12½' ft width have been using as their pathway till today. The defendants in violation of terms and conditions as contained in their deeds dated 20-8-1974 most unfortunately entered into an agreement with the developer, the defendant No. 5 for development of the property by constructing multi-storied building without excluding the property prescribed for pathway of the plaintiffs. And the developer obtained building plan showing the entire land as land of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 which they cannot do as per their deeds as well as existing condition of the suit property. It is also stated that the defendant No. 5 by using their force trying to encroach the existing road under which all the facilities such as WASA, Telephone and Gas line have been installed and, as such, they prayed for an order of injunction. Both the courts below considering the facts and circumstances as well as balance of convenience and finding prima facie case in favour of the plaintiffs granted an order of status quo directing both the parties which in fact caused no harm and or injustice to the parties to the suit.

8. Mr AFM Mezbah Uddin, Senior Advocate with Mr Oziullah and Mr Kamal Hossain, Advocates appearing for the petitioners submit that admittedly the disputed property along with non-suited property belong to present petitioners who purchased the same in the year 1974. But there is a condition in the purchase deed that the plaintiffs will have the right of use of the pathway running from east to west measuring 53'6" x 8' ft just north side of the petitioners' property. Accordingly as per sale deed 53'6" x 8' ft road is now existing and the plaintiffs are using the same. He further submits that there is no dispute about the pathway described in the deeds of the parties. But subsequently on 24-1-1997 by deed No. 358 the petitioners purchased 0055 sataks of land from the original owner Golam Rahman and others. The said property is the adjacent property of the petitioners and it is not part and parcel of the existing pathway at all.
