But the plaintiffs taking advantage of existing pathway as mentioned in the deeds of the year 1974 tried to claim that the property purchased in the year 1987 by the petitioners was for the purpose of widening the road for their use. It is absolute unbelievable and beyond the probability that the petitioners by their own money purchased the land for the benefit and use of the plaintiffs who already got a pathway on the property of the petitioners. He further goes to submits that the plaintiffs never raised any dispute regarding width of the pathway of the plaintiffs but while the plaintiff entered into agreement for development of the property with the defendant No. 5, developer the plaintiffs with a view to harass the petitioners and create disturbance most unfortunately raised a claim that the property purchased by the petitioners in the year 1987 is part of the pathway and the plaintiffs have been using the same as integral part of the existing road and on that claim they filed the present suit for injunction though in the cause title it has been described that the suit is for declaration and injunction. He further argued that a suit for injunction claiming easement right is not maintainable without prayer for a declaration of that right. It is also submitted that the trial court in its impugned order discussed no case of the parties and without disposing the application on merit passed the impugned order merely saying "both the parties are directed to maintain status quo in respect of the pathway". The appellate court also without going through the present position of the suit land and appreciating the case of the petitioners disallowed the appeal affirming the order passed by the trial court.

9. It is argued that in disposing an application for injunction the courts below ought to have framed issues to the effect that whether the plaintiffs have a good prima facie case, balance of conveniences and whether in the event of refusing injunction the plaintiffs shall suffer irreparable loss. Both the courts below in passing the impugned orders did not follow the principles enunciated for granting injunction. As such, the order under challenged is liable to be set-aside.

10. Mr Nurul Amin, learned Senior Advocate with Mr Md Ramzan Ali Sikder, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that, this is a case relating to pathway of the plaintiffs. Both the parties admit that there is a pathway as mentioned in the deed of the petitioner-defendants. It is not the case of the parties that the plaintiffs are not using the pathway since their purchase in the year 1974. Mr Nurul Amin further submits that the sale deed of the petitioners clearly shows that a pathway measuring 53'.6" x 8' ft kept open just northern side of the petitioners' land for use of the plaintiffs. Subsequently, for widening of the pathway of the plaintiffs, as well as the defendants both the parties by two separate sale deeds dated 24-1-1997 purchased 0055 sataks land each from the original owner and the said property situated just northern side of the existing road. As per deed of the petitioners the plaintiffs-opposite parties are entitled to use and enjoy the pathway and the petitioners are entitled to construct building on the land excluding the land prescribed for the road. But the present petitioners in violation of the terms and conditions of the sale deed of the year 1974 entered into an agreement with the defendant No. 5 developer for the entire property covered by the sale deeds of the year 1974 and 1987 which they cannot do.

11. He further submits that taking advantage of giving entire property to the developer by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 the defendant No. 5 obtained a building plan on the property showing entire land to be the land of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 but in fact after exclusion of the property covered by the pathway the defendants are entitled to get sanction or approval of building plan only on 0.0654 sataks of land not on the land measuring 0.804 sataks. It is also argued that had the defendants given the property to the developer excluding the land of the existing pathway there would not have arisen any dispute regarding pathway of the plaintiffs. He further goes to submits that the defendant No. 5, developer obtained building plan from RAJUK on the property beyond entitlement of the defendants. If the developer is allowed to continue with the construction work and to build the building, violating the Rules in this regard, the pathway of the plaintiffs will be absolutely obstructed and, as such, to prevent abuse of the process of the court and multiplicity of suits the trial court considering facts and circumstances of the case granted an order of status quo directing both the parties which in no manner caused injustice to anybody including the defendants. The appellate court maintained the order of the trial court by disposing the application on merit holding that the defendants admitted existence of a pathway to be enjoyed and used by the plaintiffs and, as such, defendants ought to have excluded the said property from their agreement entered with the defendant No. 5. As such, both the courts below rightly passed the order directing the parties to maintain status quo. In support of his submissions he has referred to the case of Sikam Fashion Ltd. vs Miaco Ltd. reported in 10 BLT (AD) 39 (para 4).

12. Heard the learned Advocates for the parties, have gone though the revisional application, impugned judgment and order of both the courts below, plaint in suit, application for injunction along with other annexures, such as, the sale deeds of the parties, agreement executed in between the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 5 annexed thereto.

13. In the present suit both the parties admitted that the plaintiffs got a pathway over the property purchased by the defendants in suit. The pathway is admittedly measuring 53'.6" x 8' ft. running from east to west. Further case of the plaintiff is that the defendants by a sale deed dated 24-1-1987 purchased 0055 sataks land from the same plot situated in the north of the existing pathway and the defendants are trying to build the proposed building by encroaching the said strip of land which is the part and parcel of the existing pathway of the plaintiffs. By a sketch map the plaintiff-opposite party tried to impress upon the court that the property purchased by the defendants in the year 1987 is situated just adjacent north to the existing road and not adjacent to the land of the defendants as per boundary given in the deed of the year 1987 and, as such, the defendant cannot extend proposed building by encroaching over the existing road. On the other hand the petitioner-defendants submit that the property purchased in the year 1987 is the property situated just adjacent north to the defendants present land and adjacent south to the existing pathway and the property in question was never purchased for widening the pathway. It is also claimed that the sale deed of the year 1987 does not say and disclose any such condition that the property purchased for the widening of the road like the sale deed of the year 1974.

14. Had it been purchased for the purpose of widening the road there must have been a condition in the sale deed like the deed of the year 1974. It is also claimed that it is unusual that the defendants on their own initiative and with their own money purchased some quantum of land for the benefit of the plaintiffs instead of purchasing the same by the plaintiffs. From the papers and documents available in record this Court finds that there is no dispute regarding a pathway measuring 53'.6" x 8' ft but the dispute is whether the property purchased by the defendants on 24-1-1987 is the adjacent land to the north of the plaintiffs pathway and whether the property measuring 53'.6" x 4½' is lying just north side of the existing road as claimed by the plaintiffs. In this situation unless the position of the property is inspected or investigated physically by an Advocate Commissioner appointed by the court and obtained report thereof it cannot be said that the present existing road is measuring 12' ft or 8' ft width.

15. Both the courts below while disposing the application for injunction failed to ascertain present position of the suit pathway and to consider the admission made by the plaintiffs in last part of paragraph No. 11 of the plaint in suit to the effect that the plaintiffs have already been dispossessed from 21' x 3' width land in question much before filing of the suit. Moreover, from the annxures 3 and 4 annexed to the counter affidavit, the agreement entered in between the developer defendant No. 5 and irrevocable power of attorney executed by the defendants empowering the defendant No. 5 show that the defendants executed the said agreement and power of attorney for entire property covered by deeds dated 28-6-1974 and 24-1-1987 without excluding the property covered by pathway and showing existence of the pathway in question which led both the courts below to find that the defendants in violation of the terms of the sale deed executed the agreement with the developer for the entire property which they cannot do and considering such aspect the appellate court in the impugned order has observed that the defendants ignoring the existence of the pathway and excluding the property covered by it executed the agreement for entire property which compelled the plaintiffs filing of the present suit and found an arguable case in favour of the plaintiffs. This court finds that there is a dispute between the parties regarding present position of the existing road and its measurement. I think that the length and width of the existing road and its position is required to be ascertained first and without ascertaining the present position of the disputed pathway, effective disposal of the application for injunction as well as the suit could not be done.

<u>16. In view of the above observations this Court thinks that it would be justified and justice will be met if a direction is given to the trial court to hold an investigation of the suit pathway to ascertain its present measurement and position by appointing an Advocate Commissioner and to hear the application for injunction afresh giving both the parties opportunity of being heard maintaining the order of status quo till disposal of the injunction matter.</u>

17. In the result, the Rule is disposed of with the direction given above, without any order as to costs.

18. The trial court is, hereby, directed to dispose of the injunction application after holding local investigation or inspection within 1 (one) month from the date of receipt of this judgment and order without fail.

19. Communicate a copy of this judgment and order to the court concerned.

Order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule stands vacated.

End.

lawyer:
Rukonuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate with Tanzibul Alam Advocates ------- For the Petitioner. 
Rafiqul Haque, Senior Advocate ------- For the Respondents No.3.
parties:
Rokeya Akhter Begum ------- Petitioner
VS
Bangladesh and others --------- Respondents
full_judgment:
AHM Shamsuddin Chowdhury J : The Rule under review was issued at the instance of one Rokeya Akhtar Begum, who, the incumbent Acting Principal of the celebrated institute named, Viqarunnisa Noon School and College, being aggrieved by a commercial, published in Daily Ittefaq, dated 8th March 2010, through which the Chairman of the Governing Body of the aforementioned institute, respondent No. 3, invited applications from potential candidates with a view to appoint the regular Principal for the institute.

2. By the Rule, the respondents were asked to show cause as to why the respondent No. 2's failure to prevent the respondent No. 3 from acting in derogation to the contents in the tenure of job extension approval letter, bearing Memo No. 43/ka/she/84 (ansha-2) /2029, dated 15-1-2009 issued by the respondent No. 2, and the impugned decision taken at the meeting dated 21-3-2010, by the respondent No. 3 and, the impugned decision to issue advertisement, seeking application from potential candidates to fill in the post of the Principal for Viqarunnisa Noon School and College and, the notice of employment published in Daily Ittefaq on 8-3-2010, with a view to recruit the Principal for the said institute, shall not be declared to have been done illegally, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

3. The petitioner's grievance was hurled at the fact, and it is her complaint, that since she was appointed as the "Acting Principal" for a fixed term of two years, with effect from 31 January 2008, it was beyond the competence of the authorities to dislodge her from that position before the stipulated period expires.

4. She averred that she had been in the concerned institute's teaching employment for as many as 32 years, inputting her best efforts, in consequence of which she earned the fame of a well reputed teacher. In recognition of her experience, competence, efficiency and ability, the respondent No.3, assigned upon her the duty of the Acting Principalship in the event of the departure of the incumbent Principal with effect from 31st January 2008.

5. As she was due to retire on 6th February 2009, having reached the age of 60 years, the aforementioned respondent, reckoning her outstanding performance etc., at it's meeting dated 10th January 2009 resolved to place her retirement in abeyance for a period of two years, i.e. upto the 6th February 2011. This decision was transmitted to the Secondary and Higher Secondary Education Board, Dhaka, the respondent No. 2, which body obliged the respondent No. 3 by according approval of the said proposal for extension which factum was signified by the respondent No. 2 vide its aforementioned communication dated 15th January 2009. The undermentioned conditions were embodied in the said extension approving Memo:

(a)	Viqarunnisa Noon School and College will provide salary after she attains the age of 60.

(b)	Viqarunnisa Noon School and College will appoint a full time Principal as per the Government regulations as soon as possible and will intimate the respondent No. 2 of the same.

(c)	The respondent No. 2 may cancel such approval if that creates any legal complication.

6. Having procured the extension, the petitioner continued with her duties to the satisfaction of all concerned. On 8th March 2009, however, she was taken by a total surprise viewing the advertisement in question. It is her complaint that the respondent No. 3's attempt to recruit a new regular Principal, when the petitioner was performing her duties with almost competence, and when extension of her tenure attracted no complication, was not only  illegal, but was also reflective of malafide consideration.

7. She insisted that because of her competence, the students of the institute had done extraordinarily well in the SSC and HSC examinations, yet the respondent No. 3 and its Chair exerted pressure upon her to bear to admit students of their choice and it is because of her declination to give in to their pressure, that she fell out of their favour, and hence their decision to appoint a new Principal in her substitution, notwithstanding the subsistence of the period for which she was accorded extension. She directed legal notice to the respondents but with no avail, and hence this petition.

8. Very comprehensive affidavits to rebut the petitioner's assertion and claims were filed by the respondent. No. 3.

9. Their primordial contention is rooted at the question of maintainability of the petition, as they reckon that the Governing Body of non-government institution cannot be subjected to judicial review under Article 102 of the our Constitution, because such an institute is neither a government body nor a local authority.

10. Admitting that the petitioner's length of service was extended by two years when she approached her normal retirement age as on 6th February 2009, with the approval of the respondent No. 2, they do nevertheless bank upon the fact that one of the conditions, subject to which the respondent No. 2 accorded approval was that the respondent No. 3 would appoint a regular Principal without delay and that by inviting applications through the impugned commercial, the respondent No. 2 simply acted to comply with the aforesaid condition.

11. They further averred that the respondent No. 2 is equipped with no legal power to compel the respondent No. 3 to refrain from removing the petitioner and hence, her claim is misconceived.

12. They also disclosed that the petitioner herself responded to the impugned commercial and applied for the job of the regular Principal though she was not qualified to be inducted to the post because of her age.

13. They further asserted that the petitioner applied for extension as an Assistant Professor, which is her basic post, not for an extension as the Acting Principal and that the position of Acting Principal being of temporary duration, cannot be extended and hence, the petitioner's claim that the tenure of her job was extended as Principal, is not reflective of the reality, and is devoid of substance.

14. They insist that the respondent No. 3, with the approval by the respondent No.2, under the relevant regulation extended the petitioner's tenure only to work as an Assistant Professor, not a the Acting Principal.

15. As the Rule matured for consideration, M Rukonuddin Mahmud, the learned Senior Advocate made appearance for the petitioner, while Mr Rafiqul Haque, the learned Senior Advocate represented the respondent No.3.

16. Mr Mahmud, toeing the line laid down in the petition, submitted that once the respondents extended the petitioner's job for a fixed term, they lost their liberty to remove her before the efflux of the term so fixed. He was rather vehement in arguing that the claim that extension was not as Acting Principal, was a fallacy. He drew our attention to the extension granting resolution and the approval that it secured. He also submitted with commendable vigor and his characteristic aura of oration and rhetoric, that in deciding the question of judicial reviewability, the status of the body concerned is of little relevance as it is the nature of the function of the body that matters.

According to him the respondent No. 3 is amenable to judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution because the function it performs is of public nature. He did also remind us that what the petitioner has challenged, and the terms on which the Rule was issued, was the passivity of the respondent No.2, which is undoubtedly a public functionary any way.

17. Mr Rafiqul Haque, in his turn, with equally forceful and florid eloquence and exhibition of persuasion, put greater emphasis on the question of the respondent No. 3's amenability to judicial review. He was emphatic that it is essentially the respondent No. 3's decision to appoint a new Principal which has been challenged and that the said respondent, not being a statutory functionary, cannot be subjected to writ jurisdiction.

18. On the factual side he followed the line of argument as have been inscripted in his client's affidavits to the effect that the petitioner's tenure was extended for the post of Assistant Professor, not for that of the Acting Principal.

19. Perusal of papers divulged to us that the Rule was issued on two terms, namely whether the respondent No. 2 by persistently failing to restrain the respondent No. 3 from the latter's move to appoint a regular principal, adhered to unlawfulness and, secondly whether the Governing Body itself have acted unlawfully by inviting application from potential candidates for the Principal's job.

20. The first issue is indeed quite a narrow one. It is only the second issue that calls for in-depth consideration.

21. To address the first issue, all we need to do is to analyse the acts resorted to by the respondent No. 3, which, according to the petitioner, the respondent No. 2 should have put a stumbling block on, whereas to address the second leg of the Rule, we are really required to examine the reviewability of the decision of the Governing Body, i.e. the respondent No. 3. If either issue is answered in the affirmative, the Rule will merit to receive absoluteness.

22. Facts, as admitted, reveal that, the respondent No. 3, by it's decision dated 6th February 2009, resolved to extend the tenure of the petitioner's job for a period of two years to end on 6th February 2011. This was done pursuant to petitioner's application to that effect just before her normal retirement fell due.

23. It is crystal clear from the document annexed as Annexure 1 to the respondents No. 3's supplementary affidavit at page 13 that the petitioner sought extension as an Assistant Professor, though at the relevant time she was performing the job of the Acting Principal simultaneously.

24. At this point it is incumbent to dissect the legal provisions by which the government retains control over the terms and conditions of services of the teachers of private institutions like the instant one. The same is figured in a secondary legislation titled, "The Reorganized non-Government Intermediate College Teachers (The Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka) Terms and conditions of Service Regulation 1979, which had been framed under power conferred by "Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961" pursuant" to which the Board regulates the terms and conditions of service of such teachers.

25. Regulation 27 of the said subordinate legislation is the pertinent one as that determines the question of a teacher's extension beyond the date of his/her retirement. Under this regulation, reproduced below, the Governing Body of the institute concerned can resolve to extend the employment period of a teacher beyond her birthday, on which he would, unless extended, retire.

26. Regulation 27 reads:

(1) A teacher may, in exceptional circumstances, be allowed extension in service of the college on receipt of prayer from the teacher concerned.

(2) In the case of Principal, the Board on the recommendation of the Governing Body by two thirds majority, in the case of other teachers, the Chairman of the Board on the recommendation of the Governing Body may grant the extension of service to a teacher under sub-regulation (I).

(3) The grant of extension under the regulation shall be subject to the following conditions, namely:

(a) no extension shall be granted beyond the age of 65 years.

(b) no extension shall be granted for a period of more than two years at a time; and

(c) no extension shall be granted unless a certificate of physical and mental fitness is produced by the teacher from a registered medical practitioner approved by the Governing body.

27. So, what is clear from Regulation 27 is that the extension cannot be granted suo moto, but only on an application preferred by the extension seeker. This necessarily follows that the Board, at the recommendation of the Governing Body can, in exceptional circumstances, grant extension for the post applied for. Hence, in so far as the petitioner applied for extension as an Assistant Professor, it was beyond the respondent No. 2's power to grant extension as the Acting Principal. The fact that the extension granting letter required the respondent No. 3 to recruit a regular principal as soon as possible, further vindicates said respondent's claim that extension was granted for the post of an Assistant Professor, not for the post of Acting Principal. The first issue is thus resolved against the petitioner.

28. This sways us to examine the second leg of the Rule, the more broader question, namely whether the respondent No. 3, a non governmental institute, is susceptible to writ jurisdiction:

29. To locate the correct answer to the dichotomy springing from divergent submission proffered by the learned counsels of the respective parties, we have examined the legal concept in juxtaposition with authorities of unimpeachable preponderance both from the English as well as our own and Indian jurisdiction, discussed below. We have also endeavoured to trace the embryogenesis and the gestation of the Prerogative Writs in nutshell to underscore the trend of their development to the present position, expecting that to shed a flood of light as to their ambit and applicability with undistorted precision.

30. The origin of the Writs of Certiorari, Mandamus and Prohibition can be traced in such antiquities as the Common Law itself, more precisely, during the reign of Henry II, in the 12th century. By these Writs the Monarch, through the Star Chamber and the Court of King's- Bench kept the inferior bodies within their power.

31. In the earliest times, the Royal Writs were sealed governmental documents, drafted in a crisp, business like manner, by which the King conveyed notification or orders (Van Caenegem Royal Writs in England from the conquest to Glanville: Studies in the early history of common Law, Seldom Society, 1959).

32. From the earliest times proceedings in the local courts and the local communities, as well as those instituted before borough courts were removable into the Kings Court at Westminster (Holsworth, History of English Law, II, 395). Usurpation of authorities by municipal corporation gave rise to activities to impugn the validity of byelaws (ibid 398). Quo-Warrant proceedings, and later, applications for Writs of Scare Fascias were also aimed at the borough councils. 33. When the Justices of the Peace emerged as the principal organ of local administration, the court of Kings Bench, which, of all common law courts, was most closely connected with the business of government, assumed superintendence over their proceedings, a superintendence that was facilitated by the fact that the administrative functions of the' Justices of the Peace were discharged in a judicial form.

34. It was not, however, until the 17th century that what was to become the modem concept of judicial review, took shape (Edith G Henderson, Foundation of English Administrative Law, 1963).

35. The word "Certiorari", a derivative of the phrase "certify", was essentially a Royal demand for information, the King wishing to be 'certified' of some matter, orders, that the necessary information be provided for him. Thus the King wished to be more fully informed of allegations of extortion made by his subjects in Lincoln and thereafter appointed Commissioners to inquire into them (Placitorum Abbreviation 155 49 Hen 3).

36. From about 1280, the judicial forms of the Writ of Certiorari' were in common use, issued on the application of ordinary litigants (Seldon Soe-Vo/s 55, 57, 58, 74, 76, 82 and 88 edited by GD Sayles).

37. Certiorari was historically associated with the King' s person as well as with the King's Bench; it was of high importance for the control of inferior tribunals, particularly with respect to the administration of criminal justice. It was a writ of course for the King but not for the subjects. The concept has been lucidly expressed in a modern Canadian Case in following terms:

"The theory is that the sovereign has been appealed to by someone of his subjects who complains of an injustice done to him by an inferior court, whereupon the sovereign, saying that he wishes to be certified certiorari of the matter, orders that the record etc. be transmitted into a court in which he is sitting (R vs Titchmarsh, 1915, 22 DLR 272).

38. During the Tudor period, by the middle of the 17th Century, these Writs firmly received Prerogative characteristic, though it was not until 1759 that they were classified as a group by Mansfied (R vs Lowle 1759, 2 Bnrn 834, which case seems to be the first one where reference to a "Certiorari" as a "Prerogative Writ", used to correct the errors of the Justices of the Peace, was made). "When in 17th and 18th century the term 'Prerogative' was applied to the Writ, this was because they were considered to be closely connected with the rights of the Crown; no doubt it was the reason they issued chiefly from the King's Bench Court." (De Smith, Judicial Review, apple).

39. Bracton described the emergent Court as 'Aula Regea, where the King's justice 'praprias causa Regis terminant (De Legibus f150 b). The origin of the term "Prerogative" is attributable to the political inclination of certain judges in the 17th century who sought to associate themselves with the King's personal solicitude. Mansfield and Bracton were responsible, if not for the invention of the 'Prerogative Writ', at least for it's acceptance as part of the lawyers' vocabulary.

40. During the late Tudor and early Stewart period the Writ of Certiorari frequently issued to bring the proceedings of inferior Courts of Common Law before the Chancellor. From the 14th to the 17th century the main purpose of Certiorari had been, in addition to controlling the functions of the Justices of the Peace, to supervise proceedings of inferior tribunals of specialized jurisdiction such as Commissioners of Swear, Courts of Merchants, Courts of Admiralty, Courts of Forest, to obtain information for administrative purposes, for example, to direct the Sherif to find out whether one who has been granted the 'King's protection in tarrying in the city, instead of journing forth in the King's service', the Escheator to certify into the Chancery the value of the Knights, to bring into the Chancery or the Common Law Courts judicial records for wide diversity of purposes, to remove Coroners' investigation and indictments into the King's Bench and so on.

41. One casualty of the 17th century constitutional conflict was the use of executive organ i.e. the Kings Council and the Star Chamber to enable the national government to control the acts of the local officials, most importantly those of the Justices of the Peace, who were the most important functionaries in the local tiers of administration. With them the enforcement of criminal Law and the local administration were inextricably blended. Executive power were usually performed in judicial form. So in R vs Glamorganshire Inhabitants (1700, 1Ld. Raym 580), rate levied by county Justices of the Peace to pay for repairs to a bridge was reviewed by having recourse to Prerogative Writ.

42. During the 18th and early 19th century there was little administrative or political control over the activities of the Justices of the Peace, but their exercise of power could be challenged in the courts of Kings Bench by recourse to the Prerogative Writs.

43. By the first half of the 19th century a reaction set in against prevalent tendency to treat nearly all of an inferior courts finding as touching it's jurisdictions which made it possible to construct a coherent theory of the concept of jurisdiction without which the scope of judicial review would have been seriously limited.

44. When new departments of central government emerged, towards the end of the 19th Century, the court of Kings Bench extended its controlling jurisdiction to include them as well.

45. Since all these bodies were exercising statutory powers, it was natural that disputes about the limits of their power should be settled by the courts by recourse to Prerogative Writs. Thus it was that judicial control which originally served to check the powers of inferior courts, which was adapted to review the exercise of statutory powers first by the local authorities and then, in the 20th Century, by Ministers of the Crown (Board of Education vs Rice 1911 AC 179, Local Government Board vs Aldridge (1915 AC 120).

46. Though with the passage of time, particularly towards the end of the 19th century, the court of King's Bench spread it's wings to bring under it supervisory control, by resorting to Prerogative Writs, the local authorities and the departments of central government, which, as the House of Lords stated in the case of Draymond vs South West Water Authorities (1976 AC 609), was "a long step from reviewing the rate levied by the Justices of the Peace to reviewing statutory regulations made by a Secretary of State", yet, in principle it is the same kind of control which the courts exercise, even today, whether they are reviewing a point of law raised in the Magistrates courts or the excess of jurisdiction by a government department or a local authority.

47. As early as 1922, the House of Lords held, "That supervision goes to two points, one is the area of inferior jurisdiction and the qualification and conditions of it's exercise; the other is the observance of the law in the course of it's exercise" (R vs Not Bell Liquors Ltd. 1922 Act 128).

48. It is obvious from the history of the development of the doctrine of judicial review that traditionally it only applied to public, as opposed to private law domain. The existence of a divide separating public and private law, according to jurists of acclaimable standing, probably causes greater controversies and. it is not always easy to erect an acceptable fence between the two. The distinction between the public and the private law plays a crucial role in determining (1) when it is necessary to bring proceeding by way of judicial review and; (2) by whom and against whom proceedings which raise public law issue can be brought.

49. For a great many years the way the courts have identified activities which are subject to law is by deciding whether or not they are activities to which the High Courts supervisory jurisdiction through judicial review may be invoked by an aggrieved person. In the past it was mainly done by asking what was the source of the power being exercised by the decision maker whose action was impugned. Where the power was statutory or derived from Prerogative, no problem to invoke judicial review would occur. Where, however, the power did not emanate from an Act of Parliament, a Prerogative or a Delegated Legislation, judicial review, generally, was not available. Prof. (Sir) Wade and Prof Forsyth's following expression, represents the traditional as well as the changed view:

"Judicial Review is designed to prevent access and abuse of power and neglect of duty by public authorities. In the past there was clear test for determining the limits of the Courts' jurisdiction: power meant power conferred by Parliament. The law, however, has been driven from these familiar moorings by the impetus of expanding judicial review which has been expanded to two kinds of non-statutory actions. One is where the bodies are unquestionably governmental, do things for which no statutory power is necessary, such as issuing circulars or other forms of information. The other category is where judicial review is extend to bodies, which by the traditional test, would not be subject to judicial review, and which, in some cases, fall outside the sphere the government altogether. A variety of commercial, professional, sporting and other activities are regulated by powerful bodies which are devoid of statutory status and may yet have an effective monopoly. In their willingness to 'recognise the realities of executive powers' (per Lord Donaldson MR in Take-Over Panel case, below) and their desire to prevent it's abuse, the Courts have undertaken to review the decisions of a number of such bodies, while in others they have refused". (Administrative Law, 9th Edition, page 638). The said learned authors went on to say, "This judicial forays into areas beyond the law have constitutional implication. The rule of law now operates in territory previously supposed to be beyond it's reach." (page 639).

50. So, today the English courts have come to recognize that the traditional approach is too restrictive and instead of ' looking at the source of the power exclusively they are now inclined to analyse the type of function performed by the decision maker as well (R vs Panel on Take over and Merger, exparte Datafin PLC (1987 QB 815). So, where a body is carrying out a public function, such as that undertaken by a non-government regulatory organization in relation to an area of activity, which is subject to its control, the courts will consider intervening to require compliance with the principles of judicial review. This is so, even if the body is non- statutory, exercising powers which are not derived either from legislation or Prerogative.

51. There are, hence, presently, two kinds of situation namely source or origin based situation and function based situation that enjoy recognition by the English courts. (Lloyd LJ expressed in "Panel of Take over " case, supra. "I do not agree that the source of power is the sole test whether a body is subjected to judicial review.)"

52. Source or origin based approaches needs no explication as they are axiomatic. The "function based approach" is erected on the theme that a body performs "public function" when it seeks to achieve some collective benefit for the public or a section of the public and is accepted by the public, or section thereof, as having authority to do so. In the case of P. ,elf-regulatory body, the general consent to the exercise of it's power by business in a particular sector establishes it's legitimacy.

53. Lloyd LJ in Panel on Take-Over, expressed, "But in between these extremes there is an area in which it is helpful to look not just at the source of the power but at the nature of the power. If the body in question is exercising public law functions, or if the exercise of its function have public law consequences, then that may, as Mr Lever submitted, be sufficient to bring the body within the reach of judicial review. It may be said that to refer to "public law" in this context is to beg the question. But I do not think it does. The essential distinction, which runs through all the cases to which we referred, is between a domestic or private tribunal on the one hand and a body of persons who are under some public duty on the other." He went on saying, "So I would reject Mr Alexander's argument that the sole test whether a body is subject to judicial review is the source of it's power. So to hold in my judgment impose an artificial limit on the developing law of judicial review."

54. This may happen in a wide variety of ways. For instance a body is performing a public function when it provides 'public goods' or other collective services, such as health care, education and personal social services, from fund raised by taxation. They may also do so, if they regulate commercial and professional activities to ensure compliance with proper standard. Public functions need not be the exclusive domain of the state. Charities, self-regulatory organizations and other nominally private institutions such as universities, the stock exchange, religious ecclesiastical bodies, may also perform some types of public function. As Sir Gordon Borrie observed, "non-governmental bodies such as these are just as capable of abusing their powers as is government". (Regulation of Public and Private Power 1989 PL 552).

55. Hence such private, non-governmental bodies like IMRO, FIMBRA, and LAUTRO, which were officially recognized under the Financial Services 'Act, 1986, for regulating sectors of financial markets, were part of a statutory system, were held to be amenable to judicial review; although their own powers or source of power were not statutory (Bank of Scotland vs Investment Management Regulatory Organizations Ltd. 1989 SLT 432). Decisions of Stock- Exchange, were likewise held reviewable (R vs International Stoc: Exchange of the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland Ltd. Ex-parte Else, (1993 QB 534).

56. In the case of R vs Press Complaints Commission ex-parte Stewart Brady, (1997,, 9 Admin LR 274), as well as in the case of R vs Code of Practice Committee of the British Pharmaceutical Industry ex-partf Professional Counselling Aids Ltd. (1990, 3 Admin LR 697), the High Court held that notwithstanding absence of statutory foundation, decision of these bodies were reviewable as they had public law elements.

57. The prevailing English judicial view is that as it is through the principles of judicial review that the rule of law and other constitutional principles are given practical effect, the supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court should ensure that bodies, whether nominally public or private, when performing public functions, comply with the law and achieve acceptable standard of administration.

58. Subsequent to the decision in the tide turning case of R vs Panel on Take- Over and Mergers, ex-parte Datafin PLc, (supra) where the question of a private body's amenability to judicial review was extensively and intensively explored, English Courts went on to elaborate a variety of overlapping criteria designed to particularize the broad based functional approach, enunciated by Sir Donaldson MR in the above cited case. They include the following tests:

(1) The "but for" test i.e., whether but for the existence of a non- statutory body, the government would itself almost inevitably have intervened to regulate the activity in question (R vs Advertising Standard Authority ex parte Insurance Service PLC, 1990 2 Admin LR 77 DC, where Lord Justice Glide well stated that in the absence of the Advertising Standard Authority, its function, would, no doubt, be exercised by a government functionary).

(2) Whether the government has acquiesced or encouraged the activities of the body under challenge by providing "underpinning" for it's works, has woven the body into the fabric of public regulation (as observed by Sir Thomas Bingham MR in R vs Disciplinary Committee of the Jockey Club, ex parte Aga Khan 1993 1 WLR 909, CA) or that the body was established under the authority of the government (per Lord Justice Lloyd in Panel of Take-Over, supra). Here the question is not what might happen, but what has actually occurred.

(3) Whether the body was exercising extensive or monopolistic powers, for instance, by effectively regulating entry into a trade, profession or sport.

(4) Whether the aggrieved person consensually submitted to be bound. (Reproduced from "Principles of Judicial Review" by De Smith, Woolf of Jowdis, page 68.)

59. Thus, the functions of Criminal Injuries Compensation Board, a non-statutory body, constituted merely administratively, to compensate victims of violent crimes, was held to be reviewable in R vs Criminal Injuries Compensation Board, ex parte Lavin (1967 2QB 864). Lord Parker CJ said, "the exact limit of the ancient remedy by way of Certiorari have never been and ought not to be specifically defined and should be extended to meet changing condition."

60. In R vs Panel on Takeover and Mergers, ex-parte Datafin Pic, supra, the Court of Appeal refuted the contention that in view of the Panel's non-statutory character, which is an unincorporated association in the city of London, engaged to monitor rules promulgated by itself, which governs company take overs and mergers and is without a visible source of legal support, having neither statutory nor contractual powers, is not amenable to judicial review. Although it refused to interfere on merit, nevertheless, observed, by recognizing that the Panel was susceptible to judicial review as it wielded immense power de facto, since violation of the code, adjudged by itself, may lead to expulsion from the stock exchange or investigation by the Department of Trade and Industry or other sanction. In expressing a positive view on amenability, Sir Donaldson MR, holding that notwithstanding the Panel's non-governmental status, it performs public duty, expressed, 'I should be very disappointed if the court could not recognise the realities of executive power and allowed their vision to be clouded. Given that it is really unthinkable that an the absence of legislation  the Panel should go cocooned from the attentions of the courts in defence of the citizenry, we sought to investigate whether it could be controlled by established  private law Suffice it to say that the result was wholly unconvincing."

61. Lloyd LJ in that case termed it as "an implied devolution of power" observing, "Possibly the only essential elements are what can be described as a public element, which can take many different forms, and the exclusion from the jurisdiction of bodies whose sole source of power is a consensual submission to their jurisdiction".

62. Subsequent to the innovation of this generous formula by the Court of Appeal through the case of "Panel on Take Over", based on the 'recognition of real executive power' in defining "public element" the English courts intervened to review decisions taken by a host of non-governmental, non-statutory bodies like the General Medical Council (R vs General Medical Council ex-parte Gee 1986, 1 WLR 1247), a private school administered under a trust deed when the impugned dismissal of the governor was carried out by the trustees (R vs Trustees of Roman Catholic Diocese of Westminster, ex-parte Andrew, 1990 COD 25), a voluntary school, whose articles were made under statute (R vs Board of Governor of the London Oratory School, ex-parte Regis, The Times, February 1988) a private City Technology College, which was maintained under an agreement with the Secretary of State under statutory powers, whose refusal to admit pupil was held reviewable (R vs Governors of Haberdashers Aske's Hatcham College Trust, exparte Tyre11, 1995 COD 399 The Times, 19th October 1994), the Advertising Standard Authority, set up by advertising industry for voluntary self-regulation (R vs Advertising Standard Authority ex-parte Insurance Service PLC 1990 2Admin LR 77 and R vs Advertising Standard Authority ex vernous Oganisation Ltd., 1992 1 WLR 1289, where the Court said, if the Advertising Standard Authority had not existed, the government would, no doubt, have acted, like the Take-Over Panel, and that the Authority played a part in a system of governmental control), the Press Complaints Commission, a purely non-statutory body (R vs Press Complaints Commission, 1997 a Admin LR 274), the Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd (R vs Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd, ex-parte Bowden, 1996 AC 261, where the House of Lords stated that though the body concerned is a joint stock company, it is, nonetheless amenable to review because it is charged with administrating the rules of the scheme which are made by the Securities and Investment Board, exercising statutory power delegated to them by the Secretary of State, and, as such, is interwoven with a system of statutory or governmental control, the Institute of Chartered Accountants (R vs Institute of Chartered Accountants, 1998 All BR 14, where the Court observed that, a non statutory though, the Institute performs important responsibilities under the Companies Act 1989), the Life Savings Society (R vs Life Saving Society, ex-parte Heather Mary Rose Howe, 1990 COD 440 in which case the Court of Appeal indicated, obiter, that if the decision of the non-statutory body was not based on contract and if it raised a public law issue, review may be available, although the Court refused to intervene because the applicant was seeking to remedy a private grievance in that she suffered harm to her reputation at the action of the body and hence no public law claim was involved).

63. The English Courts, however, continued with their declination to review decision of bodies whose power are purely based on contracts. Hence, they had refused to review decision of private sporting bodies created by contracting parties like the Jockey Club (R vs Jockey Club ex-parte Massingberd-Mundy 1993, 2 ALL ER 207), (R vs Jockey Club, ex parte Aga Khan, 1993, 1 WLR 909), football Association (R vs Football Association Ltd. ex-parte Football League Ltd. 1993, 2 ALLLR 833), (although in the case of Jones vs Welsh Football Union, (The Times 6th January 1998) the High Court did intervene, and the Court of Appeal affirmed the High Court's decision, saying that sports now being a big business, it would be naive to pretend that it could be kept out of reviewability as used to be the case many years ago.

64. The English courts also refused to intervene in non-governmental ecclesiastical bodies like the Jewish synagogue (R vs Chief Rabbi ex-parte Watchman) and the Muslim Mosque (R vs Imam of Bury Park Jame Masjid ex-parte Sulaiman Ali 1994, COD 142). They also refused to review decision by Greyhound Racing Club (Law vs National Greyhound Racing Club Ltd. 1983 1WLR 1302), Lloyd Corporation's decision (Corporation of Lloyds vs Briggs 1993 1 Lloyds Report 176), by an independent school (R vs Fern hill Manor School ex-parte Brown 1992, 5 Admin LR 159, stating that such schools are, generally, not amenable to judicial review as the relationship between those attending and the school is based on contracts with parents and there is no sufficient statutory underpinning to render their decisions amenable to judicial review).

65. The Rt. Hon'ble The Lord Woolf MR and Prof Jeffrey Jowell in their book "Principles of Judicial Review," summarized the legal position generally and also in respect to contractual matters, in following terms (page 73):

(1) The test of whether a body is performing a public function, and is hence amenable to judicial review, may not depend upon the source of its power or whether the body is ostensibly a "public" or a "private " body.

(2) The principles of judicial review prima facie govern the activities of bodies performing public functions.

(3) However, not all decisions taken by bodies in the course of their public functions are the subject matter of judicial review. In the following two situations judicial review will not normally be appropriate even though the body may be performing a public function:

(a) Where some other branch of the law more appropriately governs the dispute between the parties. In such a case, that branch of the law and its remedies should and normally will be applied; and

(b) Where there is a contract between the litigants. In such a case the express or implied terms or the agreement should normally govern the matter. This reflects the normal approach of English law, namely, that the terms of a contract will normally govern the transaction, or other relationship between the parties, rather than the general law. Thus, where a special method of resolving disputes (such as arbitration or resolution by private or domestic tribunals) has been agreed by the parties (expressly or by necessary implication), that regime, and not judicial review, will normally govern the dispute.

66. The English Courts had also invented a device to draw distinction between two types of functions performed by the same body, one type being amenable, while the other type is not. So in the case of R vs independent Broadcasting Authority (The Times, 4th March 1986), the authority's decision in so far it relates to the exercise of statutory power was concerned was reviewable, while it's voting power in the applicant company was not.

67. Having dissected the English position, we should now concentrate our attention to our own system. Is it at variance with that of the UK?

68. There are two obvious and notable differences; the English position derives from the Common Law, whereas ours emanate from Article 102 of the Constitution, and secondly while in our Constitutional scheme, two divers types of situations, reflected vide Article 102(1) and Article 102(2) respectively, as to the availability of judicial review, depending on whether or not fundamental rights are engaged, no such distinction, for obvious reason, exists in the English judicial review jurisprudence.

69. That said, however, it should not skip from our mind that our constitutional provisions are not totally divorced from those of the English Common Law. As a matter of fact, the nomenclatures Mandamus, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto, Prohibition, Habeas Corpus do not have a place in our Constitution. They have been infused into our Constitutional Law through case laws, borrowed from the English Common Law.

70. Article 102 reads: "Power of High Court Division to issue certain order and directions, etc—(1) The High Court Division on the application of any person aggrieved, may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution.

(2) the High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law—

(a) on the application of any person aggrieved, make an order—

(I)	directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do; or

(II)	declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the Affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect; or

(b) on the application of any person, make an order

(I) directing that a person in custody be brought before it so that it may satisfy itself that he is no being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner, or

(II) requiring person holding or purporting to hold a public office to show under what authority he claims to hold that office.

(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing clauses, the High Court Division shall have no power under this article to pass any interim or other order in relation to any law to which article 47 applies.

(4) Where on an application made under clause (I) or sub- clause (a) of clause (2), an interim order is prayed for and such interim order is likely to have the effect of—

(a) prejudicing or interfering with any measure designed to implement any development programme, or any development work; or

(b) being otherwise harmful to the public interest the High Court Division shall not make an interim order unless the Attorney General has been given reasonable notice of the application and he (or an advocate authorised by him in that behalf) has been given opportunity of being heard, and the High Court Division is satisfied that the interim order would not have the effect referred to in sub-clause (a) or sub-clause (b).

(5) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires, "person " includes a statutory public authority and any court or tribunal, other than a court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force or a tribunal which Article 117 applies'.

71. So, as far as Article 102(1) is concerned i.e., when fundamental rights are relied on, the question of status of the impugned person or authority loses it's relevance because the phrases "any person or authority", in the said sub-Article necessarily refers to a person or an authority, irrespective of his/it's status. (Shri Anadi Mukta Sadguru Shree Muktajee Vandasjiswami Suvarna Jayanti Mahotso vs Smarak Trust vs VR Rudani AIR 1989 (SC) 1607). Decisions by such a person or an authority is, whether he /it is a public functionary or a private one, is hence reviewable, provided however, that infringement of one of the fundamental rights, figured in Part III of the Constitution, is in question. In so far as such a person need not be a public functionary, little complication arises in fundamental rights oriented cases.

72. On the other hand, intricacies appear when fundamental rights provisions are not engaged, i.e., when the petition is hoisted on Article 102(2). In such a circumstance the body or the person, whose decision has been impugned, must be the one that performs the function in connection, either with the affairs of the 'Republic' or in connection with the affair of a local authority.

73. In this respect, it is necessary to dispel widely held, yet, a very obfuscating view that the body concerned must necessarily be a local authority. Article 102(2) does definitely not say that the body itself has to be a 'local authority' What it really says is that the body or the person concerned shall be the one that performs the functions in connection with affairs of the Republic or (in connection with the affairs of) a local authority. (The Bengali version of Article 102(2) makes it clearer) and from that point of view the individualistic status of the body or the person is not necessarily decisive because a non-government officer or a non-local authority officer can also 'perform function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority'.

74. A "local authority" has been defined by section 3(28) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 to, inter alia, exclude such corporations, bodies or authorities, as are not constituted by the government under any law; law is defined by Article 152, and hence no scope of any maneuvering exists to expand the area of local authority itself. But, when this is borne in mind that Article 102(2) is not concerned with the status of the body or the person itself but with the question as to whether the body or the person 'performs the function of a local authority,' we should not encounter much hurdle to infuse the 'public law' doctrine, enunciated in 'Panel on Take Over' case, where the Court of Appeal stated that all such bodies are likely, in principle to be amenable to judicial review, since they are intended to 'perform functions' properly seen as falling within the responsibility of the state.

75. We cannot be oblivious of the fact that there are scores of people and bodies, not officials of any local authorities, or of the Republic, who are, nevertheless, engaged in performing functions, of such authorities or of the Republic, like contractors, consultants, agents, sub-agents, delegatees and so on, acting really as the alter ego of the local authorities or of the government, who can, no doubt, be susceptible to review under sub-Article (2).

76. It would be in defiance of the notion of purposive interpretation to say that by the passages, "a person performing the function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or a Local Authority", the framers of our Constitution meant to confine the list within public servants or the servants of local authorities. If that was their intent, they would have so limited the ambit with expressive words. The additional words "in connection with" is significant. If the framers meant to confine liabilities on the government or local authorities or their officials only, they would not have inserted those additional words and would have simply stated "performing functions of the Republic or of a local authority". This is to be remembered that "Parliament does nothing in Vain". The list of people or bodies performing functions in connection with the affairs of the republic or of a local authority cannot be cloistered in this way. Hence, no reason exists as to why persons, including juristic ones, not in the employment of the government or of statutory bodies, yet performing important public functions for or in substitution of them, like private universities, private hospitals etc. (arguably the decision in the case of Manjurul Huq vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR 239, would have been different if the issue was not confined to the Canteen of the Bangladesh Diabetic Association), cannot be held to be "performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or (affairs of) a local Authority" as they are not only performing duties of utmost public importance and public character, but are doing so virtually in substitution of the government or of the local authorities either under licenses granted by the state or by the local authorities or as their agents or delegatees and that, had these private bodies not been there to perform the said public oriented duties, the government or the local authorities would have, invariably, been required to step into their toes as it is one of the fundamental obligations of the state and of the local authorities to provide education, healthcare etc. It is worth mentioning that under section 3(39) of the General Clauses Act 1897, the phrase 'person' includes artificial i.e., juristic persons as well.

77. So no reason would justify keeping at the bay the ratio expressed by the Court of Appeal in the "Panel on Take-Over" Case, supra, as well as other cases that followed' "Panel's" principle, while interpreting the ambit of both the sub-Articles of Article 102 of our Constitution. In fact, in addition to the ratio in the case of 'Panel Take-Over', plentitude of authorities, cited below, are there from our as well as from Indian jurisdiction to lend support to our view.

78. In the case of Zakir Hossain vs Bangladesh, 55 DLR 130, this Division expressed that in so far as providing, establishing and maintaining cellular phones remained confined to the exclusivity of authority of the government under applicable statutes, a person who performs the government's said function as a grantee of the government's aforementioned power under an agreement and license, does in fact perform the governmental and sovereign function of the latter as it's agent and the person concerned, a mobile phone provider company is, hence a 'person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic', as it's agent and is, as such amenable to review under Article 102(2) of the Constitution, notwithstanding it's own non-statutory status.

79. Similarly, by a perspicacious judgment in the case of Farzana Moazzem vs Securities and Exchange Commission, 54 DLR 66, this Division proclaimed that a body, though not created by a statute, would nevertheless, be amenable to Writ jurisdiction if it performs the job as a subordinate functionary or as a instrumentality of a statutory body by performing several duties cited in a statute or in the preamble to a statute. This decision obviously reflects a broad-based, purposive and innovative interpretation, expanding the realm of 'Judicial Review', and is in total concord with the ratio expressed in the 'Panel of Take Over' case, supra.

80. In Conforce Ltd, vs Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Co. Ltd. 42 DLR 33, this Division held that Titas Gas, though a limited company was, nevertheless amenable to Writ jurisdiction because, it performs the function of distribution sale etc. of gas substance under the direct control of a statutory corporation and also under the government acting through the Ministry of Mineral Oil and Gas Resources.

81. Likewise the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Shri Anadi Mukta Sadguru Shree Muktajee Vandasjiswami Suvarna Jay anti Mahotsov Smarak Truot vs VR Rudani AIR 1989 (SC) 1607, expressing that the term 'authority' used in Article 226 must receive a liberal meaning, observed 'The word any person or authority used in Article 226 are, therefore not to confine to statutory authorities and instrumentalities of the state. They may cover any other person or body performing public duty. The form of the body Concerned is not very much relevant. What is relevant is the nature of the duty imposed on the body.' The Supreme Court went on to say, 'The law relating to mandamus made the most spectacular advance. Article 226 confers wide powers on the High Courts to issue writs in the nature of prerogative writs Under Article 226 writs can be issued to any person or authority. It can be issued for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights and for any other purpose.' The Court also emphasized, 'The judicial control over the fast expanding maze of bodies affecting rights of the People should not be put into watertight compartments'. The Court further observed, "It has to be appreciated that the appellants trust was managing the affiliated college to which public money is paid as government aid plays a major role in the control, maintenance and the working of educational institutions. The aided institutions like government institutions discharge public functions by way of imparting education to students. They are subject to rules and regulations of the affiliating university. Their activities are closely supervised by the university authorities. Employment in such institutions therefore, is not devoid of public character.'

82. The ratio of this case is also very akin to the concept of public law domain" expressed by the Court of Appeal in Panel in "Panel on take-over" case.

83. The Bombay High Court expressed similar view in the case of Sejal Rikeen Dalal vs Stock Exchange, Bombay, (AIR 1991 Born 30).

84. In Khatri vs Bihar (AIR 1981 SC 928) the Indian Supreme Court unambiguously expressed that granting relief in case of a violation of fundamental rights the court is not helpless and it should be prepared to devise new remedies, and, if necessary, to develop new principles of liability for the purpose of vindicating those precious fundamental rights.

85. It must not skip our thought that the Indian Constitutional scheme is not different from ours in this particular respect because the term 'Authority' has not been defined by either Constitution (Art. 12 of Indian Constitution merely conjoins it with "state") or by the General Clauses Act and, that Act, instead of defining 'person', has only stated what it includes. Hence the divergence in the contents of the two Constitutions in other respect, is of little significances so far as reliance on the above cited case is concerned.

86. We are, hence not tempted to accede to the generalized nature of the submission proffered on behalf of the respondents suggesting that if the body concerned is not per se a local authority as per the definition given by section 3(28) of the General Clauses Act 1897, 'cul-de-sac. We hold that although the status of the body or the person cannot always be ignored, private bodies or persons can, in certain circumstances, notwithstanding their non-statutory status, perform functions "in connection with the affairs of the republic" or "the affairs of local authorities" nonetheless, as narrated above. We are hence, inclined to endorse Mr Mahmud's submission that the source or the origin of the power alone is not decisive as the nature of the function, founded on "function based" theory is also of utmost importance. His preferment goes glove in hands with the ratio expressed in the 'Panel of Take Over' case, and of course with the cases decided at our as well as Indian jurisdictions, discussed above.

87. That said, however, we must now turn to the other side of the coin which catalogues the reverse postulations, portraying situations where review is not available, when sub-Article (2) alone is engaged. A rather big list of English authorities in this context have already been figured above, and hence we must now turn to our and Indian authorities. They refer to a class of cases where the bodies are not themselves created by statute and are not as such per se local authorities, and do not otherwise perform the functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or in connection with the affairs of a local authority. They are, therefore, not amenable to review under Article 102(2), albeit that they are subject to regulation by certain statutory provisions.

88. The case of Noor Alam Jahangir vs Government of Bangladesh, 60 DLR (AD) 12, represents a glaring example of this class. In that case the Appellate Division refused to review the decision taken by the authorities of a private school run by Bangladesh Rifles, holding that Rifles Public School and College, though run by the Bangladesh Rifles, is not a local authority as it is not a statutory creation.

89. Likewise, in Mofizul Huq vs Mofizur Rahaman, 48 DLR (AD) 121, the Appellate Division refused to review a decision of a private institute, saying that to be a statutory body it must, first of all, owe it's existence to a statute and that a distinction exists between a body or an institute which is created by or under a statute and a body not so constituted but is only governed by certain statutory provisions for it's proper maintenance and administration.

90. The ratio of the decisions in these two private school cases is not different from that of the English case of R vs Fernhil Manor School, 1992, 5 Admin LR 159.

91. There was nothing in any of the two above stated non statutory school cases to show that the impugned decision had any public law element or that the impugned decision formed part of any function performed in connection with the affairs of the Republic or in connection with the affairs of any local authority.

92. With the same theme this Division refused to review decisions by Bangladesh Diabetic Association in respect to it's canteen (Manjurul Huq vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR 329).

<u>93. Surely, the Diabetic Association which is not by itself a statutory emanation, was not performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority while dealing with it's canteen, although function of public nature, like medical service provided by the aforementioned Association, in appropriate cases, may very well espoused with duties performed in connection with the affairs of the Republic" or in breach of fundamental rights so as to render it prone to I review under Article 102(2) and (1) respectively.</u>

94. Review, on the same counts, were also refused against the decisions of a private arbitration tribunal (45 DLR 360), of an election appeal board created under the Trade Organisation Rules, 1994, (47 DLR 209), of the officials of the Muktijodha Command Council (on the ground that although they were government officials, they did not act as such in taking the impugned decision, (1995 BLD 124) as well as of the authorities of a school run by a sugar mill under the Bangladesh Food and Sugar Mills Corporation, (48 DLR 431).

95. Now, in the instant case although in ground (iii) the petitioner purported to engage fundamental rights, essentially and in substance this petition does not attract any aspect of fundamental rights, as cited in Part III of the Constitution but turns upon a purely contractual relationship between herself and the respondent No. 3. She cannot, as such, really rely on fundamental rights factors and invoke sub-Article (1).

96. It does also deserve to be mentioned that although the extension was granted by the respondent No. 2, it was granted on a recommendation of the respondent No. 3, and hence the decision was that of the respondent No. 3.

<u>97. Her claim, in our view, cannot be drawn to the domain of Article 102(2) either because the same hung upon nothing else than sheer contractal tie, which remains confined to private law realm. The action under challenge goes nowhere to touch the ceiling of public law threshold because by no stretch of imagination can her case be enveloped within the connotation of 'public law', as she does not divulge that element even by microscopic proportion.</u>

98. Viqarunnisa Noon College per se is obviously not a local authority as per the definition given by section 3(28) of the General Clauses Act 1987. Notwithstanding it's status, it or it's Governing Body can, nevertheless, in appropriate circumstances, be deemed to be performing functions in connection with the affairs of the republic or in connection with the affairs of a local authority. But to say that they performed such functions in the situation under consideration, would be tantamount to putting the truth topsy turvy. Indeed the facts of the present case are such that the ratio expressed in the cases reported in 60 DLR (AD) 12, and 48 DLR (AD) 121, squarely fits into it. The ratio in the case of R vs Fernhil Manor School, supra, also lend support to this view. We also reminisce the Indian Supreme Court's observation 'if the rights are purely of a private character no Mandamus can issue, if the management of the college is purely a private body with no public duty, Mandamus will not lie' (Shri Anadi Mukta Sadguru Shree Muktajee Vandasjisqami Suvarna Jaynti Mahotsav Smarak Trust vs VR Rudani, supra.)

99. The Rule is, therefore, destined to founder as being devoid of any merit and, the same is, hence, discharged.

100. There is however, no Order as to cost.

The Order of stay granted at the time of the issuance of the, Rule is hereby vacated.

End.
