          37. The respondent No. 2 acted in the transaction as the collecting Bank and the presenting Bank, having acted under the collection instructions of the remitting Bank, i.e. Brac Bank Limited (respondent No. 4). Under the aforesaid instructions, respondent No. 4 authorized the respondent No. 2 to handle documents on a collection basis and to release documents to the respondent No. 1 (Milestone Clothing Resources LLC) upon receipt of respondent No. l's letter of undertaking to pay the collection in 90 days. Respondent No. 2 duly carried out its obligations in such capacity and released the documents to respondent No. 1 after receiving their signed letter of undertaking.

          38. Thus, the contractual relationship under URC-522 existed between respondent No. 2 and respondent No. 4 (remitting bank), to which the petitioner-company had no privy. In a "Documentary Collection" under URC-522, it is now established that URC-522 does not create privity of contract between the principal/seller and the collecting Bank. As the collecting Bank is the agent of the remitting Bank, there is no privity of contract between him and the customer, i.e. the seller. This is based on the principle that there is normally no privity of contract between a principal and his sub-agent. Even if the remitting Bank engages a collecting Bank, which is specifically nominated by the customer and who is not one of the remitting Bank's usual correspondences, there is no privity of contract between the collecting Bank and the customer. The High Court of Justice, Queen's Bench Division, Commercial Court, in the case of Grosvenor Casinos Limited vs National Bank of Abu Dhabi, reported in 2 All ER (Comm) 112, held that URC-522 does not create privity of contract between the principal and the collecting Bank. To conclude the issue in a simpler version, all that I record here is that there being no 'offer' by the petitioner-company to Wells Fargo Bank, resultantly, there is no 'acceptance' from Wells Fargo Bank and, thus, there is no consideration and, therefore, it is crystal clear that there is no existence of any contract between the petitioner-company and the respondent No. 2.

          39. I would, now, take up the third issue, namely, whether the legal notice sent by the petitioner's lawyer to the collecting Bank and the reply thereto by the collecting Bank compose an implied form of arbitration agreement under the provisions of section 9(2)(b) & (c) of the Arbitration Act.

          40. It would be useful, if we look at the provisions of section 9 of the Arbitration Act, which run as follows:

          9. Form of arbitration agreement—

          (1) An arbitration agreement may be in the form of an arbitration clause in a contract or in the form of a separate agreement.

          (2) An arbitration agreement shall be in writing and an arbitration agreement shall be deemed to be in writing if it is contained in—

          (a) a document signed by the parties;

          (b) an exchange of letters, telex, telegrams, fax, e-mail or other means of telecommunication which provide a record of the agreement; or

          (C) an exchange of statement of claim and defence in which the existence of the agreement is alleged by one party and not denied by the other.

                   Explanation—The reference in a contract is a document containing an arbitration clause constitutes an arbitration agreement if the contract is in writing and the reference is such as to make that arbitration clause part of the contract.

          41. From the marginal note (Head note) of section 9 of the Arbitration Act, it is vividly clear that the provisions of this section are about the form of arbitration agreement. Section 9(2) of the Arbitration Act provides, among others, that an arbitration agreement must be in writing and the agreement may be deemed to be in writing if it is contained in a contract signed by the parties or contained in written communication as elaborated in clauses (a) to (c) under section 9(2) of the Arbitration Act. It further appears that section 9(2)(b) of the Arbitration Act is not an alternative to section 9(1) of the Arbitration Act, but an explanation to determine whether an arbitration agreement is in writing or not. As per section 9(1) of the Arbitration Act, an arbitration agreement can be in the form of a clause in a contract or as a separate agreement. Section 9(2) of the Arbitration Act went further to explain that such agreement as mentioned in section 9(1) of the Arbitration Act should be in writing, in other words, oral agreement is not acceptable. In addition, section 9(2) of the Arbitration Act also enlightens that an arbitration agreement will be considered as written if any of the conditions, laid down under it, is satisfied.

          42. For determining the existence of an arbitration agreement through section 9(2)(b) of the Arbitration Act, the following conditions are to be satisfied: (1) the subject matter of agreement i.e. arbitration agreement shall be mentioned in a letter, telex, telegram, email, fax or any other medium and (2) the party on whom such agreement has been served shall agree to such communication. If the second condition as aforesaid is disregarded, and section 9(2) of the Arbitration Act is found independent, then it would make arbitration obligatory only on the willingness of one party.

                   43. For determining the existence of an arbitration agreement through section 9(2)(c), the following conditions are to be satisfied: (1) the subject matter of agreement i.e. arbitration agreement shall be mentioned in an exchange of statement of claim or defence and (2) the agreement is alleged by one party, and not denied by the other. It appears from the second condition that the affirmation to enter into an arbitration agreement is confirmed, by the party to whom such statement of claim of defence has been served, through omission to decline such proposal.

          44. In other words, under section 9(2) of the Arbitration Act, an arbitration agreement must be in writing though no special form is prescribed for that. Such an agreement can be in one document or can be gathered from several documents also. It can be gathered from correspondences consisting of letters, fax messages, telegrams or even telex messages. An arbitration agreement can also be constituted when the existence of the agreement is depicted in a statement of claim and defence and the existence of the contract is alleged by one party and not denied by the other. The arbitration clause may exist either in the circumstances by way of incorporating an arbitration agreement or in the situation as contemplated in section 9 of the Arbitration Act. An arbitration agreement may be included by way of implied terms. For example, the agreement in World Cotton Association by way of implied term may incorporate an arbitration clause. Similarly, in documentary collection, if the parties by express term decide to include ICC Arbitration Rules in their contract, then the parties shall be bound by such term. In the instant case, from the documents on record, it appears that there is no implied term for any arbitration.

          45. From the above discussions, it leads me to hold that in order to constitute an arbitration agreement, a written document must be present, which states or refers or demonstrates the ad idem intention of the parties to adopt a quasi judicial method, i.e., a private tribunal as to dispute resolution, whose decision shall be binding upon both the parties.

          46. In Thomson Press India Limited vs NCT of Delhi, reported in 1999 (1) Arb LR 421, the Court decided that even though, an arbitration agreement does not necessarily have to include words like 'arbitrator' or 'arbitration', the words used for the purpose must be words of choice and determination to go to arbitration.

          47. In Jagdish Chander vs Ramesh Chander (2007) 5 SCC 719, the Court decided that the essential elements of an arbitration agreement are, (i) the agreement should be in writing; (ii) the parties should have agreed to refer any dispute between them to the decision of a private tribunal; (iii) the private tribunal should be empowered to adjudicate upon the disputes in an impartial manner and (iv) the parties should have agreed that the decision of the private tribunal in respect of the disputes shall be binding upon them. Ujwala Raje Shah vs Veer Corp. 2014 (2) RAJ 598, connotes "Arbitration Agreement" as, "If the terms of the agreement indicate intention on the part of all the parties to refer the dispute to the arbitral tribunal for adjudication and their willingness to be bound by the decision of such tribunal, such agreement would amount to arbitration agreement."

          48. If I now turn back to the facts of the present case with a view to see the applicability of the above principles of law, it would appear that since Wells Fargo Bank expressly declined their intention to settle the dispute through arbitration, the existence of an arbitration agreement can be found neither under section 9(2)(b) of the Arbitration Act, due to the lack of their consent to enter into such agreement, nor under section 9(2)(c) of the Arbitration Act, due to their express denial. In other words, from the communications dated 5-10-2017 and 14-11-2017 between the petitioner and the respondent No. 2, there seems to have no indication or reference to any expression of either party to a pre-meditated consensus to refer any potential dispute to an arbitrator for dispute resolution and hence, while considering whether there exists an arbitration agreement between the parties under reference, the communications dated 14-11-2017 and 5-10-2017 do not attract section 9(2)(b) & (c) of the Arbitration Act. By merely raising a dispute, an arbitration does not come into play as a matter of course. Thus, I find that the petitioner's legal notice dated 5-10-2017 to the respondent No. 2, and the reply dated 14-11-2017 to the legal notice do not attract section 9(2)(b) and (c) of Arbitration Act. Section 9(2)(b) and (c) of Arbitration Act would have applied only if the aforesaid legal notice by the petitioner and the reply by the respondent No. 2 contained an agreement, i.e. meeting of the minds, to refer disputes between these parties to arbitration. The reply dated 14-11-2017 issued by the respondent No. 2 does not contain indication whatsoever that the respondent No. 2 was willing to refer the dispute to arbitration. To the contrary, the respondent No. 2 clearly stated that if the petitioner was to pursue any legal action against the respondent No. 2, the only proper forum would be USA Courts. Thus, there was no arbitration agreement between the petitioner-company and Wells Fargo Bank, even through written correspondence. By no stretch of imagination, thus, it can be said that there exists any arbitration agreement between the petitioner-company and Wells Fargo Bank under sections 9(2) &(3) of the Arbitration. Act. However, since Coreattire Fashion (respondent No. 6) through its reply letter dated 4-2-2018 (Annexure H) made the statement "My client proposes to appoint one arbitrator for my aforesaid client himself" (at paragraph 6), this scenario satisfies all the conditions under section 9(2)(b) of the Arbitration Act, for, the above-quoted statement amounts to a consent to settle the dispute through arbitration.

          49. Now, let me deal with the issue No. 4, namely, if the arbitral tribunal is not formed by appointing an arbitrator, whether the petitioner-company is going to be non-suited or remains remediless.

          50. There is no scope under the Arbitration Act to refer a dispute to arbitration only on the ground of financial hardship or any other inconvenience of a party, as has been pleaded in this case that since the petitioner is a Bangladeshi party and the counterparty to the dispute is a resident in USA, it would not be feasible to contest the suit in the USA Court given the value of the subject-matter of arbitration is trivial. The basis for appointing an arbitrator is the existence of an arbitration agreement, and not the supposed inconvenience of a particular party. If it is possible to appoint an arbitrator without the existence of an arbitration agreement, any and all parties can apply to the Court for appointment of arbitrators by pleading inconvenience in pursuing the relevant remedy under the applicable law. This would make arbitration agreements, which are foundations of all arbitrations and the law of arbitration, entirely redundant. If this Court takes a view that a party may maintain an application under section 12 of the Arbitration Act even in the absence of a prima facie arbitration agreement on the ground of inconvenience, the whole scheme of the Arbitration Act would become frustrated and a floodgate would open allowing a party to any civil dispute to apply to Court for constitution of an arbitral tribunal. In my opinion, such a result would be opposed to public policy.

          51. There is no bar to a suit against the importer and the collecting Bank in Bangladesh if a case of fraud or otherwise can be established. The plaint in such event has to disclose a valid cause of action to maintain the suit in Bangladesh. If the Bangladeshi party can establish that the cause of action arose wholly or in part in Bangladesh, a Court in Bangladesh may also exercise jurisdiction over such dispute (section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908). The difficulty lying here may be that there is no reciprocity of enforcement of judgment between USA and Bangladesh. Therefore, even if a verdict is obtained in Bangladesh, the same cannot be enforced in USA. However, the verdict of Bangladeshi civil Court may be enforced, in a roundabout manner, with the assistance of Bangladesh Bank and other scheduled Banks. For example, if the petitioner-company somehow comes to know that the importer or the Wells Fargo Bank has any money in any Bank in Bangladesh or has stored any goods anywhere in Bangladesh, it may seek to attach the same by the order of the Court. My considered view, thus, is that since the petitioner-company is free to sue the respondent No. 2 (Wells Fargo Bank) and respondent No.1 (importer) either in the competent Court of USA or in Bangladeshi civil Court and, further, since the petitioner-company can commence arbitration in Bangladesh any time with the importer (respondent No. 1), the petitioner-company is not going to be either non-suited or remain remediless.

          52. The last issue to be dealt with by this Court is whether the collecting Bank is under any obligation to recover money from the drawee (importer). In case of a transaction through letter of credit ("L/C"), an issuing Bank (the buyer's or importer's Bank) unconditionally guarantees to pay the seller's Bank when the shipping documents, as listed in the L/C, are presented in an acceptable condition. However, in a `Documentary Collection' arrangement ("D/A"), as per Article 16 of the URC-522, the collecting Bank is responsible to make payment only if it has collected payment from the buyer. It has no independent obligation to make payment, if the buyer has not made payment of the agreed amount to the collecting Bank. URC-522 clearly sets out the respective obligations of the parties, and does not contain any provision requiring the collecting Bank to make any payment if it has not received the amount concerned from the buyer. Thus, the difference between an L/C transaction and D/A transaction is that in the former case the buyer's Bank guarantees to the L/C beneficiary Bank (i.e. exporter's Bank) that it would make payment on receipt of compliant shipping documents, whereas in the latter case the buyer's Bank does not provide any such independent guarantee/undertaking.

          53. In this case, the collecting Bank had engaged in a 'Documentary Collection' with an obligation to send the money to the remitting Bank, only when the importer will make payment under D/A. Under the provisions of `URC-522', the collecting Bank is under no obligation to take any collateral security towards securing the deferred payment (D/A) at the time of releasing the documents to the drawee, unless the collecting Bank is otherwise instructed by the drawer. URC-522 does not impose any obligation upon the collecting Bank to obtain collaterals from the drawee; it merely obliges the collecting Bank to comply with the collection instructions provided by the drawer. In order to protect its interest, the collecting Bank, sometimes, becomes tempted to release the documents under a trust receipt. Under such a document a genuine trust is constituted, the drawee being the trustee, the collecting Bank being the beneficiary and the proceeds of sale of the goods collected by the drawee being the trust property. In other words, the collecting Bank may enter into any arrangement with the drawee for securing the collecting Bank's interest; so long such arrangements do not contravene the collection instructions by the drawer or the remitting Bank.

          54. In this case, the collecting Bank had received instructions from the remitting Bank merely to pass the documents onto the importer upon taking an undertaking from the importer that the latter shall pay within 90 days and, accordingly, the collecting Bank has performed its duties. Whether the collecting Bank has acted in good faith and has exercised reasonable care in dealing with the petitioner-company's 'Documentary Collection', as per the provisions of Article 9 of the URC-522, or it has violated any provisions of Unified Commercial Code (UCC), which has been termed by the learned Advocate for the petitioner-company to be a law of the USA, is a question of fact to be examined by the Court, in absence of any arbitral tribunal which could not be constituted due to non-incorporation of an arbitration clause in the correspondences of "Documentary Collection". Now-a-days, many of the remitting Banks inscribe the provisions of arbitration in the L/C and Documentary Collection. It has become a frequent custom to incorporate the provision of arbitration in dealing with Documentary Collection, more particularly in dealing with transactions relating to Documents by Acceptance (D/A). Since the practice of "Documentary Collection" is highly specialized and often counter-intuitive to the general commercial lawyer, the judicial process has not generally afforded speedy, final and sound relief desired by the parties to a dispute under Documentary Collection. To resolve this predicament, International Centre for Letter of Credit Arbitration INC was founded in 1996, which is located in Washington DC, USA. This Centre has established a set of rules, namely. ICLOCA Rules of Arbitration. These rules are modelled to assist in the resolution of disputes arising out of international banking operations, including Letters of Credit, Confirmations or Advices, Documentary Collections, Funds Transfers etc. The interested parties of the transactions may refer the dispute under ICLOCA Rules by inserting a clause into the undertaking or agreement providing that all future disputes, arising out, or in connection to the agreement be subjected to the Centre for Resolution under those Rules. There are two circumstances in which a dispute might be referred to arbitration under ICLOCA Rules and administered by the centre: (i) a clause may be inserted into the undertaking or agreement providing that all future dispute arising out of, in connection with or relating to, that undertaking or agreement be submitted to the centre for resolution under these rules, (ii) an existing dispute may also be referred to the centre for resolution by agreement of the parties, even if there was no advance agreement to arbitration.

          55. There are different models of law governing the contractual relationship between the parties. Once the parties adopt any such model in their contractual relationship, the arbitration clause incorporated in such model impliedly becomes applicable in their contractual transactions. For example, if the parties adopt 1CC Rules of Arbitration or Rules of the International Cotton Association Limited, the arbitration clauses incorporated therein become impliedly applicable and binding in their contract. Therefore, in "Documentary Collection", if the parties by express term decide to include ICC Arbitration Rules or ICLOCA Rules of Arbitration in their contract, then the parties shall be bound by such term.

          56. The parties to a transaction have the flexibility to agree to the dispute resolution mechanism to be applied to a transaction. Such agreement varies from one transaction to another, depending on various commercial and legal considerations. There is no uniform practice of any specific dispute resolution mechanism. The URC-522 does not contain any provision to the effect that the parties to a D/A transaction shall refer their dispute to arbitration.

          57. Since there is no privity between the principal and the collecting Bank, in England, the customer/principal may invoke the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act, 1999 to sue the collecting Bank. Since no such Act is prevalent in Bangladesh, the principal cannot sue the collecting Bank. In such circumstances, the proper remedy of the customer would be to request the remitting Bank, in return for an indemnity against the incurred expenses to claim against the collecting Bank.

          58. In this case, admittedly the transaction of this case took place under the URC-522 and since the collecting Bank has no obligation to take any collateral security towards securing the deferred payment at the time of releasing the documents to the drawee (importer) under the URC-522, the collecting Bank is not bound to take any initiative to recover the collections (money) from the importer.

          59. After carrying out the examination of all the five issues, as framed by me for the purpose of adjudication of this case, I find that this case (application under section 12 of the Arbitration Act) is liable to fail against the respondent No. 2 (collecting Bank), mainly, on the grounds of non-existence of the arbitration agreement, albeit the learned Advocate for the petitioner has put his best effort to make out a case on the strength of Preamble, section 2(c) and section 9(2)(b) of the Arbitration Act, 2001. He has particularly emphasized on the Preamble of Arbitration Act, 2001 in an expectation to pursue this Court that the scheme and object of repealing the old law of arbitration and enacting the new Arbitration Act in 2001 is to facilitate arbitration for any 'international commercial dispute' to be held in Bangladesh. In order to address the above submissions, it would be pertinent to briefly know about the history of arbitration in our jurisdiction. In this part of the world (sub-continent), the concept of arbitration is known to the people from time immemorial. In good old days, disputes between private individuals used to be placed before `Panchas' and `Panchayats'. Likewise, commercial matters were decided by `Mahajans' and 'Chambers'. Formal arbitration proceedings, however, had come into existence after the Britishers started commercial activities in India. The provisions relating to arbitration were found in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1859 (CPC) and, then, in subsequent CPCs. A full-fledged law pertaining to arbitration in India was the Arbitration Act, 1899. A consolidated and amended law relating to arbitration was passed in 1940, known as the Arbitration Act, 1940. Protracted, time-consuming, atrociously expensive and complex Court-procedures impelled the commercial world to an alternative, less formal, more effective and speedy mode of resolution of disputes by a Judge of choice of the parties which culminated into passing of an Arbitration Act. Experience, however, belied expectations. Proceedings became highly technical and thoroughly complicated. The provisions of the Act made 'lawyers laugh and litigants weep'. Representations were made from all quarters of the society to amend the law by making it more responsive to contemporary requirements. Moreover, apart from arbitration, conciliation has been getting momentum and worldwide recognition as an effective instrument of settlement of disputes. There was no composite statute dealing with all matters relating to arbitration and conciliation. The United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) adopted a Model Law in 1985 on International Commercial Arbitration. The General Assembly of the United Nations recommended its member-States to give due consideration to the Model Law to have uniformity in arbitration procedure which resulted in passing of the Arbitration Act, 2001. The Act is almost a complete Code in itself and consolidates and amends the law relating to domestic arbitration, international commercial arbitration and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards. The Preamble expressly refers to International Commercial Arbitration.

          60. Thus, with the passage of time, the customs and laws relating to arbitration of disputes have achieved the status of the finest law of our jurisdiction, as now it contains both procedural and substantive laws. It has clearly now categorized the provisions for local arbitration and the international arbitration. The latest position of the laws relating to arbitration of all the countries of the world is, which has now become an inviolable law, like Veda's statement, that there cannot be any arbitration without any arbitration agreement. I find the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner-company to be a desperate attempt to bring his case within the purview of arbitration agreement, although his agreements do not attract the Preamble, section 2(c) and section 9(2)(b) in any manner. Since, this Court finds that there is no existence of any arbitration agreement with the Well's Fargo Bank, this application cannot succeed against it. However, the arbitration may be held with Coreattire Fashion Ltd (respondent No. 6) who had consented to the proposal of arbitration given by the petitioner-company.

          61. Before parting with the judgment, I find it pertinent to make an observation that the legislature may consider incorporation of a provision at an appropriate place in the Arbitration Act that the Court (the District Judge Court and the High Court Division) shall examine the issue of existence of an arbitration agreement without entering into the merit of the case, when an application for any interim order or for appointment of an arbitrator is made before the Court.

          62. I must record here the invaluable assistance rendered by Mr Ahsanul Karim who appeared before this Court as an amicus curiae. He took the pain of going through all the relevant laws of Bangladesh and the up-to-date Legal Instruments on International Trade and presented a very precious written submission, significant portions of which have been used by me in this judgment. Although, currently, Mr Ahsanul Karim is an Advocate of this Court with a single star, however, it is hoped that very soon he will be honoured with double stars by the Honourable Appellate Division, for, in my estimation, he possesses all the qualifications, knowledge, experience and professional etiquette to be endowed with the professional status of a 'Senior Advocate'. Also, the performances of the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr Syed Mohidul Kabir and the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2 Dr Sharif Bhuiyan were highly commendable in assisting this Court.

          63. In the result, this application is rejected. However, there shall not be any order as to costs.

         The Office is directed to send a copy of this judgment to the Legislative Division of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for their consideration as to incorporation of the proposed provision, as observed by this Court in the penultimate para of this judgment.

End.

full_judgment:
On an application of the petitioner, Akkas Ali being dead his heirs 1(a) Mrs Romija Khatun and others under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure the Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 2-9 and 14-18 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 10-4-1995 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1993 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 29-11-1992 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Comilla in Partition No. 289 of 1980 dismissing the suit should not be set-aside.

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Partition Suit No. 289 of 1980 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Comilla for partition of the suit land contending inter-alia that his grandfather Mozu Gazi was the owner of the suit land who during his lifetime by way of a registered Heba deed dated 11-7-1914 gifted the suit land to his two sons namely Modhu Miah alias Kala Miah, father of the plaintiff, Asmat Ali and one daughter Khatoon Bibi and delivered the possession of the suit lands to them. The CS khatian was wrongly recorded in the name of Mozu Gazi in place of Asmat Ali, Modhu Miah and Khatoon Bibi,. Modhu Gazi died leaving behind one wife Manikjan Bibi, Asmat Ali and Modhu Miah as two sons, Khatoon Bibi as one daughter as his legal heirs. Manikjan got 1 decimal from Mozu Gazi as widow and she purchased 16 decimals from one Sona Miah, husband of Khatoon Bibi and thereby she got total 17 decimals of land. Asmat Ali died leaving the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 namely Jabbar Ali and Moidhar Ali as 2 sons and thereafter Jabbar Ali died leaving defendant Nos. 4-9 as his heirs. Moidhar Ali died leaving defendant Nos. 10-13 as his heirs. Khatoon Bibi died without issues leaving Modhu Miah as full brother and Sona Miah as husband. Modhu Miah purchased 16 decimals from Sona Miah by registered Kabala dated 16-1-1929 and got 1.80 acres by dint of inheritance from Khatoon Bibi and thereby Modhu Miah, father of the plaintiff got 2.36 acres by way of aforesaid Heba deed dated 11-7-1914, 2 decimals by way of inheritance from father, 16 decimals from Sona Miah and 1.80 acres from Khatoon Bibi, in aggregate 4.34 acres of land. Modhu Miah during his lifetime by way of registered Heba deed dated 3-10-1980 gifted the said 4.36 acres to plaintiff and defendant Nos. 15-17 four sons of Modhu Miah and delivered possession to them and thereby plaintiff is the owner and possessor of 1.09 acres on the total in the suit land, but the defendants are not willing to partition the suit land upon several tagids and thereby cause of action arose on 18-11-1980 and plaintiff filed the suit on 27-11-1980.

3. Further case of the plaintiff is that the suit plot No. 1338 is homestead of the plaintiff appellant and he is in peaceful possession and residing in the suit land having his 7 tin shed huts and four chat huts and 10 coconut trees and 12 mango trees and other trees in the same. The defendant No. 20 Rahman Ali alias Abdur Rahman is not a son of original owner Modhu Gazi. He is the son of another Mozu Gazi of a different village Nabipur and his mother Manikjan Bibi was married to Mozu Gazi, as his 5th wife after the death of the father of the defendant No. 20 and he got 17 decimals from his mother Manikjan Bibi only, but did not inherit anything from Mozu Gazi, grandfather of the plaintiff. Hence the suit.

4. The suit was contested by the 3 sets of defendants by filing separate written statements.

5. The defendant No. 3 ultimately supported the case of the plaintiff and stated that Mozu Gazi was the original owner of the suit land and that CS khatian was recorded correctly in the name of him and she also admitted that Mozu Gazi gifted the suit land to his two sons Modhu Miah and Asmat Ali and one daughter Khatoon Bibi by registered Heba deed dated 11-7-1914. Manikjan Bibi earlier was married to one Mozu Gazi and Khatoon Bibi died leaving behind two full brothers Asmat Ali and Modhu Miah and husband Sona Miah and she supported the case of the plaintiff and prayed for separate saham.

6. The case of the defendant Nos. 2, 5 and 12 is that Mozu Gazi was the original owner of the suit land and he gifted the suit land by registered Heba deed dated 11-7-1914 to his two sons Asmat Ali and Modhu Miah and one daughter Khatoon Bibi and delivered possession to them and the CS khatian was wrongly recorded in his name and that defendant No. 20 who is not the son of Mozu Gazi and that Khatoon Bibi died leaving Sona Miah as husband and Asmat Ali and Modhu Miah as two brothers as her heirs and that the suit was bad for defect of parties and Asmat Ali was the owner and possessor of 3.26 7/9 acres of land. They ultimately supported the case of the plaintiff but claimed that the suit is bad for defect of the parties and claimed their saham.

7. The case of the defendant No. 20 is that Mozu Gazi was the original owner of the suit land and Manikjan Bibi was the 3rd wife of Mozu Gazi and he is the son of Mozu Gazi and Manikjan was not married to Mozu Gazi. Though Mozu Gazi executed and registered Heba deed dated 11-7-1914 in favour of his two sons and one daughter but he was in possession of the suit lands. Mozu Gazi died in the year 1966 leaving behind Manikjan as one widow, Asmat Ali, Kala Miah father of the plaintiff as two sons and Khatoon Bibi as one daughter. Manikjan got 89 ½ , decimals, and each son got 1.79 acres and daughter got 89 ½ , decimals and defendant No. 20 got 2.68 ½ acres from his father and mother and Khatoon Bibi died leaving Sona Miah as husband and one Charu as her son. The suit is liable to be dismissed.

8. At the trial the parties adduced oral as well as documentary evidence to prove their respective cases.

9. The trial court after hearing the parties and considering the evidence on record dismissed the suit by its judgment and decree dated 29-11-1992.

10. Against the said judgment and decree of the trial court the plaintiff-petitioner preferred Title Appeal No. 34 of 1993 before the learned District Judge, Comilla. The said appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Comilla who after hearing the parties and considering the evidence on record disallowed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the trial court by its judgment and decree dated 10-4-1995.

11. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree of the courts below, the plaintiffs-petitioners filed this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

12. Mr. Abdul Kuddus Miah, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf the opposite party No. 27 through Vokalatnama to oppose the Rule.

13. Mr. Md. Tajul Islam the learned Advocate along with Mrs. Sabikun Nahar, Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner argued that both the courts committed error in law in dismissing the suit. He argued that this is a suit for partition and the plaintiffs as well as the defendants prayed for their respective saham, in such a case the courts below ought to have given saham to the parties without dismissing the suit which they committed error in law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He argued that both the courts after consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit on the ground of barred by defect of parties whereas it appears that the defendants initially raised the question of defect of parties and accordingly, the plaintiff filed an interrogatory on 24-5-1987 to supply the name of the parties who were left out and ultimately the defendants failed to produce the same and court vide its order dated 16-11-1987 waived the question of defect of parties so without considering the said material facts of the case both the courts erroneously passed the impugned judgment. He referred the decisions reported in 17 BLT (AD) 25 = Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest, volume-XII-37 and 17 BLT (AD) 164= Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest, volume-XII-37. He further argued that the plaintiffs claimed that the original owner Modhu Gazi, the grandfather of the plaintiff, gifted his entire portion of the suit land through gift deed dated 11-7-1940 in favour of his two sons Ashmat Ali and Modhu Miah @ Kala Miah and daughter Khatoon Bibi and in support of the same the plaintiff filed certified copy of the gift deed in the trial court and filed original gift deed in the appellate court through firishti form and since the said gift deed is 30 years old document produced from the proper custody of the plaintiff so as per provision of section 90 of the Evidence Act the said deed has presumptive value unless the same was rebutted by the defendants but the trial court did not consider at all the same and the appellate court opined that which was not acted upon, which is erroneous decision of the courts below. He cited the decision reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76. He further argued that both the courts opined that the plaintiff failed to prove their possession over the suit land so he is not entitled to get decree whereas in partition suit possession of the co-sharer in a joint land even more than 12 years shall not constitute adverse possession against others relying upon the decision reported in 6 ADC 74 = Supreme Court Digest, volume-XII (2009) 34. The learned Advocate further argued that in the case of partition there is no question of limitation at all and a co-sharer in possession of land less than his share he is always entitled to pray for partition relying upon the decision reported in 27 BLD (AD) 239 = Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest, volume-X-48. He argued that admittedly the plaintiff is a co-sharer of the case land and it is not a case of declaration of title and in such a case if it is found that the plaintiff has entitlement of the land even he can claim his portion of land from each of land and the court should have considered the same since in the instant case not only the plaintiff but all the defendants prayed for their respective saham so, without dismissing the suit the courts ought to have given saham to the parties since in partition suit the plaintiffs as well as the defendants all should be treated as plaintiffs and in such a case this Court can interfere with the concurrent finding of facts of the courts below in revisional jurisdiction relying upon the decision reported in 1 MLR (AD) 282. He prayed for making the Rule absolute.

14. On the contrary Mr. Abdul Kuddus Miah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 27 argued that both the courts after consideration of the evidence on record rightly passed the impugned judgment which cannot be interfered with in revisional jurisdiction. He argued that the plaintiff claimed that he has entitlement of the suit land on the basis of the gift deed dated 11-7-1940 and subsequent deed (exhibit-2) dated 30-10-1980 which was executed by the father of the plaintiff Modhu @ Kala Miah in favour of his four sons including the plaintiff and, as such, the court opined that the said gift deed dated 11-7-1914 has not been acted upon and also opined that the deed executed by the father of the plaintiff dated 30-10-1980 is nothing but a collusive deed for making out the case and the same has not been considered by the court. He argued that in the instant case since the plaintiff did not claim that he has entitlement of the land as a co-sharer by inheritance the court rightly dismissed the suit. The learned Advocate further argued that the plaintiff trying to establish that defendant No. 20 Abdur Rahman is not the son of Mozu Gazi but both the courts after consideration of the evidence on record opined that Abdur Rahman is one of the son of Mozu Gazi, in such circumstances of the case the courts below also disbelieved the case of the plaintiff and rightly dismissed the suit. The learned Advocate further argued that both the court since opined that the plaintiff failed to prove his case by adducing sufficient evidence which is finding of facts and the finding of facts of the courts below cannot be interfered with in revisional jurisdiction. He prayed for discharging the Rule.

15. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment of the courts below, the papers and documents as available on the records. This is a suit for partition. The plaintiff claimed that the original owner Mozu Gazi, the grandfather of the plaintiff, gifted his entire share to his two sons and one daughter namely Asmat Ali, Modhu Miah @ Kala Miah and Khatoon Bibi through gift deed dated 11-7-1914. The plaintiff also claimed that Manikjan the wife of Mozu Gazi also inherited some portion of the land from Mozu Gazi. The further case is that Abdur Rahman is not the son of Mozu Gazi since before she was married to Mozu Gazi, Manikjan the mother of Abdur Rahman was earlier married with another Mazu Bhuiyan and Abdur Rahaman is the son of said Mazu Bhuiyan. The plaintiff's further case is that his father Madhu Miah @ Kala Miah obtained 2.36 acres of land on the basis of gift deed dated 11-7-1914 and Khatoon Bibi obtained 2.37 acres of land by the said gift deed dated 11-7-1914 executed by Mazu Gazi and after her death her full brother Modhu Miah @ Kala Miah obtained ¼ portion of the said land and her husband Sona Miah obtained rest ¾ portion of land. The plaintiff claimed that his father also purchased 0.02 and 0.03 acres of land through separate deeds and obtained 1.80 acres of land from sister Khatoon Bibi and 0.02 acres as a heir from the rest portion of the land of Mozu Gazi and also obtained 1/3 portion i.e. 0.16 acres from the land which was surrendered by Sona Mia through deed dated 16-1-1919. Thus they claimed that Madhu Miah obtained total 4.37 acres of land. Thereafter he gifted the said portion of the land to his four sons through gift deed dated 30-10-1980, by this way the plaintiff is entitled to get 1.09 acres of land. The defendant Nos. 2, 5 and 12 the heirs of Asmat Ali ultimately supported the case of the plaintiff and they claimed their separate saham for 3.26 7/9 acres of land. The defendant No. 3 also supported the case of the plaintiff and she prayed for her separate saham.

16. The defendant No. 20 Rahman Ali contested the case. He claimed that he is the son of Mozu Gazi through her mother Manikjan. Mozu Gazi died leaving behind wife Manikjan, three sons Asmat Ali, Modhu @ Kala Miah and Rahman Ali and one daughter Khatoon Bibi. He denied the gift deed dated 11-7-1914 executed by Mazu Gazi in favour of two sons Asmat Ali and Modhu @ Kala Miah and one daughter Khatoon Bibi. His further case is that his mother Manikjan inherited two anna shares of Mozu Gazi and rest portion was inherited by three brothers Asmat Ali, Modhu @ Kala Miah and Rahman Ali and one daughter Khatoon Bibi. This defendant also admitted that Khatoon Bibi is the full sister of Modhu @ Kala Miah. This defendant also claimed that the alleged gift deed dated 11-7-1914 executed by Mazu Gazi is a fabricated document since after the aforesaid transfer of the land the CS record was prepared in the name of Mozu Gazi and accordingly SA record was prepared in the name of Asmat Ali, Modhu @ Kala Miah and Rahman Ali, the three sons of Mozu Gazi.

17. The trial court after consideration of the evidence on record opined that the plaintiff failed to prove his case by adducing sufficient evidence. The trial court further opined that the gift deed dated 30-10-1980 executed by the father of the plaintiff has no basis since the plaintiff made him defendant and no corroboration about the said case even which was not proved by the deed writer or by the attesting witnesses and thus opined that by the said deed the plaintiff cannot claim his title. The trial court also opined that the defendant as well as some PWs admitted the possession of the defendant No. 20 and, as such his title has been established. The trial court also considering the case of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 20 opined that Rahman Ali is one of the son of Mozu Gazi. The trial court further opined that the deed dated 11-7-1914 is not proved as genuine by any evidence since the certified copy of the original deed is a secondary evidence which should be proved by adducing sufficient evidence. Though the trial court opined that the plaintiff can get saham for some portion of land as a co-sharer of the case jote but opined that since the case is bad for defect of parties and the plaintiff failed to prove his possession by adducing sufficient evidence has taken a view that the suit is not maintainable and accordingly dismissed the suit.

18. The appellate court after consideration of the evidence on record opined that the deed executed by Mozu Gazi dated 11-7-1914 has not been acted upon since the CS record was prepared in the name of Mozu Gazi even SA record was also prepared in the name of three brother i.e. Asmat Ali, Modhu @ Kala Miah and Rahman Ali. The appellate court stated that the certified copy of the said deed as exhibit 4 but on perusal of the record I find no certified copy of the said deed in the record. It appears that at the appellate stage the plaintiff filed the original gift deed dated 11-7-1914 executed by Mozu Gazi in favour of Asmat Ali, Modhu @ Kala Miah and Khatoon Bibi through firishti form and also filed an application for considering the same as additional evidence but the appellate court without any order and without exhibiting the same passed the impugned judgment. It is found that the plaintiff filed the said original deed through firishti form in the appellate Court and which is available in the record but the appellate court though did not disbelieve the said deed opined that which was not acted upon since CS record was prepared after the execution of the deed in the name of Mozu Gazi and also the SA record was prepared in the name of three brothers as such the appellate court opined that the said deed has not been acted upon. It also appears that both the court concurrently found that Rahman Ali the defendant No. 20 is one of the son of Mozu Gazi and on perusal of the record it is found that the defendant No. 20 admitted that Khatoon Bibi was the full sister of plaintiff, and the plaintiffs and others defendants claimed that two sons Asmat Ali and Modhu @ Kala Miah and one daughter Khatoon Bibi from the womb of Lalzan Bibi, 2nd wife of Mozu Gazi. So, admittedly the defendant No. 20 is not the full brother of the Madhu Gazi.

19. It appears that both the courts after consideration of the evidence on record opined that the suit is bad for defect of parties. I have gone through the record; it is found that when the defendant No. 20 raised the question of defect of parties the plaintiff filed an application for interrogatory on 24-5-1987 and finally on 16-11-1987 the court decided on making an opinion that the defendants derived from raising the question of defect of parties so it appears that both the courts without considering the earlier order erroneously took view that the case is bad for defect of parties which is clear misappropriation of facts of the case and the same cannot be sustained. Since the revisional court has every right to interfere with the findings of the courts below if it finds misreading or misappropriation of fact. Our Apex Court in the case of Gazi RafIqul Islam @, Manzu vs Mosharaf Hossain reported in 17 BLT (AD) 25 = Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest, volume-X11-37 held that the plea of defect of parties is to be raised at the earliest stage of the suit, otherwise such plea should be deem to have been waived. Similar view has been taken in the case of Sufia Khatun-vs Amir Hossain Mondal and others reported in 17 BLT (AD) 164 = Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest, volume XII-38. And since the court by its order dated 16-11-1987 waived the question of defect of the parties but both the court did not consider the said vital facts of the case which is clear non consideration of the material facts of the case by the courts below. We disapproved such non consideration of the material facts of the case of the Court below.

20. 1 have also perused the entire matter of the case, it is found that the plaintiff is the co-sharer of the case jote and it is admitted that he is one of the grand son of original owner Mozu Gazi and no case that he is deprived to get his saham. If this Court has taken a view that the said deed dated 11-7-1940 has not been acted upon even in such a case the plaintiff also not ousted on that grounds since he is one of the co-sharer of the suit land and in such a case the entire portion of the case land devolved upon the heirs of Mozu Gazi and they are entitled to get their respective saham.

21. It has already been decided that Asmat Ali, Modhu @ Kala Miah are the full brothers of Khatoon Bibi so after her death her portion should be devolved upon her full brothers and husband Sona Miah. It also appears that Sona Miah transferred his portion to Ashmat Ali, Modhu (@), Kala Miah and Manikjan Bibi. In such a case, the said portion should be divided in equal shares among those three persons. It also appears that the plaintiffs claimed that his predecessor purchased 0.02, and 0.03 acres of land through register deed and also claimed that 1.80 acres of land from Khatoon Bibi as heir. The same also should be considered by taking evidence.

<u>22. This is a partition suit, so the suit cannot be dismissed on the ground that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession over the suit land. It is settled principle that the possession of a co-sharer in a joint land even more than 12 years shall not constitute adverse possession against other co-sharers. This principle is supported by the case of Probir Kumar Rakshit vs Abdus Sabur reported in 6 ADC 74 = Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest, volume XII-34. And in the case of Md Abdul Noor Cunnu Miah @ Md Laisuzzaman reported in 27 BLD (AD) 239 their lordships held that a co-sharer in possession of land less than his share is always entitled to pray for partition by bringing a suit in a court of competent jurisdiction and if his claim is proved he is entitled to get land partitioned through court. A co-sharer in possession of excess land than his share is bound to part with the same. Considering the aforesaid facts and discussions above, it is clear that both the courts without considering the said vital facts of the case erroneously passed the impugned judgment.</u>

23. It is also found that the trial court opined that the deed dated 30-10-1980 executed by Modhu @ Kala Miah by which the plaintiff is not entitled to get saham since Modhu @ Kala Miah was alive at the time of filing the suit and he was made party. But it is not a correct view since his father executed the said deed in favour of his four sons and he was made a party but did not contest the suit or raised any objection by filing any written statement, even none of the brothers also made any objection about the same. In such a case the findings of the trial court is an erroneous one. But it appears that the defendant No. 20 claimed that by the said deed Modhu @ Kala Miah transferred more than that of his share and the said matter should be considered by the courts below on taking evidence and considering all the materials documents as adduced by the parties.

<u>24. It is found that the plaintiff as well as defendants claimed their respective saham so, since it is a partition suit the court should dispose of the same giving the parties respective saham as per evidence on record but cannot dismiss the suit avoiding their responsibility. And since this is a long pending case and the appellate court being the final court of facts should dispose of the case on merit considering the evidence on record as available on the record and also giving the parties opportunity to give scope to prove their respective cases and the discussions as made above. The appellate court is empowered to consider the case afresh, can frame issue or issues and can take the same for consideration and also can take additional evidence or evidences if required as provided under section 107 and Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, so it is better to send back the case on remand to the appellate court to dispose of the appeal on merit afresh.</u>

25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 10-4-1995 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Comilla in Title Appeal No. 34 of 1993 is hereby set-aside. The Title Appeal No. 34 of 1993 is hereby sent back on remand to the appellate court to dispose of the appeal afresh giving the parties opportunity to prove their respective cases and considering the observations as made above.

26. Since, this is a long pending case the appellate court is directed to dispose of the appeal as early as possible preferably within 6 (six) months from the date of receipt of the judgment.

Send down the Lower Court's records at once.

End.

Kamal-ul-Alam with Shahnaj Akther Advocates—For the Petitioner. 

Md Al-Amin Sarker DAG with KM Masud Rumy and Md Nasim Islam AAGs—For the Respondents.
